## **1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

## **1.1 Ripretinib overview and positioning in ≥fourth-line advanced GIST** 

Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) is a rare, life-threatening sarcoma that affects the gastrointestinal tract; it commonly develops in the stomach and small intestine (60-70%) but can occur anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract.[1-3] The median age at presentation is 60-65 years, with an incidence of 1.5 out of every 100,000 people.[4] GIST is a highly complex disease, with the potential for many mutations to drive treatment-resistance and disease progression. Central drivers of tumour development are mutations in the KIT proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase (KIT) and/or platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRA). 

There is no cure for advanced GIST and there remains a significant unmet need for effective treatment options. In the UK, imatinib is the standard first-line (1L) treatment for patients with advanced disease.[4,5] Upon progression or intolerance to imatinib, the standard second-line (2L) treatment is sunitinib.[4,6] For patients whose disease progresses on or fails to respond to imatinib and sunitinib, regorafenib is the standard third-line (3L) treatment option.[4,7] Patients often develop secondary drug-resistance mutations and, as a result, generally progress rapidly through the available treatment options, receiving only moderate clinical benefit.[8-13] The median progression free survival (PFS) for patients receiving 3L regorafenib is 4.8 months, and the objective response rate (ORR) is 4.5%.[8,9,14] 

UK clinical practice guidelines from the British Sarcoma Group (BSG) recommend ripretinib as the preferred option for fourth-line treatment in patients with inoperable, progressive, or metastatic GIST after treatment with imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib. However, ripretinib is not broadly available to patients in the UK.[4] Current fourth-line treatment, and the most appropriate comparator for ripretinib, is best supportive care (BSC), which includes medication for symptomatic management, for example analgesics, laxatives, and antiemetics.[15,16] Patients having BSC have poor 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 15 of 181 



<!-- page 18 -->

survival and health-related quality of life (HRQoL).[17-19] Clinician and patient expert testimony both state that there is a high unmet need for an effective fourth-line treatment that broadly targets KIT and PDGFRA mutation-positive and wild-type GIST and has the potential to extend life and improve patient HRQoL.[20] 

Ripretinib is a once-daily oral treatment and is the only switch-control tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) specifically designed to broadly inhibit wild type and mutated KIT and PDGFRA kinases, with a unique dual mechanism of action.[21,22] 

In a randomised, placebo-controlled trial (INVICTUS) in patients with advanced GIST previously treated with three or more TKIs, ripretinib significantly improved median PFS compared with placebo (6.3 months vs 1.0 month), thereby reducing the risk of disease progression or death by 85% (HR 0.15; 95% confidence interval [95% CI] 0.09 to 0.25; p<0.0001).[15] 

Ripretinib achieved a clinically meaningful 64% reduction in the risk of death (HR 0.36; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.62), leading to an 8.5-month improvement in median overall survival (OS) vs placebo in the primary analysis.[15] By the January 2021 data cut-off, this had increased to a 11.9-month improvement in median OS over placebo, 18.2 months vs 6.3 months respectively (HR 0.41).[23] As such, ripretinib nearly tripled OS for these patients, after an initial median follow up of 6.3 months and an additional 19 months of follow-up after the initial analysis.[23] Importantly, ripretinib showed durable, clinically meaningful disease control.[23] Despite advanced disease, patients receiving ripretinib maintained HRQoL and function over approximately 8 months, while the same measures declined sharply for patients receiving placebo after just 1 month.[16] Ripretinib was well-tolerated and demonstrated an acceptable safety profile.[15,23]

## **1.4 Health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway** 

## **1.4.1 Disease overview** 

GIST is a rare, life-threatening and heterogeneous subset of soft tissue sarcoma (STS), and the most common mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Although occurring anywhere in the GI tract, GIST most frequently develops in the stomach (60% to 70% of cases) or small intestine (25% to 35% of cases).[1-3,25] The colon and rectum are involved in approximately 4% to 5% of cases.[1-3,25] 

GIST is a highly complex disease, developing in specialised interstitial cells of Cajal within the GI tract and primarily driven by mutations in the KIT transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase and the related receptor tyrosine kinase, platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRA).[26,27] Approximately 80% of GIST has primary mutations in KIT, and 5% to 10% have a mutation in homologous PDGFRA.[1,28,29] 

Most primary KIT mutations involve a single mutation at diagnosis.[1] However secondary mutations can develop over time in response to treatment with targeted TKI therapies, leading to treatment resistance.[28,30] These acquired secondary resistance mutations are seen in up to two thirds of GIST cases that progress after TKI treatment. 

As a result, the disease is heterogenetic and the patient may have multiple mutations.[28,31,32] There is, therefore, an unmet need for a treatment that is able to target both primary and secondary KIT and PDGFRA resistance mutations. 

## _Clinical presentation and burden of disease_ 

The median age at GIST presentation is 60-65 years, with an incidence of 1.5 out of every 100,000 people.[4] There are approximately 900-1,000 new cases of GIST per year in the UK; of these, approximately 173 will progress to fourth-line treatment for advanced GIST.[4,8,33-36] 

The clinical presentation of GIST can vary based on the tumour size and site.[3,37] Symptoms of advanced disease include gastrointestinal bleeding and anaemia, whilst larger tumours may present with abdominal pain/discomfort, obstruction and a Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 21 of 181 



<!-- page 24 -->

palpable mass. Some patients may have non-specific systemic symptoms such as extreme tiredness, weight loss, night sweats and fever.[4] 

Patients with fourth-line advanced GIST have particularly poor survival outcomes. Median overall survival (OS) for patients with advanced GIST receiving BSC after 3 prior lines of therapy with TKIs can be as short as 1.8 months, although this is a worst-case scenario.[15] When clinicians were consulted on the anticipated survival of patients with ≥4L advanced GIST if only treated with BSC, they anticipated OS to be 2 to 3 months.[38] 

The humanistic impact of advanced GIST is substantial. Patient HRQoL deteriorates severely as the disease progresses, with a significant reduction in cognitive and social functioning.[16] Over half of patients with advanced GIST experience high levels of fear of disease progression, often related to the lack of later-line therapeutic options, leading to significant psychological distress.[39] The psychological burden often leads to patients with GIST having difficulties in making and maintaining relationships, as well as experiencing body image concerns, low mood and depressive symptoms.[40] Furthermore, the toxicity of currently available later-line therapies makes them difficult to tolerate. For example, results from the phase 3 randomised controlled trial (RCT) GRID showed that regorafenib is not associated with any statistically significant benefit in HRQoL. This was attributed to the severe adverse events associated with regorafenib dosing.[41] Many patients therefore require dose adjustment or treatment interruption, which can contribute to rapid progression through the available therapeutic options.[42,43] This is then accentuated by an increased financial burden and the result this has on a patient’s well-being.[44] 

In addition to the impact on patients, caring for someone with GIST also imposes a significant emotional, financial, and social burden. Carers often take on numerous responsibilities, such as providing emotional support, accompanying patients when leaving their home and on medical and non-medical appointments, and assisting with communication and travel. According to the National Sarcoma Survey 2020, more than half of GIST carers had to stop working or studying, either temporarily or permanently.[45]

## **1.4.2 Clinical management of advanced GIST and place of ripretinib in the treatment pathway** 

There is no cure for advanced GIST. Approximately half of patients present with metastatic or unresectable GIST at diagnosis and around 40% to 90% of patients who have had surgery develop subsequent postoperative recurrence or metastasis.[35,36] Targeted therapy with TKIs is the standard of care for metastatic or unresectable GIST. Conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy are not effective in this advanced patient population.[39,46,47] 

In patients with metastatic or unresectable disease, imatinib is the 1L standard treatment in the UK.[4,5] Disease progression after imatinib treatment occurs mostly due to primary resistance or secondary KIT mutation. If progression or imatinib intolerance is confirmed, the standard 2L treatment is sunitinib. Most patients will again relapse within 6 months to 1 year due to additional or alternative secondary mutations in KIT, or due to multiple different KIT mutations occurring in different areas of the tumour.[11] In addition, some patients with imatinib-resistant disease have primary resistance to sunitinib due to the specific secondary mutation(s) that arise during imatinib treatment.[8] Regorafenib is regarded as standard therapy for the 3L treatment of patients whose disease has progressed on or failed to respond to imatinib and sunitinib.[7] 

Patients with advanced GIST progress quickly through available therapies. For patients who progress on 1L treatment with imatinib, subsequent lines of TKI therapy have moderate clinical benefit due to the development of secondary drug-resistance mutations.[8] Response rates are generally lower in later lines of treatment and median PFS becomes shorter.[8,9,14] Median PFS for patients receiving 3L regorafenib is 4.8 months, and the ORR is 4.5%.[8,9,14] This is primarily as the three available TKIs only block a subset of clinically relevant secondary resistance mutations.[9,10,12] Therefore, given the heterogeneous nature of KIT and PDGFRA mutations in advanced GIST, it is desirable to use a treatment that inhibits as many mutations as possible.[48] 

There is no established standard of care in the UK for patients who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors, including imatinib. Importantly, 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 23 of 181 



<!-- page 26 -->

clinicians and patient experts have highlighted the substantial unmet need for a treatment that is effective in patients with TKI resistance.[20] Current treatment, and the most appropriate comparator for ripretinib, is BSC which involves symptomatic management using analgesics, laxatives, and antiemetics.[17-19] 

In clinical practice, regorafenib may continue to be used after disease progression because of the lack of alternative treatment options.[4,7,18,38,49] However, clinical experts noted that post-progression regorafenib is a last resort after seeking relevant clinical trials or other therapies via compassionate use.[18,20] This is because it only has benefits for a limited time and is associated with toxicities that often outweigh any potential clinical benefits after progression.[18] 

Ripretinib is currently recommended as a later line treatment option for patients with advanced/metastatic GIST in British (BSG) and European (ESMO) clinical practice guidance.[4,49] Prior to this, the recommended approach for patients with advanced/metastatic GIST who had progressed through 3 previous lines of therapy was BSC and enrolment onto clinical trials.[49,50] 

There remains a substantial unmet medical need for a treatment which provides broad inhibition of KIT and PDGFRA kinase activity, including wild-type and secondary drug-resistance mutations, to extend life and improve patient HRQoL.[48,51] It is therefore proposed that the place of ripretinib would be in the fourth-line of treatment, alongside BSC, as shown in Figure 1.

## **2 Clinical effectiveness** 

## **2.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

Clinical and HRQoL systematic literature reviews (SLR) were originally conducted from January 2000 to July 2020 to identify the clinical, HRQoL and economic evidence relevant to ripretinib, respectively. Specifically, the clinical SLR was conducted in the target population of patients with advanced (unresectable or metastatic) GIST to assess the relative efficacy and safety of ripretinib and comparators in fourth-line or later. The SLRs were subsequently updated five times including July 2021 (Ovid search conducted on June 24, 2021), March 2022 (Ovid search conducted on March 21, 2022), May 2023 (Ovid search conducted on May 17, 2023), April 2024 (Ovid search conducted on April 8, 2024) and March 2025 (Ovid search conducted on March 10, 2025). 

For the clinical SLR, a total of 1,574 records were identified using the Ovid platform on March 10, 2025. Of these, 114 records were selected for full-text review, after screening by title/abstract. Overall, following a full-text review and the addition of studies from congress, bibliographic search, and clinicaltrials.gov, a total of 39 records from 2 original studies were selected for data extraction in the clinical SLR. 

Please see Appendix B and F for details on the clinical and HRQoL SLR methodology and process used to select the clinical and HRQoL evidence for ripretinib in the fourth and later-line setting (≥4L) for the treatment of advanced GIST, including Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagrams. 

## **2.2 List of relevant clinical effectiveness evidence** 

The clinical SLR identified 39 reports, 15 of which were relevant to this submission (Table 3). Of these publications, 10 were regarding the original pivotal phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial (INVICTUS), which provided direct head-to-head evidence on the clinical benefits of ripretinib vs placebo in patients with advanced unresectable or metastatic GIST who had progressed following imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib. The remaining 24 were deemed not relevant as the

Results of a phase 2 single-arm, open-label study (NCT04282980) of ripretinib 150 mg once daily in adult patients with advanced GIST who had progressed on three or more prior kinase inhibitors (n=39) are reported in two publications. Efficacy and safety results were broadly consistent with the INVICTUS trial and are not discussed further in this submission.[52,53] 

The clinical SLR also identified two publications, relating to the phase 1, non-randomised study (NCT02571036) of ripretinib that included a dose escalation and expansion phase of patients with GIST in the 2L, 3L, and ≥4L setting who were treated with ripretinib at the 150 mg QD dose.[54,55] Efficacy and safety results were broadly consistent with the INVICTUS trial and are not discussed further in this submission. 

The HRQoL SLR identified four further relevant publications reporting HRQoL analyses of INVICTUS, in addition to Blay et al., 2020,[15] Becker et al., 2021,[56] Reichardt et al., 2021,[57] and Bauer et al., 2023.[58] These include a key publication by Schoffski et al., 2022[16] and three posters: two were presented at the 2020 ASCO Annual Meeting by Heinrich et al., 2020 and George et al., 2020 and one was presented at ISPOR 2022 by Jones et al., 2022.[59-61]

In addition to published data, three advisory boards with oncologists based in the UK were conducted in August 2022, July 2024 and April 2025. All participants had extensive experience in the treatment of advanced GIST and were familiar with the INVICTUS trial and, in the case of the July 2024 and April 2025 meetings, the Royal Marsden expanded access program as well. Insights were used to provide additional evidence relevant to UK clinical practice and to validate the assumptions made in the cost-effectiveness model, and are used throughout the document.[18,38,70] 

## **2.3 Summary of methodology of the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence** 

## **2.3.1 INVICTUS methodology** 

## _**Trial design**_ 

INVICTUS was an international, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 129 patients who had received 3 or more prior anticancer therapies for advanced GIST. It compared the efficacy of ripretinib plus BSC (hereafter referred to as the ‘ripretinib’ group) and placebo plus BSC (hereafter referred to as the ‘placebo’ group) in patients who had received prior treatment with at least imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib.[15] The study was conducted at 29 specialised hospitals across 12 countries in North America, Europe, and Asia, including two in the UK.[15] 

Patients were randomised 2:1 to receive ripretinib 150 mg once daily (QD) or placebo orally in 28-day cycles until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Randomisation was stratified by:[15] 

- Patients who had received 3 vs 4 or more prior anticancer treatments 

- Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 vs 1 or 2 

As a part of BSC, permitted concomitant medication included medications for symptomatic relief such as analgesics, laxatives, and antiemetics (Table 5). Medications that increased gastric pH, with the exception of proton pump inhibitors,

Patients, investigators, and research staff were unblinded to the study drug assignment upon disease progression, as determined by blinded, independent, central review (BICR). Upon disease progression by mRECIST, based on independent radiologic review (IRR), patients randomised to ripretinib 150 mg QD were given the option to continue at an increased dose (150 mg twice a day [BID]), to continue their current dose at 150 mg QD, or to discontinue treatment with ripretinib.[15] Patients randomised to placebo were able to crossover to ripretinib 150 mg QD upon disease progression or discontinue the study, also by mRECIST based on IRR. Patients who crossed over to ripretinib and then experienced a second disease progression were given the option to continue at an increased dose (150 mg BID), to continue their current dose at 150 mg QD, or to discontinue treatment with ripretinib (Figure 2).[15] The option to dose escalate was included to give patients another therapeutic option after disease progression given the limited options at this point in the treatment pathway.

## _**Primary and secondary endpoints**_ 

The primary efficacy endpoint in the study was PFS, defined as the date from randomisation to the date of progressive disease (PD) or death due to any cause, as assessed by radiologic BICR using the mRECIST version 1.1 criteria.[15] Additionally, during some analysis PFS was subdivided into PFS1, defined as the time from randomisation until PD, and PFS2, defined as the time from the first dose of ripretinib 150 mg BID to PD or death. 

The key secondary efficacy endpoint was ORR, defined as a confirmed complete response (CR) or partial response (PR), as assessed by BICR and during the initial assigned study treatment.[15] Other secondary endpoints were OS, time to progression (TTP), time to best response, and duration of response (DOR). HRQoL was assessed

using the EuroQol 5 dimensions 5 levels (EQ-5D-5L), EuroQol visual analogue scale (EQ-VAS), and European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire for Cancer 30-item (EORTC QLQ-C30) - physical and role functioning domains only.[15] These were all pre-specified analyses in the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP). 

Analysis of time to treatment discontinuation (TTD) was undertaken post-hoc to provide data on continued treatment with ripretinib post-progression required for the cost-effectiveness model.[72] 

Safety assessments included clinical laboratory tests, ECOG performance status, vital signs, weight, 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) measurements, left ventricular ejection fraction, physical examinations, and dose reductions, interruptions, or treatment discontinuations.[15]

## **2.3.3 Patient baseline characteristics: INVICTUS** 

Patient characteristics were generally well-balanced across the two treatment groups. There was a similar proportion of males (55% vs 59%), patients in the ECOG performance status strata of 1 or 2 (56% vs 61%) and patients with three prior lines of therapy (64% vs 61%) between the ripretinib and placebo groups, respectively. In both groups, over half of patients were outside the US (53% vs 55%) and the median age was 59 and 65 years, respectively (Table 8).[15] 

The ripretinib group had a lower proportion of patients aged ≥75 years than the placebo group (9% vs 23%) and a slightly higher frequency of primary gastric tumours (47% vs 41%).[15] A lower frequency of KIT exon 11 mutations was seen in the ripretinib group (55% vs 64%) and PDGFRA mutations were present in 4% in the ripretinib group and none in the placebo group.[15] 

Subsequent subgroup analyses have shown that these slight imbalances in patient baseline and disease characteristics across the arms of INVICTUS are unlikely to significantly impact the overall treatment effect of ripretinib.[15]

## **2.3.4 Royal Marsden expanded access study methodology** 

The Royal Marsden Hospital, London, UK independently published observational data from the ripretinib expanded access program; Deciphera Pharmaceuticals had no involvement in collecting, analysing or publishing of this data.[69] 

## _**Study design**_ 

The objective of this retrospective observational study was to describe the outcomes and safety of treatment with ripretinib in a cohort of patients treated in a real-world setting, as part of the expanded access program for ripretinib in the UK prior to EMA/MHRA approval. The use of ripretinib in the UK and Europe prior EMA/MHRA approval was through a free-of-charge expanded access program provided by Deciphera Pharmaceuticals on an ‘as needed’ basis, driven by clinicians’ unsolicited requests following Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval up until EMA/MHRA approval. Patients who already had access through the expanded access program remained on treatment until clinical benefit was no longer observed or until unacceptable toxicity was seen.[69] 

A retrospective review of all patients with advanced (unresectable or metastatic) GIST who commenced ripretinib at The Royal Marsden Hospital, London, UK, between January 2020 and October 2021 was performed. Patients without a confirmed histological diagnosis of GIST and patients who did not start ripretinib at the Royal Marsden (because they were too unwell or they started treatment at a different institution) were excluded.[69] 

All patients treated had imaging available for retrospective assessment of radiologic response according to mRECIST 1.1 and had at least one measurable lesion.

## _**Study conduct**_ 

Baseline patient characteristics that were collected included but were not limited to: age in years at first ripretinib dose; primary mutation status (KIT and PDGFRA); ECOG performance status (PS); and number and type of previous lines of treatment. 

During treatment with ripretinib, patients received a ripretinib starting dose of 150 mg QD but were given the opportunity to dose escalate to 150 mg ripretinib BID at the time of disease progression determined by their treating physician. Due to the possibility for intrapatient dose escalation (IPDE), patients were retrospectively assessed as two groups: those receiving 150 mg ripretinib QD; and those with dose escalation upon tumour progression to 150 mg ripretinib BID.[69] 

During treatment with ripretinib, information was collected on radiological response, toxicity (according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events Version 5.0 [CTCAE v5]), dose reduction, IPDE to 150 mg BID dosing, treatment duration and cause of treatment interruption. When documenting the reason for treatment discontinuation, clinical PD was defined as worsening patient-reported symptoms in the presence of radiological signs of PD that did not reach the level required for confirming mRECIST PD. The radiological signs required to reach mRECIST PD include a progressively growing tumour nodule withing a pre-existing tumour mass where the lesion was at least 2 cm in size or the lesion had to be expanding on at least 2 sequential imaging studies.[69,71] 

Given the observational nature, the analysis had no predefined sample size and all patients meeting the inclusion criteria were analysed.[69] 

## _**Outcomes**_ 

Retrospective mRECIST measurements were used to assess PFS, best ORR and time to best response. 

Due to the possibility of IPDE, specific PFS endpoints were defined: 

- PFS QD was defined as the time from the date of the first 150 mg ripretinib QD dose to the time of mRECIST progression while on this dose or death, 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 41 of 181 



<!-- page 44 -->

whichever occurred first.[69] This endpoint is equivalent to PFS (the primary endpoint) in INVICTUS. 

- PFS BID was defined in the subgroup of patients undergoing IPDE, as the time from date of the first 150 mg ripretinib BID dose to the time of mRECIST progression while on this dose or death, whichever occurred first.[69] This endpoint is equivalent to PFS2 in INVICTUS. 

- PFS ITT was defined as the time from the first 150 mg ripretinib QD dose to: the time of mRECIST progression at this dose for patients who did not undergo IPDE; the time of mRECIST progression at the 150 mg BID dose for patients who did undergo IPDE; or time of death, whichever occurred first.[69] This endpoint was defined to capture the overall duration of ripretinib treatment regardless of dosage. There was no equivalent endpoint in INVICTUS. 

TTD endpoints were defined for the same groups as PFS endpoints. TTD was the time from the first day of ripretinib treatment (at a specified dose) to the last day of ripretinib treatment (at a specified dose) regardless of the cause of treatment discontinuation.[69] 

TBP assessed ripretinib treatment beyond disease progression and was defined as the time patients remained on ripretinib between the PFS event and the TTD event dates if the TTD event date was more than 28 days after the PFS event date.[69] 

OS was defined as the time from the date of the first 150 mg ripretinib QD dose to the time of death from any cause.[69]

## **2.3.5 Expert elicitation or expert opinion** 

Advisory boards with oncologists based in the UK were conducted in August 2022, July 2024 and April 2025.[18,38,70] The aim of the advisory boards was to elicit expert insights on: 

- the unmet need in advanced GIST in the UK; 

- the generalisability of INVICTUS to UK clinical practice, supported by observations from Royal Marsden; 

- the assumptions used in the health economic model, including the OS extrapolation and utility values; 

- the clinical management of advanced GIST in the UK. 

Medical oncologists specialising in the management of advanced GIST in the UK were identified either through their work in specialist sarcoma units/services, their contribution to GIST treatment guidelines and/or their participation as an investigator in GIST clinical trials. 

The advisory board held in 2022 included 4 specialists in GIST.[70] The 2024 advisory board included 7 specialists in GIST, 6 based in the UK and one based in Scotland. A health economist was also present at the advisory board to moderate selected discussions on the cost-effectiveness model.[18] The 2025 advisory board included 3 specialists in GIST all based in the UK.[38] All participants across the advisory boards had extensive experience in the treatment of advanced GIST and were familiar with INVICTUS and the Royal Marsden study. 

The materials for the three advisory boards included data from INVICTUS, the Royal Marsden expanded access cohort study (2024 and 2025 only) and analyses from the economic model to facilitate the discussion.

## **2.4 Statistical analysis and definition of study groups in the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence** 

## **2.4.1 INVICTUS** 

## _**Statistical analysis**_ 

Primary efficacy analyses were based on the ITT population, defined as all randomised patients (n=129).[15] The safety population was used for safety analyses and included all patients who received at least one dose of study drug (n=128).[15] 

A sample size of 120 patients (ripretinib, n=80; placebo, n=40) was calculated to provide both power for efficacy and size for the safety database with an assumed 15% patient dropout.[15] Analysis for PFS was stratified by the same factors used for randomisation (3 vs ≥4 prior lines of therapy and ECOG performance status 0 vs 1 or 2).[15] The p-value was from a 2-sided stratified log-rank test at 0.05 significance level in testing the hypothesis of no difference between ripretinib and placebo to provide over 90% power to detect a difference in PFS between ripretinib and placebo.[15] This power assumed a median PFS of 4.5 months for ripretinib and 1.0 month for placebo and approximately 80% power to detect a 20% difference in objective response, assuming an ORR of 22% and 2% for ripretinib and placebo, respectively.[15] 

A Cox regression model was used to obtain the point estimate of the hazard ratio with treatment and randomisation stratification factors as fixed factors and its 95% CI was obtained using Wald method. PFS time was summarised using the Kaplan-Meier methodology, with associated 2-sided 95% CIs. The proportional hazards assumption was examined by visual inspection of the log (-log) plot.[15 ] The same methodology was used for other time-to-event endpoints (PFS, OS, TTP, and time to best response). 

To control for family-wise type I error, a statistical hierarchical testing procedure was used. The hypothesis tests to evaluate the difference between the two treatment Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496]

groups were done at a 2-sided 0.05 level of significance sequentially in the following order:[15] 

1. The primary endpoint - PFS 

2. The key secondary endpoint - ORR 

3. OS 

4. HRQoL for change from baseline to Cycle 2 on Day 1 in the physical and role functioning domains of the EORTC QLQ-C30 (each at 0.025 level of significance) 

If a hypothesis test was found to be non-significant at the α=0.05 level, subsequent analyses in the hierarchy were reported as descriptive statistics[15] . Other endpoints (e.g. TTP, time to best response) were not included in the hierarchy due to insufficient power.[15] 

ORR was analysed by an unstratified two-sided Fisher’s exact test (using a 0.05 significance level) to evaluate treatment difference, and the 95% CI of the treatment difference was calculated with the Newcombe method. 

Descriptive statistics were used to summarise safety data and HRQoL variables.[15] HRQoL outcome assessments that were pre-specified in the SAP compared the change from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1 in scores on the EQ-5D-5L, EQ-VAS and the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaires.[16] A t-test was conducted to evaluate changes between groups in EQ-VAS scores from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1. Analysis of covariance models (ANCOVA) were used to assess change from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1 in role and physical function domain scores between groups on the EORTC QLQ-C30.[15] EQ-5D-5L was summarised overall by number and percentage for each level of each dimension. For the EQ-5D-5L index (utility) score, an ANCOVA model was used to assess change from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1 between groups.[16] 

The efficacy of ripretinib in patients dose escalating to ripretinib 150 BID in the open-label period following disease progression was an exploratory endpoint of INVICTUS, pre-specified in the SAP.[66,68] The “post intrapatient dose escalation” analysis was conducted on the safety population of patients who were treated with

## _**Handling of missing data**_ 

Patients who had first disease progression or died after two or more consecutive missed/non-evaluable assessments were censored for the primary PFS endpoint at the time of radiologic assessment immediately prior to the two or more consecutive missed/non-evaluable radiologic assessments.[19] For the secondary endpoint of ORR, patients with an unknown or missing response were categorised as non-responders and were included in the denominator when calculating the proportion.[15,19,71] 

## _**Subgroup analyses**_ 

Subgroup analyses of the primary endpoint of PFS were pre-specified.[15] In each subgroup, the hazard ratio (HR) was from Cox regression with treatment as a fixed factor, and the 95% CI of the HR was based on the Wald method. The following subgroup analyses were performed:[15] 

- Age (18 to 64 vs 65 to 74 vs 75 years or older) 

- Gender (Male vs Female) 

- Race (White vs non-White vs not reported)

## **2.4.2 Royal Marsden expanded access program** 

## **Statistical analysis** 

Patient characteristics at baseline were reported as median (IQR) or percentages of the total population for continuous and categorical variables, respectively. Median follow-up time was estimated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. Survival curves were constructed using the Kaplan–Meier method, and univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to assess the prognostic value of baseline covariates. Variables with univariate p value <0.2 were selected for the multivariate models. HR along with their 95% CI were reported. The validity of the Cox proportional hazard assumption was tested for all multivariable models. All analyses were performed using R software version 4.0.3.[69] 

## **Handling of missing data and patient censorship** 

Patients not experiencing the event were censored at the date of their last radiological evaluation for PFS endpoints, and to the date of their last clinic appointment for TTD and OS.[69] Two patients with symptomatic and progressive disease were discharged to the local palliative care team for BSC and were then lost to follow-up. To avoid informative censoring, these patients were considered to have experienced an OS event 2 weeks after their last clinic visit.[69]

## **2.5 Critical appraisal of the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence** 

## **2.5.1 INVICTUS** 

INVICTUS was a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled study, which is the gold-standard study design for interventional clinical trials that minimises the risk of confounding factors and allows direct comparison of the relative efficacy of interventions. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Council for Harmonisation Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice.[15] Randomisation was carried out appropriately, with patients, assessors, and investigators and site staff all blinded to treatment assignment during the double-blind period. There were no imbalances in drop-outs between groups and primary efficacy analyses were based on the ITT population, where the ITT population was defined as all patients who signed the informed consent and were randomised. Therefore, the trial design of INVICTUS was sufficiently robust to answer the decision problem, in assessing ripretinib versus BSC in adult patients with advanced GIST who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors, including imatinib. 

The handling of missing data is described in Section 2.4. and please refer to Appendix B for complete details on the quality assessment undertaken in the clinical SLR. 

## **2.5.2 Royal Marsden expanded access program** 

The Royal Marsden observational data is included in this submission as supporting evidence to demonstrate the generalisability of the results of INVICTUS to UK clinical practice. As a non-randomised and non-controlled retrospective study, there are inherent limitations to the statistical validity of the results. Retrospective studies can suffer from limited or missing data, less rigor in data collection (no pre-study analysis plan or protocol) and recall bias, all of which are distinct disadvantages. However, these limitations have been acknowledged by the sponsors and in the original analysis of the data. 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 49 of 181 



<!-- page 52 -->

The study reviewed patients from a single institution meaning the populations might not be completely representative of the advanced GIST patient population in the UK. Covariate and multivariate analyses were undertaken to identify any confounding factors and consider these in the interpretation of the results. In particular, the cohort included an unusually high prevalence of small bowel GIST; however, it is unlikely to have had a major impact on the results, as the site of tumour origin was not associated with PFS or OS in multivariate analyses.[69] 

## **2.6 Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant studies** 

## **2.6.1 Summary of clinical effectiveness** 

**Ripretinib significantly improved median PFS vs placebo (6.3 months vs 1.0 month), reducing the risk of disease progression or death by 85% (HR 0.15; 95% CI 0.09 to 0.25; p<0.0001) in the INVICTUS phase 3 double-blind RCT.[15]** 

- Ripretinib, when used to treat patients through an expanded access program at the Royal Marsden Hospital in London, resulted in a median PFS of 7.9 months (95% CI 5.6–19.3), similar to that achieved in INVICTUS.[69] 

**Median OS was 18.2 months in the ripretinib group vs 6.3 months in the placebo group (HR 0.41; 95% CI 0.26 to 0.65) after a median initial follow-up of 6.3 months and an additional 19 months of follow-up.[23]** 

- At primary analysis, ripretinib showed a clinically meaningful improvement over placebo in median OS (15.1 months [95% CI 12.3–15.1] vs 6.6 months [4.1– 11.6]; HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.62).[15] 

- The median OS observed in the Royal Marsden expanded access cohort (14.0 [95% CI 9.9–N/A] months) supports the clinical effectiveness of ripretinib in UK real-world practice.[69] 

**Ripretinib demonstrated durable, clinically meaningful disease control: 56 patients (66%; 95% CI: 55-76) receiving ripretinib experienced stable disease (SD) at 6 weeks and 40 patients (47%; 95% CI 36-58) at 12 weeks, vs 9 patients (20%; 95% CI 10-35) and 2 patients (5%; 95% CI 1-16) treated with placebo, respectively.[15]**

<!-- page 53 -->

- Additionally, fewer patients treated with ripretinib had progressive disease than patients who received placebo; 19% vs 64%, respectively, at primary analysis.[15] 

- Ripretinib demonstrated a clinically meaningful benefit to patients, with most patients achieving PR or SD (75%) compared to only 20% in the placebo arm, at primary analysis. 

- In patients treated under the Royal Marsden expanded access program, 85.7% had a best response to ripretinib QD of PR or SD, supporting the real-world effectiveness of ripretinib in UK clinical practice.[69] 

## **Ripretinib is well-tolerated and has an acceptable safety profile.** 

- The majority of treatment-related treatment emergent adverse events in patients receiving ripretinib were grade 1-2, and were alopecia (49%), myalgia (27%), nausea (25%), fatigue (24%), palmar–plantar erythrodysesthesia (21%) and diarrhoea (20%).[15] 

- Treatment-related serious adverse events were reported in eight (9%) of 85 patients who received ripretinib and three (7%) of 43 patients who received placebo.[15] 

- Rates of discontinuation (5% vs 2%) and dose reduction (6% vs 2%) due to adverse reactions were low across both the ripretinib and placebo arms, respectively.[15] 

- The safety profile of ripretinib in the Royal Marsden expanded access program was in line with INVICTUS.[69] 

## **Despite advanced disease, patients treated with ripretinib maintained quality-of-life (QoL) and function over approximately 8 months; the same measures declined sharply for patients on placebo after just 1 month.[16]** 

- Patients having ripretinib reported stable scores on all pre-specified patient- reported outcome (PRO) measures (EQ-5D-5L VAS and EORTC QLQ C30) up to Cycle 10. In contrast, PROs declined sharply in the placebo arm.[16] 

- Patients receiving ripretinib demonstrated clinically-relevant differences vs placebo in self-reported health (+3.7 vs -8.9; p=0.004), physical function (+1.6 vs -8.9; p=0.004) and role function (+3.5 vs -17.1; p=0.001).[16]

- Patients receiving ripretinib had a longer time until definitive deterioration (TUDD) in all assessed PRO measures compared with placebo.[56] 

- The median TUDD for overall health and QoL was not reached at 56 weeks for patients receiving ripretinib vs 7.7 weeks for patients receiving placebo.[56] 

- When considering individual INVICTUS patients, the median TUDD in the pre-specified PROs was greater than median PFS, suggesting that patients’ use of ripretinib is not limited by toxicity and QoL is maintained during post progression use of ripretinib.[56] 

## **2.6.2 INVICTUS** 

## _**Patient disposition**_ 

A total of 129 patients were enrolled in the trial, of whom 85 were randomised to the ripretinib arm, and 44 were randomised to the placebo arm (Figure 3). Patient withdrawals in the ripretinib and placebo group were equivalent (2.4% vs 2.3%) in the double-blind period (ITT population) and no patient was lost to follow-up. One patient randomised to the placebo group was not treated and not included in the safety population (n=128).[15] 

Of patients randomised to the placebo group, 29/44 crossed over to open-label ripretinib 150 mg QD after disease progression. At primary analysis, 21.1% (n=27) of patients remained on their blinded treatment in the double-blind period (26 in the ripretinib group and one in the placebo group.[15] Twenty percent of patients in the ripretinib group and 30.2% in the placebo group discontinued treatment in the double-blind period; the most common reasons were clinical progression (ripretinib, n=4; 4.7% vs placebo, n=3; 7.0%) and death (ripretinib, n=3; 3.5% vs placebo, n=4; 9.3%), respectively.[15]

The median relative dose intensity in the double-blind period was 100% (IQR 98.1 to 100.0) for the ripretinib group and 97% (86.5 to 100.0) for the placebo group.[15] Treatment compliance was high (≥80%) in both groups during the double-blind period (98.8% of patients in the ripretinib arm and 83.7% in the placebo arm).[15,51] The mean (standard deviation [SD]) treatment duration for the ripretinib arm (24.44 [13.941] weeks) was longer than the treatment duration for the placebo arm (8.25 [6.757] weeks).[19,51] 

At data cut-off of 10 August 2020, 65 patients in the ripretinib group had progressed, of whom 43 dose-escalated to ripretinib 150 mg BID; 22 patients either continued ripretinib 150 mg QD or discontinued (Figure 4).[66] Based on the ITT population, 66% of patients randomised to placebo switched to ripretinib after disease progression (n=29 of 44 patients; 1 patient did not receive the allocated treatment, 4 patients died and 10 patients did not switch to ripretinib).[15,66] Of the 29 patients who crossed over from placebo to ripretinib 150 mg QD, 34% escalated to ripretinib 150 mg BID following a second disease progression (n=10 of 29; 10 continued with ripretinib 150 mg QD and 9 discontinued treatment). 

As of January 2021, 63 of the 85 patients originally randomised to ripretinib had entered the open-label period following disease progression based on independent radiological review.[74] Of those, 19 continued to receive 150 mg QD and 44 underwent IPDE to 150 mg BID. A final total of 30 participants (68%) who received placebo in the double-blind period crossed-over to receive ripretinib 150 mg QD in the open-label period; 16 subsequently dose escalated to 150 mg BID following progression with QD dosing.[74] 

Clinicians in a UK advisory board estimated that approximately 80% of patients would be expected to continue ripretinib post-progression in UK clinical practice.[38] This aligns with the proportion of patients continuing ripretinib post-progression in INVICTUS. Clinicians also estimated that approximately 50% of those on post-progression ripretinib (i.e., 40% of the total population) would dose escalate if such dosing was routinely commissioned.[38] This is lower than that seen in INVICTUS, likely due to patients in routine clinical practice being less fit than those recruited to clinical trials.

## _**OS – secondary endpoint**_ 

OS analyses were conducted for the full on-treatment period, including the double-blind and open-label periods. Patients achieved a clinically meaningful survival benefit when treated with ripretinib vs placebo. As of data cut-off on 31 May 2019, 31% of patients in the ripretinib group (69% censored), and 59% in the placebo group (41% censored) had died (Table 14).[15] Median OS was 15.1 months (95% CI 12.3 to 15.1) for the ripretinib group and 6.6 months (4.1 to 11.6) for the placebo group.[15] Ripretinib reduced the risk of death by 64% vs placebo (HR 0.36; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.62).[15] The estimated 12-month OS rate was 65.4% (95% CI 51.6% to 76.1%) for the ripretinib group and 25.9% (95% CI 7.2% to 49.9%) for the placebo group.[15] 

The OS endpoint was not evaluated for statistical significance as a result of the hierarchical testing procedure and the ORR not reaching statistical significance.[15] 

From analysis of more mature OS data (data cut-off 15 January 2021), estimated median OS was 18.2 months for the ripretinib group (95% CI 13.1 to 30.7 months) (Figure 8). Median OS remained the same for the placebo group (6.3 months; 95% CI 4.1 to 10.0 months; HR 0.41; 95% CI 0.26 to 0.65). At analysis, 54% (n=46/85) of patients in the ripretinib group and 82% (n=36/44) of patients in the placebo group had died.[23] This improvement in median OS seen in longer-term analyses supports the ability of ripretinib to confer a clinically meaningful survival benefit; the continued low

## _**OS post hoc analyses: OS after IPDE to ripretinib 150 mg BID**_ 

A number of post hoc analyses were considered and UK clinician advisory boards were undertaken to quantify the impact of dose escalation on OS in INVICTUS. 

## **Open-label BID vs QD OS analysis** 

As of data cut-off of 10 August 2020, 43 of the 85 patients randomised to ripretinib 150 mg QD dose escalated to 150 mg BID following disease progression on by BICR (Figure 9). Of those randomised to ripretinib 150 mg QD with disease progression, 22 did not undergo IPDE but either continued with ripretinib 150 mg QD or discontinued study treatment. The median OS for patients who underwent IPDE was 18.4 months Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496]

This post hoc analysis presents a naïve OS comparison of patients randomised to ripretinib 150 mg QD who did and who did not undergo IPDE at disease progression. In addition to the inherent limitations of post hoc analyses (reduced statistical power, 

risk of confounding/bias), this analysis was not adjusted for possible predictive or prognostic factors.[75] In particular, at the time of progressive disease, 51% of patients who dose escalated had an ECOG of 0 whereas 18% who remained on QD dosing had an ECOG of 0.[66] ECOG has been identified as a prognostic factor, and a lower score is significantly associated with longer survival in patients with advanced GIST.[46,76,77] A UK advisory board confirmed that ECOG is a key treatment effect modifier for this patient population. Therefore, an imbalance in ECOG status would have contributed to the perceived benefit in the IPDE population vs the population who did not undergo IPDE. ## **Censored BID-dosing analyses** 

To further understand the impact of IPDE on the OS, two other post hoc sensitivity analyses were undertaken. The first analysis censored patients who underwent dose increase to 150 mg BID after progression in the open-label phase of the study. OS was analysed over the full study duration and all patients who dose escalated (whether originally randomised to ripretinib or placebo) were censored in the analysis. This analysis estimated a longer median OS for both groups and an improved OS HR at the primary analysis and subsequent data cut-offs compared with the pre-specified OS analysis (Figure 11).[78]

## **Cox proportional hazards time-varying analysis** 

A Cox proportional hazards time-varying analysis was undertaken to allow for adjustment of clinically relevant covariates and their change over time to estimate an effect on survival. Comparison of ripretinib BID vs QD resulted in a HR of 1.37 (95% CI 0.66 - to 2.84; p=0.397) indicating a 37% increase in the risk of death after dose escalation.[79] 

Although not statistically significant, this suggests IPDE has a negative impact on survival, which may be perceived as counterintuitive.[79] This approach avoids the risk of potential bias associated with the BID-censored analysis described; however, the primary limitation in quantifying the effect of dose escalation is not being able to adjust for all possible treatment effect modifiers or outcome predictors. This is due to the fact randomisation was broken after the first incidence of disease progression in the trial; all possible treatment effect modifiers and outcome predictors were not recorded at this point. The resulting potential for selection and survivor bias makes it difficult to Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 68 of 181 



<!-- page 71 -->

attribute differences in the risk of death directly to the dosing regimen rather than to underlying unmeasured health status factors. 

## **Two-stage adjustment** 

A 2-stage modelling approach was used to estimate the effect of patients switching to BID dosing rather than continuing with QD dosing. Only patients randomised to ripretinib QD were included (n=85) in the model, since patients randomised to placebo could only switch to BID dosing after switching from placebo to QD dosing. In stage 1, analysis of OS data using various distributions (exponential, Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic, and generalised gamma) and simple or complex covariate adjustment were fitted to obtain acceleration factors and time ratios. In all cases, time ratios were >1 which indicated prolonged survival for patients that switched to BID compared with patients who remained on QD dosing. Complex covariate adjustment resulted in survival time ratios of 1.94 to 2.72. 

The 2-stage method assumes that there is no time-dependent confounding between the time of progression and the time of treatment switch; as the difference between the two was generally small, this was felt to be true. However, the Cox proportional hazards time-varying analysis showed a lack of alignment in these results, raising questions over the certainty of this assumption and the associated result. 

## **Inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) adjustment** 

IPCW was considered as a method for assessing treatment switch from QD to BID dosing, but it was concluded that any results generated would not be reliable or informative. INVICTUS was a small trial (n=129), from a statistical perspective, and only 41 of the 85 ripretinib arm patients did not switch from QD to BID (the ‘control group’). As such, it is likely that any results would have wide confidence intervals. Given the two analyses described above, it was felt that a further analysis would not give useful insights.

## **UK clinical advisory board** 

Clinical opinion was sought regarding the effect of dose escalation vs remaining on QD dosing after disease progression. Although clinicians agreed the effect was not negligible, it was perceived that it could not be quantified based on the available data. Ultimately clinicians felt that IPDE was unlikely to have changed the shape of the survival curve. Rather, it was deemed likely that long-term survivors, who support the end of survival curves, were likely to have less aggressive disease that progresses more slowly, irrespective of whether the patient receives QD or BID dosing.[18] 

## **Conclusions** 

These analyses demonstrate the uncertainty surrounding the impact of ripretinib dose escalation on OS in INVICTUS, given the considerable variability in the magnitude of and the positive or negative nature of the effect (Table 15). A reasonable explanation as to why the statistical methodologies give differing results, with no clear trend, is the limitations in the available data. Appropriate adjustment for imbalances would require that all prognostic and treatment effect modifiers are collected at the time of potential treatment switch. Given the variability in the results, it is likely that a key factor driving the choice to dose escalate was not captured. 

Adjusting the OS curve for crossover to BID dosing in the economic model presents a significantly more complex scenario compared with adjusting for placebo crossover. The challenge is that not only had patients in the ripretinib arm switched to BID dosing; but some placebo-treated patients had already switched to active treatment before switching to BID dosing. To our knowledge, there is no established, commonly used statistical framework that provides robust and reliable estimates when adjusting for patients who switch treatment twice (placebo to QD and then to BID ripretinib). Theoretically, formal adjustment of multiple switches may be feasible in trials with sufficiently large sample size; this is less likely to be an option for smaller clinical trials concerning rare diseases.

## _**ORR – secondary endpoint**_ 

In the ripretinib group, 9.4% (n=8; 95% CI 4.2% to 17.7%; p=0.0504) of patients had a confirmed ORR as assessed by BICR in the double-blind analysis period, compared with no patients in the placebo group (Table 16). Although ORR did not reach statistical significance it was considered of clinically meaningful benefit to patients, with ripretinib demonstrating favourable disease control. A higher proportion of patients who received ripretinib had stable disease compared with those on placebo at 6 weeks (66% vs 20%) and at 12 weeks (47% vs 5%).[15]

## _**Other secondary endpoints**_ 

The secondary endpoints of DOR, TTP, and time to best response were not included in the statistical hierarchy due to insufficient power. The results reported are therefore considered descriptive and are not tested for statistical significance.[15] 

As of 31 May 2019, median time to best response was 1.9 months (IQR 1.0 to 2.7) with ripretinib, with no patients in the placebo group achieving a response. Responses in patients treated with ripretinib were durable, with median DOR not reached at the primary data cut-off; by the time of the January 2021 data cut-off, median DOR was 14.5 months.[15,23] 

Median TTP was longer in the ripretinib group (6.4 months [95% CI 4.6 to 8.4]) vs the placebo group (1.0 month [95% CI 0.9 to 1.7]).[15] A TTP event occurred in 54.1% of patients (n=46, 39 censored) in the ripretinib group compared with 72.7% (n=32; 12 censored) in the placebo group.[51] 

These results indicate durable, clinically meaningful disease control for ripretinib treatment compared with placebo.

## _**HRQoL**_ 

As ORR did not reach statistical significance, HRQoL results could not be formally tested for statistical significance owing to the hierarchal nature of the testing procedures.[16] The results reported are descriptive and statistical significance is not implied. 

HRQoL in INVICTUS was assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 role and physical functioning domains, EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1. On Cycle 2 Day 1, 71 patients were evaluable in the ripretinib arm and 32 patients were

Patients in the ripretinib group reported an improvement in physical and role functioning domains of EORTC QLQ-C30 from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1, with an adjusted mean increase in scores (indicating improvement) of 1.6 and 3.5, respectively; a decline of 8.9 and 17.1 was seen for patients in the placebo group.[16] Patients receiving ripretinib reported an improvement in HRQoL from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1, as assessed by an adjusted mean increase in EQ-VAS scores of 3.7 vs a decline of 8.9 with placebo. These differences in PRO measures between patients receiving ripretinib and those receiving placebo were considered clinically significant using a previously defined minimal clinically important difference (MCID),[82] and p-values were significant.[15] A >10% mean score change or score change of 5 points was considered the threshold to determine a MCID.[16] Based on this definition, treatment with ripretinib led to a clinically meaningful benefit compared with placebo across PRO measures (Figure 14 and Table 17).

Exploratory analysis indicated that for patients in the ripretinib group who experienced alopecia, a commonly reported treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE), HRQoL was maintained; repeated measures analysis demonstrated that overall health, physical function, and role function were maintained over time for patients receiving ripretinib irrespective of whether they had alopecia or not.[61] 

## **Time until definitive deterioration** 

Patients receiving ripretinib reported longer TUDD in all assessed PRO measures (a clinically meaningful decline in the PRO measure that does not recover based on a data cut-off of August 2020) compared with those receiving placebo.[56] This was seen for each EQ-VAS PRO measure, physical and role functioning (measured jointly), overall health, and overall QoL on EORTC QLQ-C30. For overall health, median TUDD for the placebo group was 7.7 weeks but had not been reached in the ripretinib group by 56 weeks (Figure 16). For physical and role function (EORTC QLQ-C30) and EQ-VAS score, median TUDD was 41.6 weeks in the ripretinib group vs 7.9 weeks in the placebo group (Figure 17 and Figure 18). Median TUDD was longer than median PFS (6.3 months) and median TTD (8.8 months) with ripretinib, suggesting that tolerability did not drive treatment discontinuation and that HRQoL was maintained after disease progression.[56]

## **2.6.3 Royal Marsden expanded access program** 

## _**Patient disposition**_ 

The median follow-up time in the overall patient population was 24.2 months (95% CI 19.7–29.7). At the time of data cut-off, 5 (11.1%) patients were still receiving 150 mg ripretinib QD. Ripretinib QD was discontinued for the remaining 40 patients for the following reasons: mRECIST PD in 21 (46.7%) cases, clinical PD in 17 (37.8%) cases, and toxicity in 2 (4.4%) cases. Of the 21 patients with mRECIST PD, 15 dose-escalated to ripretinib BID and 6 did not dose-escalate (2 received another TKI, and 4 declined IPDE and were referred back to their local team). Of the 17 patients with clinical PD, 10 were too unwell to continue treatment and 7 dose-escalated to ripretinib BID. In total, 22 (48.9%) patients had their dose escalated to ripretinib BID.[69] 

Of the 22 patients undergoing IPDE, 4 (18.2%) were still receiving ripretinib BID at the time of data cut-off, 4 (18.2%) had clinical progression and 14 (63.6%) had mRECIST

PD. Four patients went on to receive a further line of treatment after progression on ripretinib BID. At the time of data cut-off, 20 (44.4%) patients were still alive and 25 (55.6%) had died.[69] 

## _**Progression free survival**_ 

The median PFS for patients receiving ripretinib QD was 7.9 months (95% CI 5.6– 19.3) (Figure 19A). The median PFS for patients receiving ripretinib BID (after initial disease progression) was 5.4 months (95% CI 2.8–9.3).[69] Similar to INVICTUS, the PFS from dose escalation to disease progression on that dose was shorter compared with PFS after initial treatment with ripretinib (median PFS2/PFS1 ratio in INVICTUS was 80%).[66,69] The median PFS achieved in INVICTUS (6.3, 95% CI 4.6 to 8.1, months) is shorter than the median PFS for patients receiving ripretinib QD during the expanded access program, potentially due to the lower frequency of radiological assessment in clinical practice.[18] In the overall study population, median PFS ITT was 9.7 (95% CI 8.3–18.1) months, i.e., 9.7 months from the first ripretinib QD dose to disease progression if patients did not undergo IPDE or time until progression on ripretinib BID dosing for those who did (Figure 19B).[69]

## _**Overall survival**_ 

The median OS for the overall study population was 14.0 (95% CI 9.9–NA) months, including all patients, irrespective of post-progression ripretinib dosing (Figure 20).[69] The median OS achieved in the expanded access program was lower than the median OS achieved in INVICTUS (18.2, 95% CI 13.1 to 30.7, months) after a similar median follow up period.[15,69] The OS achieved in clinical practice is often lower than that achieved in clinical trials due to the ‘controlled by protocol’ nature of a clinical trial. Stringent recruitment criteria and intensive patient care with close monitoring and contact are maintained throughout a clinical study.[85] Analysis of cancer clinical trial control arms compared with real-world cohorts showed that poorer outcomes are generally seen in routine clinical practice unless patient populations are carefully aligned/adjusted to ensure consistency.[86] When consulted, UK clinicians agreed that clinical study populations meet strict inclusion criteria and as a result patients are often fitter than those seen in routine clinical practice.[69] 

Consistent with the reasoning above, patients in the expanded access program had poorer performance status at baseline compared those in INVICTUS (ECOG 1-2 98% vs 56%, respectively).[15,69] UK clinicians confirmed that ECOG is a key treatment effect modifier in this patient population.[18,46,77,87]

## _**Objective response rates**_ 

Three patients in the expanded access program did not undergo radiologic evaluation whilst receiving ripretinib QD, because of their rapid clinical deterioration. For the 42 patients with at least one radiological evaluation, the best responses to ripretinib QD were PR in 7 patients (16.7%) and SD in 29 patients (69.0%). The median time to best response was 2.6 (IQR 1.9–3.3) months.[69] 

Three patients did not undergo radiologic evaluation whilst on ripretinib BID; 2 patients because of rapid clinical deterioration and 1 patient was dose-escalated 2 weeks before data cut-off. In the 20 evaluable patients, the best responses to ripretinib BID were PR in 2 patients (10.0%) and SD in 9 patients (45.0%).[69] 

Rates of objective response and SD were comparable to those achieved in INVICTUS at 9% and 66%, respectively.[15,69]

An absence of objective response with ripretinib at the ≥4L of treatment or above does not preclude a clinical benefit in asymptomatic patients, particularly since objective responses are rare with any agent in this clinical setting. Unlike some other advanced solid tumours, an absence of disease progression (whether a PR or SD) is considered an important therapeutic marker of benefit and is predictive of improvements in PFS and OS in patients with advanced GIST.[66,80,81] 

## _**Time-to-discontinuation and treatment-beyond-progression**_ 

The median TTD in patients receiving ripretinib QD was similar to their median PFS, at 7.1 (95% CI 5.8–11.0) months.[69] Ripretinib QD TBP was recorded for 14 patients (31.1%). Patients with TBP generally showed no significant differences in baseline characteristics compared with patients without TBP; the only exception was site of disease and this difference is most likely due to the small sample size. The median duration of TBP was 1.9 months (IQR 1.0–3.0 months).[69] 

The median TTD in patients receiving ripretinib BID was similar to their median PFS BID, at 6.5 (95% CI 4.6–10.7) months. Ripretinib BID TBP (defined as ripretinib treatment beyond second disease progression) was observed in 6 patients (27.3%). The median duration of TBP was 2.8 months (IQR 1.0–5.4 months).[18,69] 

The median duration of TBP is comparable to that estimated for the INVICTUS ITT population (XXX).[15,72] Clinicians agreed at a UK advisory board that this aligns with their expectations for ripretinib in UK clinical practice.[38]

## **2.8 Subgroup analysis** 

## **2.8.1 INVICTUS subgroup analyses** 

## _**Subgroup analyses for PFS (pre-specified)**_ 

PFS outcomes were assessed by subgroup to understand the treatment effect of ripretinib in different patient populations. In terms of HR for PFS, the subgroup analyses consistently favour the experimental arm, as shown in Figure 21, including the stratification groups (ECOG 0 vs 1 or 2) with a HR of 0.33 and 0.10, respectively.[15] The HR values for PFS are similar for 3 prior lines of therapy (HR [CI]: 0.15 [0.08, 0.29]) compared with ≥4 prior lines of therapy (HR [CI]: 0.24 [0.12, 0.51]), and confidence intervals overlap. This confirms that there is no significant difference in treatment effect on PFS for patients who have received 3 vs ≥4 prior lines of therapy. Furthermore, the HR values for PFS are similar for ages 18-64 years (HR [CI]: 0.25 [0.14, 0.45]) and ages 65-74 years (HR [CI]: 0.19 [0.06, 0.56]), again, with confidence intervals overlapping. The PFS HR value for age ≥75 and older is more uncertain due to the small patient numbers. Clinicians consulted at a UK advisory board did not consider age or line of therapy to be treatment effect modifiers.[18] The PFS subgroup analyses for the January 2021 data cut-off shows consistent results with the May 2019 data cut-off.[23]

## **2.8.2 Royal Marsden expanded access program: subgroup analyses** 

In multivariate Cox regression models, the absence of a KIT exon 11 mutation was associated with a statistically significant reduction in PFS QD (HR 4.67, 95% CI 1.53– 14.29), PFS ITT (HR 3.06, 95% CI 1.08–8.67) and OS (HR 4.19, 95% CI 1.49–11.82) compared to when a KIT exon 11 mutation is present.[69] Furthermore, patients with three or more metastatic sites also had statistically shorter PFS ITT compared with patients with less than two metastatic sites (HR 3.00, 95% CI 1.05–8.57). Other variables tested, including number of previous lines of treatment (2 vs 3 or more) and age, were not associated with significant differences in PFS (QD or ITT) or OS, (Appendix C).[69] This is consistent with the INVICTUS OS subgroup analyses for age and number of previous lines of therapy.

Ripretinib was generally well-tolerated and associated with an acceptable safety profile in INVICTUS. The overall frequency of TEAEs was similar between the ripretinib and placebo groups (99% [84] vs 98% [42]).[62] 

At the January 2021 data cut-off, approximately half of patients in the ripretinib group experienced a grade 3 or 4 TEAE (49.4%) and 8% experienced a TEAE leading to treatment discontinuation.[23] Grade 3 or 4 TEAEs and TEAEs leading to discontinuation were reported in a similar proportion of patients in the placebo group (44.2% and 12%, respectively).[23] Grade 3 or 4 TEAEs occurring in more than 5% of patients (anaemia, abdominal pain and hypertension) were included in the economic model.

## **2.11.2 Pooled adverse reactions data** 

To perform further safety analyses, the INVICTUS patient population (129 patients diagnosed with advanced GIST who had failed at ≥3 prior lines of treatment) was pooled together with those treated in the Phase 1 Study DCC-2618-01-001, in which 277 patients with advanced malignancies were enrolled.[15,88,89] In the resulting pooled safety population (n=392), the most frequently (>25%) observed adverse reactions in patients who received at least one dose of ripretinib (150 mg) were fatigue (51.0%), alopecia (50.8%), nausea (39.8%), myalgia (37.8%), constipation (37.2%), diarrhoea (32.7%), PPES (29.8%), weight decreased (26.5%) and vomiting (25.8%). ## **2.13 Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence** 

## **2.13.1 Principal findings from the clinical evidence** 

Based on the primary efficacy analysis for the INVICTUS double-blind treatment period, ripretinib led to a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in median PFS compared with placebo (6.3 vs 1.0 months; p<0.001), thereby reducing the risk of disease progression or death by 85% (HR 0.15; 95% confidence interval [95% CI] 0.09 to 0.25).[15] Compared with placebo, ripretinib achieved a clinically meaningful 64% reduction in the risk of death (HR 0.36; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.62), leading to an 8.5-month improvement in median OS vs placebo in the primary analysis (Figure 8, Section 2.6.2).[15] With an additional 19 months follow up, this had increased to a 11.9-month improvement in median OS vs placebo; effectively tripling OS for these patients.[15,23] At the primary analysis, ripretinib resulted in a clinically meaningful ORR benefit compared with placebo (9% vs 0%).[15,51] Importantly, ripretinib showed durable, clinically meaningful disease control: 66% of ripretinib-treated patients experienced stable disease for ≥6 weeks vs 20% of patients treated with placebo; and 47% vs 5% of patients experienced stable disease for ≥12 weeks, respectively.[15] Responses in patients treated with ripretinib were durable, with the median DOR not yet reached at data cut-off (31 May 2019).[15,51] 

In INVICTUS, across all PRO measures assessed, patients treated with ripretinib maintained HRQoL and function for approximately 8 months while it quickly, and significantly, deteriorated for those receiving placebo after just 1 month.[16] Importantly, HRQoL was maintained past the point of median PFS (6.3 months), likely supported by the continued use of ripretinib post-progression in the many patients still receiving clinical benefit.[16,38] Ripretinib was well-tolerated and demonstrated an acceptable safety profile.[62] The most common treatment-related TEAEs (≥20%) among the 85 GIST patients treated with ripretinib were alopecia (49%), myalgia (28%), nausea 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 97 of 181 



<!-- page 100 -->

(26%), fatigue (26%), and PPES (21%). Most of these were grade 1 and 2 in severity.[15] Treatment-related serious adverse events were reported in eight (9%) of 85 patients who received ripretinib and three (7%) of 43 patients who received placebo. Treatment-related TEAEs leading to a dose reduction or treatment discontinuation were reported in 6% (vs 2% in the placebo group) and 5% (vs 2% in the placebo group) of patients receiving ripretinib, respectively.[15] 

Data from The Royal Marsden Hospital, London, UK, support the generalisability of INVICTUS to clinical practice in the UK.[69] After a median follow up of 24.2 months (95% CI 19.7–29.7), the median PFS was 7.9 months (95% CI 5.6–19.3) and median OS was 14.0 months (95% CI 9.9–NA), both of which are broadly in line with INVICTUS.[15,69] 

Ripretinib is able to meet a high unmet need in patients with fourth-line advanced GIST by significantly extending PFS and providing durable disease control, thereby preventing the rapid clinical decline otherwise seen in these patients.[15] Consequently, ripretinib allows patients to maintain HRQoL and provides a clinically meaningful survival benefit.[15,23] During a UK advisory board, clinicians stated that more of their patients would be alive today if ripretinib was a treatment option.[18] 

## **2.13.2 Strengths, limitations and generalisability of the clinical evidence** 

INVICTUS was a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled study, which is the gold-standard study design for interventional clinical trials, minimising the risk of confounding factors and allowing direct comparison of the relative efficacy of interventions. Stratification based on key factors such as the number of previous therapies (3 vs ≥ 4) and ECOG performance status (0 vs 1 or 2) ensured that the study accounted for important prognostic factors. 

The outcomes measured in INVICTUS were considered clinically and patient relevant by the patient groups Sarcoma UK and GIST Cancer UK. They agreed that OS, PFS, response rate (including partial response rate and DOR), AEs and HRQoL are the most applicable outcomes.[34,90] 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 98 of 181 



<!-- page 101 -->

The results from INVICTUS are relevant to clinical practice in the UK. Ten of 129 patients in INVICTUS were enrolled from two centres in the UK. Overall, the patients included in INVICTUS were representative of patients with advanced GIST in the UK and reflect the known epidemiology of GIST in the UK as reported by Bulusu et al. 2013 and confirmed by clinicians in a UK advisory board.[18,91] A further 45 patients were treated at the Royal Marsden in London under an expanded access program. The findings from the Royal Marsden retrospective review support the generalisability of INVICTUS to UK clinical practice. 

Analyses were limited by the small sample size, from a statistical perspective, which made stratifying patients by more baseline parameters difficult; although, this reflects the rarity of this disease and is aligned with the size of other pivotal trials in this patient population.[8,92,93] 

Although the ripretinib label describes a single daily dose, during INVICTUS, patients were offered the option of escalating to 150 mg BID after disease progression on ripretinib 150 mg QD. This was done on ethical grounds with the intent to provide an additional line of therapy for patients with very late-stage disease.[15] However, across the ITT population more than three-quarters (75.9%) of ripretinib exposure time was on single dose, with only the remaining 24.1% on BID. Although a high proportion (~50%) of patients dose escalated, those patients stayed on BID for a limited time overall. Specifically, only 11 of 43 patients (26%) were treated at this dose for 6 months or longer.[66] This indicates that the OS benefits seen in INVICTUS are predominantly driven by the single dose rather than BID. 

The INVICTUS trial design was, therefore, sufficiently robust to answer the decision problem, in assessing ripretinib vs placebo in patients with advanced GIST in the fourth-line treatment setting.

## **3.2 Economic analysis** 

This section describes the company’s approach to estimating the cost-effectiveness of ripretinib + BSC (ripretinib) vs placebo + BSC (BSC) for patients with advanced GIST who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors, including imatinib. Table 28 presents a summary of the economic model. Of the economic analyses identified in the systematic literature review (Appendix E), there was only one that had been conducted of fourth-or-further line ripretinib in patients with advanced GIST.[98] The model was a Markov structure and was developed from a US perspective. Health state utility values were obtained from the regorafenib pivotal trial in advanced GIST, GRID. The analysis made no attempt to adjust the clinical outcomes for the crossover to ripretinib from the BSC arm in INVICTUS, instead opting to capture the costs of ripretinib in those patients who crossed over from the BSC arm in INVICTUS. Such an approach resulted in a substantial underestimate of the clinical benefits of ripretinib and was therefore not considered appropriate to inform the _de novo_ model developed for the present analysis. The primary model used to inform the choice of a PSM structure was the model used for the appraisal of regorafenib for previously-treated unresectable or metastatic GIST, the most recent technology appraisal conducted by NICE for an earlier line of GIST treatment.[7]
