## **3.2.1 Patient population** 

The population entering the cost-utility model are adult patients with advanced GIST who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors including imatinib; this is in line with the scope and decision problem for this evaluation, the UK marketing authorisation and the INVICTUS ITT population.[104] The age at baseline for patients entering the model is 60.1 years and 56.6% of the model baseline population are male, in line with INVICTUS.[15] 

## **3.2.2 Model structure** 

Partitioned survival models (PSMs) have been extensively used to model oncology treatments in the UK healthcare setting. In a review by NICE covering the period May 2013 to February 2016, 22 of 30 (73%) oncology appraisals evaluated by NICE used a PSM.[102] 

A review of the use of partitioned survival analysis in recent technology appraisals (TAs) of cancer treatments found similar criticisms between the use of PSMs and Markov models. Although Markov models can be more flexible at modelling complex disease trajectories, they have additional data requirements over PSMs. Other model structures have been accepted during health technology assessment (HTA), including time-in-state and cumulative survival models, though these are rarely used.[102 ] 

A PSM structure was selected since it facilitates incorporation of time dependency in the models that govern partition membership over time; in addition, data requirements for partitioned survival analysis were well aligned with and fulfilled by INVICTUS clinical endpoints. A PSM structure is also consistent with previous economic models of GIST such as that used in the appraisal of regorafenib for previously-treated unresectable or metastatic GIST.[7,101] The model was developed in Microsoft[®] Excel[®] for Microsoft 365 MSO (Version 2406; Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA). The model includes three disease-related health states: progression-free (PF), progressed disease (PD), and death. To capture the effect of patients remaining on ripretinib treatment after progression, the PD state in the ripretinib arm is then further divided into PD on-treatment and PD off-treatment. 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 104 of 181 



<!-- page 107 -->

In a typical three-state PSM, the distribution of patients between the PF, PD and dead health states is estimated over time based on survival curves (Figure 22A). The OS and PFS curves are combined to estimate the proportion of patients whose disease has not progressed, who have progressed disease, and who are dead, where S(t) is the probability of survival beyond time t. The area-under-the-curve approach is then used to estimate the time patients spend in the PF and PD states. In the ripretinib cost-utility model, clinicians reported that it would be important to include the effects of continued treatment after disease progression, noting that approximately 80% of patients would be expected to continue ripretinib post-progression in UK clinical practice.[38] This phenomenon was captured by dividing the PD state into two sub-states: on treatment and off treatment (Figure 22B).

The intervention technology is ripretinib. As ripretinib is indicated for patients who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors, including imatinib, and would represent the last systemic treatment line, the most appropriate comparator was deemed to be BSC.[18,70] In the model, the base case assumption is that ripretinib would be administered to patients within the licensed indication and at the licensed dose.

## **3.3 Clinical parameters and variables** 

Clinical effectiveness parameters are based on data from INVICTUS.[15] Survival analysis extrapolation was required to inform state occupancy in the model, allowing for evaluation of clinical outcomes over a longer time horizon than that in the trial. From mature OS data for the data cut-off (15 January 2021), 46 patients (54%) in the ripretinib group experienced an OS event (39 [46%] were censored); and 36 patients (82%) patients in the BSC group experienced an OS event (8 [18%] were censored).[23] 

To validate the applicability of clinical parameters used in the health economic model, clinical experts were consulted during the advisory boards that took place in 2022, 2024 and 2025, details of which are presented in Section 2.3.5. 

## **3.3.1 Progression-free survival** 

Parametric models were fitted directly to ripretinib + BSC (ripretinib) and placebo + BSC (BSC) patient-level data to provide long-term extrapolations. Crossover of patients from BSC to ripretinib in the INVICTUS was only allowed following disease progression, therefore crossover correction was not required for PFS data. The PFS Kaplan-Meier curves for ripretinib and BSC from the INVICTUS are shown in Figure 5 in Section 2.6.2. Progression was observed within the trial follow-up period for almost all patients in both arms (84% in both, Section 2.6.2, PFS – primary endpoint).[23] 

Statistical analyses were conducted to test whether the proportional hazards (PH) assumption holds between the two INVICTUS treatment arms over the observed trial follow-up period. Two statistical tests were conducted: a complementary log-log plot and the Schoenfeld residuals test. The outcomes of these tests were used to determine whether the null hypothesis, that PH between treatment arms holds, could be rejected. 

Inspection of the log-cumulative hazards (Figure 23) and Schoenfeld residual plots (Figure 24) suggest that relative hazards are likely to vary over time; therefore it is not possible to conclude that the PH assumption holds.

Given that Figure 23 and Figure 24 demonstrate that the PH assumption does not hold, and patient-level data were available for both arms, six standard parametric independent models were fitted to each arm of the study data comprising: exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, log-normal and the generalised gamma (Figure 25). More complex models, such as piecewise spline-based models, mixture models, flexible proportional-hazards models, or proportional-odds models, were not considered as the independent parametric models appeared to be suitable for modelling PFS based on inspection of log-cumulative hazards, visual goodness-of-fit and plausibility of the extrapolated portion of the curves.[111 ]

## **3.3.2 Overall survival** 

In INVICTUS, patients who were randomly assigned to BSC were given the option to crossover to receive open-label ripretinib. 

As the true survival associated with BSC will be confounded, conventional survival analysis is likely to underestimate the survival benefit associated with ripretinib. Due to the high proportion of patients who crossed over (30 of 44 patients [68%] at data cut-off of 15 January 2021), using the results of the ITT analysis for OS in the model was deemed inappropriate. 

Treatment crossover in INVICTUS occurred following disease progression and was therefore non-random. The NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) recommends implementation of a variety of potentially appropriate crossover- adjustment approaches when adjusting for a high degree of crossover. Such approaches take into account trial characteristics, the switching mechanism, the treatment effect, and data availability.[112] The methods recommended by the DSU include: the Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights (IPCW) method, the Rank Preserving Structural Failure Time (RPSFT) model, and the two-stage approach.[112]

## _**Overall survival adjustment for crossover**_ 

## **Crossover adjustment: Inverse probability of censoring weights** 

The IPCW method was considered but not used due to the small sample size from a statistical perspective and the high proportion of BSC patients crossing over to ripretinib treatment (only 14 patients in the BSC arm did not enter the open-label period); these factors can be responsible for introducing high levels of error in treatment effect estimates and both may introduce uncertainty into the IPCW analysis.[112] 

## **Crossover adjustment: Rank preserving structural failure time** 

The RPSFTM method uses a g-estimation procedure to determine treatment effect, psi.[113] The treatment effect is estimated by balancing counterfactual event times (that is, the time that would have been observed if no treatment were received in either randomised group) across randomised groups. A key advantage of the RPSFTM method is that it is randomisation-based and requires only the randomised treatment groups, observed event times, and treatment history in order to estimate counterfactual survival times.[113] The method relies on the assumption that a ‘common treatment effect’ exists and so the treatment effect for switchers must be the same (relative to the time taking treatment) as that for those initially randomised to the experimental treatment. 

The date of first exposure and date of last exposure to ripretinib for each patient was recorded in the trial and was used in the ‘RPSFTM’ package in R to obtain the acceleration factor and time ratio associated with ripretinib treatment. The possible test options were the log-rank and the Wald test from a Cox or Weibull regression model. All three options were explored to derive the acceleration factor (exp( _ψ_ 0)) and time ratio (exp(- _ψ_ 0)) associated with ripretinib treatment in the ITT population. The log-rank, Cox and Weibull models all gave output time ratios of >15 (Table 31). When considering the counterfactual survival times in Figure 26, the dissimilarity between curves indicates that the g-estimation did not produce a robust outcome. Figure 26 shows the log-rank option but the Cox and Weibull options produced very similar 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 112 of 181 



<!-- page 115 -->

results. As patients were only allowed treatment switch following disease progression, it was considered unlikely that the ‘common treatment effect’ assumption would hold. As such, the RPSFTM method was ruled out for the base case, but was explored in scenario analyses. 

The ‘RPSFTM’ package allows for deviations from the common treatment effect to be modelled through use of a treatment-effect modifier variable, _ki_ , which modifies the counter-factual treatment-free event times by multiplying the treatment effect by _ki_ . While such modification is likely to result in an RPSFT model that is biased (in the absence of further adjustments for heterogeneity in the underlying characteristics that may drive differences in treatment effect), this option was explored. In the absence of data to inform the value of _ki_ , analyses were run in which _ki_ values were set to 1 (common treatment effect; no deviation) and 0.5 (treatment effect half as strong). With _ki_ set to 0.5, the acceleration factor exp( _ψ_ 0) changed from 0.06 to 0.07. Given the likelihood that such an RPSFT model would be biased and that the choice of treatment-effect modifier variable was arbitrary (in the absence of observed data), these analyses were not used in the base analysis, but were explored in a scenario analysis in which the best-fitting distribution to the RPSFT model with _ki_ set to 0.5 (Weibull distribution; AIC: 292.7, BIC: 296.3) was used as the basis of modelling OS in the BSC arm. An additional scenario analysis was then conducted maintaining the log-logistic distribution adopted in the base case analysis (which used the simple two-stage adjustment model).

## **Crossover adjustment: Two-stage approach** 

The two-stage approach to crossover adjustment was considered and relies on the following assumptions:[112] 

- A secondary baseline can be defined, at which point patients are at risk of crossover (for example progression) 

- There is no unmeasured confounding at the point of the secondary baseline 

- The RCT (INVICTUS) was appropriately randomised up to the point of disease progression. 

Two models were explored, one included time to progression as a co-variate (simple model) and the other included time to progression, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG), QoL (quality of life) and age as co-variates (complex model). The following assumptions were made: 

- 7 of 44 patients in the BSC group had progression censored but continued to be followed up. To avoid reducing an already small sample size, it was assumed that censored time to progression values equate to documented time to progression for these patients 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 114 of 181 



<!-- page 117 -->

- ECOG PS and QoL values recorded at the closest time to progression were used in the analysis. 

As time to progression was the only statistically significant co-variate, the use of co-variates in the complex model would add additional uncertainty to the analysis; given the small sample size, the simple model was used in the base-case analysis, while the complex model was explored in scenario analyses. 

The resulting time ratio was then used to ‘shrink’ the post-progression survival times for switching patients to derive a counterfactual dataset unaffected by switching. The base-case analysis was performed with recensoring to guard against informative censoring.[114] The resulting median OS times for the base-case analysis (simple model) and complex model are presented in Table 32. The adjusted OS BSC base-case Kaplan-Meier curve is shown in Figure 27.

The two-stage approach was ultimately chosen as the most robust estimate as switching in INVICTUS occurred only after a well-defined clinical event (giving a good basis for the ‘secondary baseline’ required in two-stage estimation). The two-stage approach also does not rely on the common treatment effect assumption, nor is it as adversely affected by a high proportion of patients undergoing crossover as the IPCW approach. 

The two-stage estimate was further validated by a UK clinician advisory board, where it was unanimously agreed that an adjusted median OS of 11.2 weeks for patients receiving BSC is clinically plausible.[38] This reflects clinical practice where patients receiving BSC after exhausting all active treatment options usually survive for 2 to 3 months.[38] 

Following crossover adjustment, tests were conducted to test if the PH assumption held between the two treatment arms of INVICTUS within the trial follow-up period. Two statistical tests were conducted: the complementary log-log plot and the Schoenfeld residuals test. The outcomes of these tests were used to determine whether the null hypothesis, that PH between treatment arms holds, could be rejected.

In addition to parametric models of OS based on INVICTUS data, the model estimates general population mortality to ensure that survival in the fourth-line GIST population does not exceed that in the general population. Adjustment for post-progression IPDE was attempted using various methodologies (Section 2.6). ## **3.3.3 Time to treatment discontinuation (TTD)** 

Post-progression ripretinib use was captured in the ripretinib arm of the model through division of the PD state into two substates: on treatment and off treatment. 

The parametric survival models used to divide the PD state into on treatment and off treatment were based on an analysis of a composite endpoint of PFS and treatment 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 123 of 181 



<!-- page 126 -->

discontinuation, defined as follows: the time from study start to a composite endpoint of PFS plus treatment discontinuation (either QD or BD) over the double-blind and open-label periods was derived. Event time was measured from the date of randomisation to the latest of PFS or treatment discontinuation. Patients without either event were considered censored and censoring time was measured from the date of randomisation to the latest of the two component times (PFS, last treatment), regardless of event/censoring for each component. Due to PFS censoring rules pertaining to two or more missing assessments (in line with the INVICTUS SAP 8.1), patients who did not either discontinue treatment and/or were considered censored for PFS, and who died were assumed to have the composite endpoint event at the time of their death. The analysis was restricted to ITT patients who were randomly assigned to ripretinib.

This aligns with experience with patients treated with ripretinib in clinical practice (at the Royal Marsden through INVICTUS and the expanded use program).[38 ] 

## **3.3.4 Subsequent treatments and drug exposure** 

As ripretinib is anticipated to be the last line of therapy for GIST in UK clinical practice, no subsequent treatments were modelled in the ripretinib arm with patients incurring only the costs of BSC after treatment discontinuation. A compliance rate and relative dose intensity of 100% and 96.5% respectively were used in the base case analysis, with the latter derived from the double-blind period of INVICTUS.[15]

## **3.4 Measurement and valuation of health effects** 

## **3.4.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials** 

EQ-5D-5L assessment was a pre-specified secondary endpoint in INVICTUS. EQ-5D-5L assessments were completed using an electronic PRO (ePRO) system before dosing on days 1 (baseline) and 15 of Cycle 1, Day 1 of subsequent cycles, and within 7 days of the last dose (end-of-treatment visit). Patients were asked to rate their health on that specific day using a vertical visual analogue scale. The five questions were scored and together contributed to the EQ-5D-5L index (utility) score of between 0 and 1 (1 being perfect health) and was calculated using the developers’ algorithm based on country-specific reference score sets (Van Hout et al., 2012).[119] An ANCOVA model with stratification factors as factors will be used to compare change from baseline to Day 1 of Cycle 2 between the two treatment arms. A summary of EQ-5D-5L index (utility) scores is shown in Table 38. 

These methods align with the NICE reference case. Although the values were not generated solely from a UK population, data from the Royal Marsden expanded use program demonstrates the generalisability of INVICTUS to UK patients with advanced GIST; this was also validated by clinicians.[38,69] INVICTUS is the most appropriate and robust data for modelling given that it is sourced from the pivotal Phase 3 trial for ripretinib in the population relevant to the NICE decision problem. No other clinical trials have collected such data to our knowledge.

## **3.4.4 Adverse reactions** 

Ripretinib was well-tolerated and associated with an acceptable safety profile in INVICTUS. The overall frequency of TEAEs was similar between the ripretinib and BSC groups (99% vs 98%).[62] Safety findings for the January 2021 data cut were consistent with the previous primary analysis results.[23] 

Approximately half of patients in the ripretinib group experienced a grade 3 or 4 TEAE (49%) with 8% experiencing a TEAE leading to treatment discontinuation.[23] Grade 3 or 4 TEAEs and TEAEs leading to discontinuation were reported in a similar proportion of patients in the BSC group (44% and 12%, respectively). ## **3.4.5 Health-related quality-of-life data used in the cost-effectiveness analysis** 

Baseline health-related quality of life estimates from INVICTUS were not used directly in the model; rather, health status utility values were least square mean values from a mixed model of repeat measures (MMRM). After mapping EQ-5D-5L responses to EQ-5D-3L responses in line with Hernandez-Alava and Pudney (2022), the MMRM was applied, adjusting for treatment arm, treatment status, PF/PD health state and all two-way and three-way interactions as fixed effects, and with a compound symmetry within-subject correlation structure per treatment arm/ treatment status/health state combination.[120] As such, health state utility values reflected all EQ-5D measurements taken while patients were within each partition of the model. Beyond the MMRM approach, no further adjustments were made to values as they were input into the 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 132 of 181 



<!-- page 135 -->

model. The model also incorporates an age adjustment for health state utility values, and utilities therefore vary over time based on a multiplier derived from general population EQ-5D estimates reported by Hernandez-Alava et al. (2022).[134] 

The cost-effectiveness analysis included four partitions: PF, PD on treatment, PD off treatment, and PD BSC. The PF partition represents patients at the start of the trial who have not experienced a progression event. This utility value was generated for both trial arms as a weighted average of patients randomised to ripretinib and those randomised to BSC. Clinicians at a UK advisory board agreed that it was reasonable to assume that patients start from the same baseline, irrespective of their randomisation.[118] Clinicians also agreed that the assumed PF value for fourth-line ripretinib (0.722) should be slightly lower than that for 3L regorafenib (0.767 in TA488).[38,101] 

The PD partition is split into PD on and off treatment as justified in Section 3.2.2. Clinicians agreed that it was logical to calculate the PD on treatment value using observations from all patients receiving post progression ripretinib, including those originally randomised to the BSC arm but who crossed over upon progression, as both populations are receiving ripretinib and have experienced progression. Additionally, clinicians felt that patients with disease progression and receiving ripretinib (PD on-treatment) are clinically closer, in terms of HRQoL, to those in the progression-free state as compared with those who have progressed and are no longer on active treatment (PD off-treatment).[38,118] In the base case analysis, a higher utility value is therefore allocated to PD on treatment vs PD off treatment.[4,18,38] Patients no longer receiving active treatment after progression (PD off-treatment), irrespective of their randomised treatment arm and whether they received post-progression ripretinib, were deemed likely to have similar quality of life. Therefore, health state utility values for PD off treatment and PD BSC were assumed to be the same in the base case. A value of 0.624 was considered reasonable by clinicians, given that the observed difference between PF and PD off-treatment utility values for ripretinib (-0.098) is comparable to that used for regorafenib in TA488 (-0.120).

## **3.5.1 Intervention and comparators’ costs and resource use** 

Drug-related costs considered include the acquisition and administration costs for ripretinib + BSC, and BSC only. 

## _**Drug acquisition costs**_ 

## **Ripretinib** 

Ripretinib is available in 50 mg capsules and the list price per 30-day supply is £18,400. Ripretinib pricing has been included ‘per pack’ in line with NICE guidance.[135] The model supports the inclusion of a PAS in calculation of the drug costs for ripretinib. The licensed ripretinib dosing is 150 mg once daily. However, as patients in INVICTUS were permitted to escalate to BID ripretinib after disease progression, the model includes an input to capture the cost of BID ripretinib in a proportion of patients in the post progression- on-treatment partition. This BID costing is implemented using a pack-wastage-adjusted tablet price of ripretinib to avoid double counting of pack wastage at the time of progression. An assumption that 50% of patients with progressed disease received the BID dose was explored in a scenario analysis based on UK clinician opinion on the likely proportion of patients who would be expected to dose escalate to BID administration after progression (Section 2.6). 

## **BSC** 

BSC costs were calculated from NICE TA488 (for regorafenib), the most recent recommended technology appraisal (TA) in GIST; TA488 used a clinician survey to estimate the proportion of patients treated with pain medication.[101] These clinicians were based in the UK, and so BSC costs from TA488 are assumed to be more appropriate to the English setting than those approximated from concomitant medications taken in the BSC arm of INVICTUS. Pain management costs were applied across both arms (ripretinib and BSC). Dosing as per TA730/TA488 was combined with costs from the British National Formulary (BNF) from January 2025 as presented in Table 44.[101,136] The assumed dose for each medication was based on the respective SmPC maintenance dose for the most common indication. In instances where the maintenance dose was a range, conservatively, the lowest dose was assumed. If the

## **3.5.2 Health-state unit costs and resource use** 

The approach to health state costs is based on TA730 and TA488.[101,128] Resource use frequencies were originally based on a survey conducted in 2013 involving 15 clinicians from the UK. These frequencies were re-evaluated in 2016 by two consultant oncologists based in UK clinical practice.[17] 

The ripretinib marketing authorisation is independent of mutational status, therefore no additional diagnostic testing is required. According to UK clinical practice guidelines, all patients with GIST are routinely tested for mutations on diagnosis.[4] Therefore, costs associated with diagnostic testing have not been included in the model. 

Table 46 presents the one-off costs of tests taken by a proportion of patients before treatment in addition to palliative surgical resection and palliative radiotherapy given to relieve or prevent symptoms. It was assumed that all patients require regular resource use, monitoring and tests as reported in Table 47.

## **3.5.3 Adverse reaction unit costs and resource use** 

The health effects of TEAEs were modelled via the incidence of grade 3-4 AEs; those occurring at a frequency of ≥5% in either treatment arm were included in the evaluation as they are likely to be associated with costs that affect decision making. ## **3.5.4 Miscellaneous unit costs and resource use** 

The approach to end-of-life costs was aligned with TA730 and TA488.[7,128] The introduction of end-of-life costs does not affect undiscounted model outcomes as the model effectively has a lifetime time horizon. All patients have died in both arms by the time horizon, so the total undiscounted cost associated with end-of-life care is identical for each arm. The costs associated with end-of-life care are relevant to discounted model outcomes when mortality differs between arms, since a larger proportion of end-of-life costs are incurred later in the arm with lower mortality. To capture this, end-of-life costs were incorporated into the cost-effectiveness model.[139 ] 

End-of-life costs were taken from NICE TA488 and inflated to 2024 prices using HCHS/NHSCII indices.[140] The original cost was taken from the study of Abel et al. ## **3.6 Severity** 

Patients with advanced GIST previously treated with three or more TKIs (Section 3.3) are anticipated to experience an additional 0.247 QALYs on BSC (over a period of 0.375 life years and based on a log-logistic model of OS in INVICTUS). This would correspond to a 98.0% proportional shortfall vs an age- and sex-matched UK population, who would be anticipated to experience an average of 12.68 QALYs based Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 144 of 181 



<!-- page 147 -->

on an adjusted, limited-dependent, variable mixture model (ALDVMM) of 2014 HSE data (Hernandez-Alava et al.; the York QALY Shortfall Calculator reference case). Table 51 and 52 present key features and inputs of the QALY shortfall analysis. 

Sensitivity analyses around general population estimates (using: EQ-5D-5L to EQ-5D-3L mapping from Hernandez-Alava et al. with HSE 2017-18 data; EQ-5D-5L to EQ-5D-3L mapping from van Hout et al. with HSE 2017-18 data; and a health state profile-based model using the 1995 Measurement and Valuation of Health [MVH] Report) showed that no general population estimates would yield less than a 98.0% proportional shortfall in patients with advanced GIST receiving BSC after three or more TKIs (Table 53).[119,143] 

Sensitivity analyses around alternative survival distributions (exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log logistic, and generalised gamma) to model INVICTUS BSC data showed only small differences in estimated QALY gain (0.18-0.24 QALYs; Table 53). Sensitivity analyses incorporating different patient characteristics were conducted in two alternative populations of patients with advanced GIST from the GRID trial and Bulusu et al.[41,91] 

Ripretinib would therefore be eligible for a 1.7x QALY weight based on the proportional shortfall rule, and analyses of this appear robust to changes in both the general population, BSC QALY estimates, and GIST population characteristics.

## **3.7 Uncertainty** 

Ripretinib was granted orphan marketing authorisation by the MHRA, with advanced GIST being rare with a prevalence of less than 3 in 10,000 people.[22] In the UK, the eligible population for ripretinib will be approximately 173 patients. The sample size of INVICTUS (n=129) may be considered small relative to other indications and this may be the cause of uncertainties in the data. However, relative to other pivotal RCTs in this patient population (regorafenib GRID trial, n=199) and given the prevalence of the disease, the sample size of INVICTUS is considered appropriate for decision-making.[8] 

There is considerable uncertainty around the clinical effects of ripretinib BID dosing and likely utilisation in UK clinical practice. As ripretinib is the last-line treatment for this patient population, dose escalation was offered at disease progression to enable patients to have a treatment option beyond ripretinib QD. IPDE was seen in 44 of the 85 patients randomly assigned to ripretinib (15 January 2021 data cut).[74] The base case analysis assumes that ripretinib will only be used within the licensed indication and in line with the licensed dose of 150 mg QD. However, the extent of usage outside of the licensed dose that may occur in routine clinical practice, and what the clinical outcomes with such use would be, is a source of uncertainty. Clinicians stated that in a scenario where BID dosing was routinely commissioned, IPDE would occur in 

Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 147 of 181 



<!-- page 150 -->

approximately 40% of all patients starting ripretinib which is lower than the 52% in INVICTUS.[38] This would be expected as the tolerability for BID dosing would probably be lower in routine clinical practice, given the strict inclusion criteria for INVICTUS resulting in a population that is often fitter than that in routine clinical practice.

## **3.11 Exploring uncertainty** 

## **3.11.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

Probabilistic sensitivity analyses (PSAs) were conducted to explore the impact of model parameter uncertainty on the results. Ten thousand simulations were performed, which combined give a distribution of incremental results and consequently an assessment of the robustness of the cost-effectiveness results. PFS and OS remain independent within the PSA as per a standard PSM. For gender proportions, event rates, compliance, relative dose intensity and utilities, a beta distribution was used to restrict draws to between 0 and 1. For costs, a gamma distribution was fitted to prevent values less than zero. Treatment costs remained fixed. 

Total costs, QALYs and the incremental cost per QALY gained with ripretinib versus BSC are presented in Table 58. An incremental cost-effectiveness plane scatter plot, cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, and cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier were produced to graphically illustrate the level of variability and uncertainty in the results, as shown in Figure 33, Figure 34, and Figure 35 respectively. In the PSA, all results fell in the northeast quadrant of the cost-effectiveness plane, representing increased costs and quality-adjusted life expectancy with ripretinib versus BSC. At a willingness-to-pay threshold of £30,000 per QALY, there was a 57.2% likelihood of ripretinib being cost-effective versus BSC. Variation between deterministic and probabilistic analyses was minimal, with the ICER only differing by £757 per QALY (£29,593 per QALY in the probabilistic sensitivity analysis versus £28,836 per QALY in the deterministic base case).

## **3.11.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

Deterministic one-way sensitivity analysis (OWSA) was conducted to explore the degree of uncertainty in the model results arising from variation in individual model parameters. The OWSA was conducted by allocating a ‘low’ and a ‘high’ value to each parameter; where confidence intervals were available, the low value was the lower bound and the high value was the upper bound of the 95% CI; in the absence of CI data, variable was altered by +/- 20%. A tornado diagram presenting the 15 most sensitive parameters is presented in Figure 36, with tabulated results in Table 59. The model was most sensitive to the PDOff health state utility value, which resulted in an increase in ICER to £31,865 per QALY at the lower bound, and a reduction in ICER to £26,333 per QALY at the upper bound. This is because patients remain in the off-treatment PD partition for considerably longer (XXX years vs XXX years in the on-treatment partition in the base case analysis). PDOff therefore has a substantial effect on QALY estimates in the ripretinib arm, particularly as the PDOff utility has no influence on the BSC arm.

Of the scenario analyses in Table 60, the approaches to modelling OS have the largest influence on ICER. Removing any adjustment to OS for crossover from BSC to ripretinib has the largest effect on the ICER, increasing it to £43,575 per QALY. Switching the OS model in both arms to use Weibull or exponential distributions (and retaining the base case crossover adjustment) increases the ICER to £37,602 per QALY and £37,434 per QALY, respectively; neither distribution was adopted in the base case analysis owing to poorer goodness-of-fit to the data than the log-logistic distribution in both treatment arms and by both measures (AIC and BIC). Furthermore, the predicted 10-year survival with these curves was deemed too low given the 10-year survival data for other TKIs in advanced GIST. Conversely, switching the OS model to use the Gompertz distribution reduces the ICER by £2,589 per QALY from the base case to £26,247 per QALY. Across all scenarios, 21 yielded ICERs that fell below a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY, while 9 yielded ICERs above a £30,000 per QALY threshold. 

Scenarios in which alternative utility values were employed all yielded ICERs below a £30,000 per QALY threshold, including an analysis that assumed no utility benefit of staying on treatment after progression. This latter scenario was not adopted in the base case as it is contrary to the utility values observed in INVICTUS in patients with progressed disease receiving treatment versus those not receiving treatment (0.699 versus 0.624, respectively). Correspondingly, maintenance of HRQoL (median TUDD) was longer than median PFS in INVICTUS. Clinicians validated this assumption, noting that patients with disease progression receiving ripretinib would be closer in terms of HRQoL to those in the progression-free state than those who have progressed and are no longer on active treatment. 

All approaches to adjusting for IPDE had a relatively modest effect on the ICER. In the case of the two-stage adjustment and time-varying Cox proportional hazards model, this was likely driven by a relatively limited exposure to the elevated mortality hazard (i.e. in the on-treatment PD state only). The effect in the two open-label BID vs QD analyses was driven by different mortality hazard trajectories over time; patients in the ‘non-progressors + IPDE progressors’ analysis had a lower mortality risk than ‘non-progressors + QD progressors’ early in the analysis; this increased to higher than Company evidence submission template for ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496] 

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 164 of 181 



<!-- page 167 -->

the QD progressors group later in the analysis, ultimately yielding very similar ICERs (£31,371 per QALY in ‘non-progressors + IPDE progressors’ vs £30,142 per QALY in ‘non-progressors + QD progressors’). An analysis was requested during a NHS Commercial Surgery in which 50% of patients in the on-treatment progressed disease partition incurred the cost of BID ripretinib yields an ICER of £32,671 per QALY gained; however, this approach deviates from the licensed ripretinib dose of 150 mg QD and was therefore not adopted in the base case. Clinicians agreed this approach reflects a scenario where BID is routinely commissioned and, if so, they expected 50% of patients who progressed on ripretinib (40% of the total population to initiate ripretinib) to dose escalate. 

## **3.12 Subgroup analysis** 

Patients with advanced GIST who have had at least 3 prior therapies, including imatinib, or have documented intolerance to these treatments comprise a small population with high unmet need. As such, further subgroup analyses have not been performed. 

## **3.13 Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation** 

The health economic analysis did not capture potential effects of the burden of advanced GIST on caregivers or of death of the patient and bereavement on caregiver and family quality of life. Data to inform on such analyses are not available but such effects are likely to exist though are not currently quantifiable. The maintenance of patients’ HRQoL, including physical and role function, while receiving ripretinib suggests a potential reduction in dependence on carers, thereby also improving carer QoL. 

The effect of having an additional line of therapy available after regorafenib on patient QoL was also not captured due to a lack of suitable data. Having an additional therapy line would give patients hope that they can live a somewhat normal life for longer than currently possible. Hope is a factor that does not come into consideration in traditional health technology assessments (HTA); however, an ISPOR taskforce found that it has

© Deciphera Pharmaceuticals (2025). All rights reserved                     Page 165 of 181 



<!-- page 168 -->

positive value, and although difficult to quantify should be considered by HTA authorities.[144 ] 

## **3.14 Validation** 

## **Validation of cost-effectiveness analysis** 

A two-stage quality control (QC) process was used during development of the cost-effectiveness model. The first QC occurred after an empty model was constructed with dummy placeholder data and was intended to: test the structure of the model; ensure that core calculations such as background mortality were correct; and confirm that no naming errors or common Excel formula errors were present. The second QC process occurred on model completion when it was put through a number of ‘binary tests’, whereby key variables are set to zero and results checked for face validity. The model also underwent a second structural test to ensure that calculations and formulae were correct. A final face validity check ensured that the context in which the variables were used was clinically and theoretically sound. The process of QC was conducted by an experienced modeller who was not the original model builder, with findings recorded against a QC checklist. The document was passed to the modelling team who implemented the QC recommendations, recording their agreement/disagreement. Where disagreement existed, the project director ensured third-party consensus resolution. 

INVICTUS is the largest mature dataset currently available informing on patients treated with ripretinib. At the 15 January 2021 data cut utilised in the model, 54% (n=46/85) of patients in the ripretinib group and 82% (n=36/44) of patients in the placebo group had died.[23] External validation of the intervention in a comparable patient population is challenging given the rarity of the disease and lack of active comparators; however, the Royal Marsden Expanded Access Program (Section 2.6) reported a median OS of 14.0 months (95% CI 9.9 to NA months) compared with the 18.2 months (95% CI 13.1 to 30.7 months) in INVICTUS.[69] Data from other studies in the advanced GIST setting are available (A618-1004 [sunitinib] and GRID [regorafenib]), these studies were conducted in earlier lines of therapy and do not include ripretinib treatment arms to validate the extrapolation.[8,145]

Opinion from an expert in crossover adjustment was sought to identify the most appropriate method to adjust for patients crossing over following disease progression, from BSC to the ripretinib. It was deemed that the two-stage approach using the time of progression as the secondary baseline was most appropriate to adjust for crossover. In TA488, the ERG deemed the switching analyses results to be generally robust to the choice of method and were satisfied with the approach taken.[101 ] 

UK clinician advisory boards including specialists in the treatment of GIST were conducted to validate specific modelling inputs and assumptions including: OS crossover adjustment and extrapolation (including the effect of dose escalation); composite PFS and TTD extrapolation; appropriate comparator therapy; treatment beyond progression; utility values; and subsequent treatment. 

## **3.15 Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence** 

In the base-case analysis, ripretinib generates 2.962 incremental QALYs and XXX incremental costs over a 40-year time horizon compared with BSC, resulting in an ICER of £28,836 per QALY gained including the PAS discount and using a 1.7 severity weighting for QALY calculations. At a willingness-to-pay threshold of £30,000 per QALY, there was a 57.2% likelihood of ripretinib being cost-effective vs BSC. Variation between deterministic and probabilistic analyses was minimal, with the ICER only differing by £757 per QALY. The model was most sensitive to the PDOff health state utility value, which resulted in an increase in ICER to £31,865 per QALY at the lower bound, and a reduction in ICER to £26,333 per QALY at the upper bound. However, scenario analyses varying utility values indicated minimal impact on the ICER. Key areas of uncertainty identified by the scenario analyses are the approaches to modelling OS and the impact of BID on clinical outcomes and cost. This is not unexpected given the limitations in data in these areas and highlight the main limitations in the model analysis. In particular, several statistical methods were explored to quantify the uncertainty around the effect of IPDE on OS, but gave contradictory results. However, incorporation of outcomes from the various approaches into the model yielded ICERs that were relatively consistent. Finally, the base case assumptions were validated externally through clinician advisory boards to

ensure they were clinically plausible and would represent UK clinical practice as closely as possible. 

This economic analysis is highly relevant to clinical practice in England: all unit costs were identified from UK-specific sources; INVICTUS included ten patients from the UK; and clinicians were supportive of the applicability of INVICTUS data to a UK population with advanced GIST. The main strength of the analysis was the use of a single, homogeneous data source as the basis of modelling the three main clinical endpoints in the model: progression, treatment discontinuation after progression, and death. 

In conclusion, based on this analysis (incorporating a 1.7x severity multiplier based on the proportional QALY shortfall in the BSC population versus the general population), ripretinib represents a cost-effective option relative to BSC for the treatment of patients in England with advanced GIST who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors, including imatinib.

## **Summary of Information for Patients (SIP):** 

## **The pharmaceutical company perspective** 

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from NICE for their treatment to be sold to the NHS for use in England.  It is a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation.  It is not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to doublecheck for marketing and promotional content before it is sent to you. 

The **Summary of Information for Patients** template has been adapted for use at NICE from the – Health Technology Assessment International Patient & Citizens Involvement Group (HTAi PCIG). Information about the development is available in an open-access IJTAHC journal article 

## **SECTION 1: Submission summary** 

**1a) Name of the medicine** (generic and brand name): 

Ripretinib (Qinlock[®] ) 

**1b) Population this treatment will be used by.** Please outline the main patient population that is being appraised by NICE: 

QINLOCK is used to treat adults with gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), a rare type of cancer of the digestive system including the stomach and bowel, that has: 

- spread to other parts of the body or cannot be removed by surgery 

- been treated with at least 3 previous cancer medicines, including imatinib.

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) are rare cancers that develop in the digestive system. Most GISTs start in the stomach or small bowel, but they can develop anywhere along the length of the digestive system (gastrointestinal tract). For example, they may also start in the gullet (oesophagus) or the back passage (rectum).[1,2] Most GISTs are usually caused by alterations in the proto-oncogene c-KIT (KIT) or the platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRA) gene. These alterations allow the tumour cells to grow.[3] 

There are around 900 new cases of GIST each year in the UK.[4] GISTs are most common in people aged 60 to 65. As GIST progresses, it can cause serious symptoms. The symptoms depend on the size of the tumour and where it is in the digestive system and so vary from person to person. Symptoms may include: discomfort or pain in the tummy (abdomen), blood in your poo (stools) or vomit, weight loss for no obvious reason, feeling tired and weak[2] . 

One of the key factors in determining the outlook for GIST cancer is the stage at which it is diagnosed. For patients with advanced GIST, the chance of being alive at 5 years after diagnosis is 53%.[5] 

People living with advanced GIST often experience a considerable impact on their daily lives, affecting their work, relationships, and ability to carry out everyday activities.[8] As the disease worsens, people may experience a sharp decline in their quality of life, including mental and social difficulties.[9] Additionally, the side effects of current treatment can make day-to-day activities challenging.[10] 

GIST can have an impact on family members, friends, and caregivers, too. Caregivers often handle many tasks: giving emotional support, cooking, cleaning, driving to appointments, helping with medicines, and sorting out bills. They may also help you dress, bathe, and stay connected with friends and family. Caregiving can be a difficult and consuming job.[11] 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

If your GP suspects you have GIST, they will refer to a specialist doctor for further testing. The primary tests to confirm a diagnosis of GIST include imaging scans, such as a computed tomography (CT) scan, and through a tissue sample (biopsy). A firm diagnosis of GIST can only be made by a pathologist looking at the tumour tissue with a microscope. Hence, there needs to be a tissue sample. A biopsy may be done endoscopically using an instrument passed into the stomach or intestines through the mouth, or anus. 

The diagnosis of GIST is confirmed if: 

- A tumour is identified in the gastrointestinal tract 

   - Imaging tests reveal the presence of a tumour in the stomach, small intestine, or other parts of the gastrointestinal tract 

- The cells of tumour carry specific markers 



<!-- page 187 -->

   - A biopsy is performed to confirm the tumour type. The tumour cells are analysed for markers, such as CD117 and DOG1, which are commonly present in GISTs 

- Genetic changes indicate GIST 

   - The laboratory will also test cells from the biopsy or surgery to look for genetic changes in the tumour cells. These changes are called mutations. Finding a positive c-KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA enzyme receptor abnormality can confirm a diagnosis of GIST[4,12] 

No additional diagnostic tests will be required to identify patients for treatment with ripretinib. 

## **2c) Current treatment options:** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

• What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines.  It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. 

- Please also consider: 

   - if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 

   - are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

Advanced GIST is considered a chronic cancer, meaning the tumours may never fully disappear. Patients often require ongoing treatment to control the disease over time. Most GISTs (around 85%) have a mutation in a protein called KIT, which causes the cancer cells to grow and divide continuously. Targeted therapy drugs, known as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), are used to block these signals.[2] 

The standard first-line treatment for GIST is imatinib. If this becomes ineffective or causes significant side effects, patients may receive second-line therapy with sunitinib, followed by thirdline therapy with regorafenib.[13] 

Current treatment pathway for advanced GIST (first-line to fourth-line): 

**==> picture [427 x 43] intentionally omitted <==**

Source: Judson I et al. 2017.[12] 

Some types of GIST do not respond well to imatinib, and over time, the cancer cells can change (mutate) in ways that help them avoid the effects of treatment. This is known as becoming resistant, meaning the treatment no longer works as well. As a result, the tumour may start to grow again. 

## **Beyond third-line treatment: Best supportive care (BSC)** 

There are no recommended drugs available after regorafenib. For patients who are no longer receiving benefit from regorafenib, they are offered BSC. This care focuses on easing symptoms, managing side effects, and preserving the best possible quality of life. This may include the use of pain relievers, anti-nausea medications, and other supportive therapies.[14-17] Patients are 



<!-- page 188 -->

recommended to try and enrol in clinical trials if possible.[6] Ripretinib would be positioned as a fourth-line treatment option, offering a further targeted drug option before BSC.

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

**Context:** 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

## **Sarcoma UK insights** 

Sarcoma UK reports that once patients with GIST have exhausted current treatment options, they may have "on average just weeks to live" if no further therapy is available, highlighting a critical unmet need.[18] 

The 2020 National Sarcoma Patient Survey had 1,117 responses including patient, family and carers. Of these, 14% of the responses concerned GIST. The aim of the survey was to understand the patient, family and carer experience of living with sarcoma. The survey found that 95% of patients with GIST reported negative mental health effects related to their diagnosis and treatment, with many also experiencing isolation, anxiety, and sadness. Furthermore, patients with GIST were reported to be the least likely amongst sarcoma patients to receive the emotional support they needed, possibly due to the rarity of the disease.[19] 

The survey also reported, more than half of carers of patients with GIST had to stop working or studying, either temporarily or permanently. Every carer also reported feeling frequently or constantly anxious or depressed since the patient’s GIST diagnosis highlighting the immense impact advanced GIST has on caregivers and family.[19] 

## **Life Raft Group Canada (LRGC) insights** 

The LRGC conducted 11 interviews with patients with metastatic GIST to capture the real-world experiences of those undergoing treatment. These interviews revealed that patients experience a wide range of severe side effects from imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib, with 39 distinct side effects identified across these treatments. Patients described "horrible" effects from imatinib such as uncontrollable diarrhoea, swelling, cramps, and chronic pain that significantly compromised their quality of life. Similarly, sunitinib was described as "extremely toxic... I had really bad diarrhoea constantly... wicked foot blisters that made it hard to walk. I couldn’t walk. It was so bad." These firsthand accounts emphasise the challenge of daily life on GIST treatments, despite their role in extending survival.[20] 

## **Patient input from first NICE technology appraisal** 

Patients highlighted the improved side effect profile of ripretinib in comparison to previous therapies. One patient shared: “Ripretinib is better than regorafenib because the side effects are 



<!-- page 189 -->

more manageable. I had to take regorafenib for three weeks then have a week off, and by week three the PPE [palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia] and diarrhoea side effects were so severe I was able to do very little other than rest with my feet raised.” 

Patients have also reported that whilst using ripretinib they are able to maintain a normal life, continuing to work, travel, and exercise. They emphasise the importance of these activities, as it allows them to lead their lives, rather than feeling defined solely by their cancer.[9] 

## **SECTION 3: The treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work?** 

What are the important features of this treatment? 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body 

Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a summary of product characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

Current therapies (imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib) are all tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and they work by blocking the KIT and PDGFRA receptor proteins on the surface of GIST cancer cells. These receptors normally control cell growth, but when they become altered (mutated) they drive uncontrolled cell multiplication leading to the development of tumours. TKIs help to keep these mutated proteins turned off by blocking them. Unfortunately, we now know that GIST cells quite often mutate again and find a way round the block meaning the tumour can start to grow again.[3,13] 

Ripretinib works differently compared with previous TKIs and binds to a different place on the protein than other TKIs. This means that for patients where imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib have become ineffective, ripretinib may still work and can improve survival. Ripretinib offers patients with GIST an effective fourth-line treatment that can work even for tumours that have many mutations that make them resistant to the other TKIs.[21-23] 

Links: Summary of Product Characteristics and Patient Information Leaflet 

## **3b) Combinations with other medicines** 

Is the medicine intended to be used in combination with any other medicines? 

• Yes / No 

If yes, please explain why and how the medicines work together. Please outline the mechanism of action of those other medicines so it is clear to patients why they are used together. 

If yes, please also provide information on the availability of the other medicine(s) as well as the main side effects.

## **3c) Administration and dosing** 

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. 

How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? 

Ripretinib will be prescribed for you by a doctor experienced in using anticancer therapies. 

The recommended daily dose is **three 50 mg tablets** (150 mg) once daily. 

**Take** the tablets at the **same time each day** with or without food. Swallow the tablets whole with a glass of water and do not chew, split, or crush the tablets. Do not take any tablets that are broken, cracked, or otherwise damaged due to unknown effects of taking tablet that are not whole. 

If you have to take certain other medicines at the same time as ripretinib, your doctor may change your dose to three 50 mg tablets (150 mg) twice daily. 

You will usually take ripretinib as long as you are benefitting from it and not suffering unacceptable side effects; however, your doctor may reduce your dose or may decide to interrupt or stop the treatment temporarily or permanently if necessary. 

If you have liver or kidney problems 

- While you are being treated with ripretinib, your doctor will monitor your liver or kidney function more closely. 

If you take more ripretinib than you should 

- If you have accidentally taken too many tablets, **seek urgent medical attention.** 

If you forget to take ripretinib 

- What to do if you forget to take this medicine, depends on when you remember the dose that has been forgotten. If it is: 

   - 8 hours or less (4 hours or less for 150 mg twice per day doses) after the time it should have been taken, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. Then take the next dose as usual. 

   - more than 8 hours after (more than 4 hours for 150 mg twice per day doses) the time it should have been taken, skip the missed dose. Then take the next dose at the usual time. 

   - Do not take a double dose to make up a forgotten dose. 

## If you are sick when taking ripretinib 

- If you are sick (vomiting) after taking this medicine, do not take an additional dose, but carry on as normal. Take your next dose of tablets the next day at the usual time and tell your doctor you have been sick. 

If you have any further questions on the use of this medicine, ask your doctor.

## **INVICTUS** 

The INVICTUS study investigated ripretinib as a treatment for patients with advanced GIST who needed a fourth (or greater) line of therapy. 

The main aim of the study was to see if treatment with ripretinib could affect tumour growth and extend survival time compared with placebo treatment (a pill with no active ingredient).[13,17] 

## Study characteristics:

|Population|Adult patients with advanced GIST who had progressed on or were intolerant<br>to imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib|
|Patient group<br>size|129 participants<br>•<br>85 patients in the ripretinib arm<br>•<br>44 patients in the placebo arm|
|Intervention|Ripretinib + best supportive care|
|Comparators|Placebo + best supportive care|
|Key inclusion<br>criteria|•<br>Males or females ≥18 years<br>•<br>Confirmed diagnosis of<br>GIST<br>•<br>Patients must have<br>progressed on imatinib,<br>sunitinib, and regorafenib<br>or have documented<br>intolerance to any of these<br>TKIs<br>•<br>At least 1 measurable tumour<br>•<br>Adequate organ function and<br>bone marrow reserve<br>•<br>An Eastern Cooperative<br>Oncology Group (ECOG) score<br>of 0–2: this measures how the<br>disease impacts daily living;<br>scores range from 0 (fully<br>active with no restrictions) to 5<br>(dead)|
|Key exclusion<br>criteria|Patients who received anticancer therapy within 14 days prior to the study|

## **Key efficacy outcomes (to determine how ripretinib effects tumour growth)** 

- Progression-free survival (PFS): How long people were able to live their daily lives before a scan showed the tumour had started growing/worsening again or before they died 

- Overall survival (OS): How long people stayed alive after joining the study 

- Objective response rate (ORR): How many patients responded to the treatment, this includes:[17] 

   - Complete response - all signs of cancer have disappeared 

   - Partial response - a reduction in the size of the tumour 

- Rate of stable disease (SD): How many patients experienced no change in the size of tumour 

## **Quality of life assessments (to determine how well patients feel when they take ripretinib)** 

The study also measured health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using the following questionnaires 



<!-- page 192 -->

which patients answered throughout the study: 

- EORTC QLQ-C30 - assesses physical and role functioning in patients with cancer specifically 

- EQ-5D-5L – measures general health status 

- EQ-VAS - measures general health status.[24] 

## **Safety assessment (to determine how safe ripretinib is for patients):** included the number of side 

effects (adverse events [AEs]) and any side effects that led to dose reduction, treatment interruption, or discontinuation.[17,22] 

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

## **Key findings from INVICTUS** 

## - Progression Free Survival (PFS) 

The main goal of the INVICTUS study was to measure how long patients lived without their disease getting worse, or before dying. 

- Half of the participants receiving ripretinib survived for 6.3 months or longer before their cancer got worse, compared with 1.0 month or longer for participants receiving placebo[13,17] 

## Objective Response Rate (ORR) 

This measures how many patients responded to the treatment. This endpoint shows how effective the treatment is in reducing or eliminating tumours. 

- Of the 85 participants receiving ripretinib, 8 had partial responses – meaning that the size of their tumor was reduced by 30% or more (as defined in a set of rules called modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors [mRECIST]). No participants in the placebo arm had partial response. 

- After the responses were analysed, they were not considered statistically conclusive. 

- More importantly for patients and clinicians is the stable disease (SD) rate, as SD is known to predict survival. At 6 weeks, 66% of ripretinib-treated patients experienced SD, which remained at 47% at 12 weeks, in contrast to 20% and 5% in the placebo group, respectively. 

- This shows that ripretinib is more effective at controlling the disease.[13,17] 

## Overall Survival (OS) 

This measures how long patients lived after starting treatment. 

- Half of the participants receiving ripretinib survived overall for 18.2 months or longer from the start of therapy, compared with 6.3 months or longer for participants receiving placebo; this included participants on placebo who were permitted to take ripretinib when their disease worsened.[22] 

## Limitations 

- Some patients who initially started on placebo, started to take ripretinib after their disease had worsened. This means that the survival in the placebo arm may be overestimated given the benefit some of these patients likely received from ripretinib. 



<!-- page 193 -->

- When disease worsened, some patients started to take ripretinib at a double dose. This dose is not included in the marketing authorisation and may have impacted the survival demonstrated in the ripretinib arm. However, clinicians agree that the extent of the effect of the double dose on how long patients live is uncertain.[15] 

## **3f) Quality of life impact of the medicine and patient preference information** 

What is the clinical evidence for a potential impact of this medicine on the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers? What quality of life instrument was used? If the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D) was used does it sufficiently capture quality of life for this condition? Are there other disease specific quality of life measures that should also be considered as supplementary information? 

Please outline in plain language any quality of life related data such as **patient reported outcomes (PROs).** 

Please include any **patient preference information (PPI)** relating to the drug profile, for instance research to understand willingness to accept the risk of side effects given the added benefit of treatment. Please include all references as required. 

## **Quality of life in the INVICTUS trial** 

On questionnaires that investigated quality of life, participants receiving ripretinib had stable scores up to treatment cycle 10 of treatment, while participants receiving placebo reported a decline in quality of life. 

- These questionnaires included evaluations of physical function, everyday capabilities, and patient perceptions of their overall health and quality of life. 

Across individual questionnaires, as measured from the start of treatment to the start of Cycle 2, ripretinib resulted in improved scores (a higher score means patients perceived their overall health and quality of life to be better) whereas scores in participants receiving placebo declined:[24] 

- Overall health (EQ-5D-5L VAS): Ripretinib improved scores by an average **+3.7 points** , whereas placebo fell **-8.9 points** 

- Physical abilities (QLQ-C30 physical function): Ripretinib improved scores by an average **+1.6 points** , whereas placebo fell **-8.9 points** 

- Everyday roles at work, home and socially (QLQ-C30 role function): Ripretinib improved scores by an average **+3.5 points** , whereas placebo fell **-17.1 points** .[24] 

Importantly, participants receiving ripretinib had a stable quality of life for about 8 months, whereas it began to drop after only 1 month on placebo.[24] Moreover, participants maintained HRQoL even when their disease worsened when receiving ripretinib. This underscores ripretinib’s ability to preserve everyday functioning.[25,26] 

Participant who experienced hair loss (a common side effect of ripretinib) reported HRQoL scores that were comparable or slightly better to those of participants who did not, indicating that patients receiving ripretinib were not negatively impacted by this side effect.[22,27] 

## **Conclusion** 

Collectively, these findings show that ripretinib can not only prolong survival but also enable patients with advanced GIST to preserve their HRQoL for longer. 

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had 



<!-- page 194 -->

treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

Ripretinib therapy is associated with some treatment-emergent side effects that are generally well controlled. Of patients receiving ripretinib in the INVICTUS trial, 5% discontinued ripretinib treatment due to side effects (vs. 2% in the placebo group).[17] 

Clinicians have noted that ripretinib’s side effects are generally mild to moderate and can be largely managed within specialist GIST/sarcoma clinics.[9] 

## **Common side effects** 

The most common side effects of ripretinib, based on the INVICTUS trial:

|Muscle aches/pain (myalgia)|27%|9%|
|Nausea (feeling sick)|25%|2%|

## **Managing side effects** 

Interrupting treatment or reducing the dose may be necessary for some patients who experience side effects. If required, the recommended dose reduction is to 100 mg of ripretinib taken orally, once a day. If a patient cannot tolerate 100 mg per day, treatment should be permanently discontinued. 

## **Serious side effects** 

Seek urgent medical attention if you experience any of the following serious side effects: 

## 1. Skin problems (called PPES) 

- PPES is a very common side effect when taking this medicine. If you develop: redness, pain, swelling, or blisters on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet, your doctor may continue your treatment, change your dose or stop your treatment until your condition improves. 

## 2. High blood pressure 

- High blood pressure is a very common side effect when taking this medicine. If you develop: headache, feeling of light-headedness, or dizziness, these may be symptoms of high blood pressure, your doctor may change your dose or stop your treatment until your condition improves. 

## 3. Heart problems (heart failure) 

- Heart failure is a common side effect when taking this medicine. If you feel: very tired, are short of breath, have swollen feet and/or ankles, these may be symptoms of heart problems. 

Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you experience: 



<!-- page 195 -->

## 4. Skin cancer 

- Treatment with ripretinib may result in certain types of skin cancer such as ‘cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma’ and ‘melanoma’. Tell your doctor if you notice any skin changes during treatment including a new wart, open sore or reddish bump that bleeds or does not heal, or a change in size or colour of a mole. Your doctor will check your skin when starting treatment with ripretinib and routinely during treatment. 

## **Conclusion** 

Overall, ripretinib offers a manageable safety profile, with side effects that can typically be addressed through dose adjustments. Monitoring and managing these side effects effectively means most patients can continue benefiting from treatment whilst minimising discomfort. 

Further information can be found in the ripretinib Summary of Product Characteristics and the Patient Information Leaflet. 

## **3h) Summary of key benefits of treatment for patients** 

Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key benefits of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. 

- Please include benefits related to the mode of action, effectiveness, safety and mode of administration 

## **Key benefits for patients** 

The results of INVICTUS showed that ripretinib provides a viable treatment option for patients with GIST who have already tried 3 or more different therapies. Ripretinib can potentially extend the time before a patients cancer gets worse and can improve survival compared to placebo.[13,22] 

Despite advanced disease, ripretinib may allow patients to maintain their quality of life and functional status over a period of approximately 8 months, compared to the rapid decline seen in patients on placebo after just 1 month.[24] 

Ripretinib has a manageable safety profile for patients. Common adverse effects include alopecia, muscle aches/pains, nausea, and tiredness.[17] 

Administered as once-daily oral tablets, ripretinib is easy for patients to incorporate into their daily routines. 

## **Key benefits for caregivers and the community** 

Ripretinib has the potential to alleviate the emotional, financial and social burden on caregivers and their communities. Ripretinib’s ability to extend survival without compromising the patient’s well-being can reduce caregivers’ fear and worry related to disease progression. Moreover, as ripretinib preserves functional status and maintains quality of life, it may reduce the need for intensive support, such as assistance with daily activities, and help patients regain some independence and as well as relieving caregivers of some of that responsibility.[9,24] 

## **Conclusion** 

Overall, ripretinib provides a much-needed further option for patients who have progressed on three previous lines of therapy. The introduction of ripretinib would offer hope to patients, carers and their communities.
