## **3i) Summary of key disadvantages of treatment for patients** 

Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key disadvantages of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. Which disadvantages are most important to patients and carers? 

- Please include disadvantages related to the mode of action, effectiveness, side effects and mode of administration 

- What is the impact of any disadvantages highlighted compared with current treatments 

## **Key considerations for patients** 

Like most cancer treatments, ripretinib can cause side effects. Whilst these are generally mild to moderate, they can still impact patients’ day-to-day lives. Common side effects include alopecia, myalgia, nausea, fatigue and diarrhoea.[17] 

In some cases, patients may need to adjust their dosage due to side effects, which may require regular monitoring and consultation with their healthcare team. This can add complexity to the treatment and may cause some uncertainty for patients. 

## **Key considerations for caregivers and the community** 

Although ripretinib has a manageable safety profile, caregivers may still need to assist with managing any side effects. The emotional and physical burden of caring for a patient experiencing these side effects may still be significant. 

## **3j) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

## **How the model reflects the condition** 

This model calculates the additional cost of one healthcare intervention (ripretinib) compared to another (BSC), for a corresponding increase in health benefit. The model development was guided by clinical and health economic experts, ensuring its relevance and alignment with UK clinical practice for patients with advanced GIST after progression on three or more TKIs.[6] The clinical benefits reflect those demonstrated in INVICTUS while the costs represent the average costs incurred to NHS England (NHSE) during the care of this patients with GIST. 

**Model structure** 

The model reflects how a patient disease progresses through different disease-related health 



<!-- page 197 -->

states. Health states represent the level of health and well-being of the patient at that point in time, informed by INVICTUS HRQoL data. Each health state is also associated with a different level of costs, informed by NHSE service costs. The amount of time a patient spends in each state is driven by data from INVICTUS. 

The three key disease-related health states are: 

1. Progression-Free (PF) – patients are alive without experiencing disease worsening on the current line of treatment 

2. Progressed Disease (PD) – patients are alive but have experienced disease worsening on the current line of treatment 

3. Death. 

## **Modelling the impact of ripretinib on survival** 

Ripretinib is expected to extend survival by delaying disease worsening. The model estimates that ripretinib increases a patient’s life expectancy by approximately 2.7 years compared to BSC alone. This reflects the significant survival benefits of ripretinib vs placebo observed in INVICTUS.[17,22] 

## **Modelling quality of life improvements** 

The HRQoL improvements with ripretinib were measured using EQ-5D-5L data from the INVICTUS trial. HRQoL was incorporated into the model through quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). 

_* A QALY, or quality-adjusted life year, is a way of measuring both how long someone lives and how good their health is during that time—one QALY means one year of life in perfect health._ 

The model estimates that 3 QALYs per patient are gained with ripretinib compared to BSC alone. This reflects the ability of ripretinib to maintain patient HRQoL for an extended period compared to BSC, even after disease worsening, as demonstrated in INVICTUS.[22,24] 

## **Modelling treatment costs** 

The model includes all relevant costs associated with ripretinib treatment, including the drug cost, disease management costs, and costs associated with side effects. Ripretinib is estimated to cost an additional £85,414 per patient compared to BSC alone. 

## **Exploring uncertainty in the model** 

To understand the uncertainties in the model results, different scenarios and sensitivity analyses are undertaken. In these instances, the values of different inputs are varied to reflect the uncertainty in the estimate e.g., healthcare costs, health state values, and long-term survival predictions. 

## **Additional considerations** 

NICE has introduced a tool called the severity modifier which NICE allows to increase the QALYs for drugs used to treat severe diseases.[28] This model increases the QALYs above by 1.7 times, reflecting the severe and life-limiting nature of advanced GIST.[28] 

The QALY calculation may not fully capture the QoL benefits associated with the use of ripretinib for patients with advanced GIST as the model does not capture the impact of ripretinib on caregivers’ QoL. 

## **3k) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see section 3f) 

**Innovation** 



<!-- page 198 -->

There are currently no approved treatments in the UK for patients with advanced GIST whose disease continues to progress or who cannot tolerate third-line regorafenib.[6] This creates a significant unmet need, which ripretinib can help address. 

Ripretinib is an innovative treatment offering clinicians and patients a new treatment option when other treatments become ineffective in the management of GIST. Ripretinib was developed for patients with advanced GIST for whom other TKIs have become ineffective meaning it may still inhibit cancer cell growth when other TKI treatments cannot. 

Clinicians and patients agree on the innovative nature of ripretinib: 

- Patient expert statement from NICE ID3805 (TA881)[9] : _“The opportunity to use ripretinib, a drug specifically designed to target the newly developed mutations and prolong life is amazing.”_ 

- Clinicians statement from NICE ID3805 (TA881)[9] : _“[Ripretinib] is a meaningful treatment option for patients with metastatic GIST in the 4th line setting who currently have no other treatment options and which is in my opinion an unmet need … [ripretinib] is a significant ‘step change’, the first in 5 years since the licensing of regorafenib.”_ 

## **Benefits not captured in the model** 

The health economic analysis did not capture the potential effects of the burden of advanced GIST on caregivers. Similarly, the model did not capture any effect of death of the patient and bereavement on caregiver and family quality of life. Data to inform such analyses are not available but such effects are likely to exist. The ability of patients to maintain HRQoL whilst receiving ripretinib, including physical and role function, suggests a potential reduction in dependence on carers, thereby improving carers QoL. 

The effect of having an additional line of therapy available after regorafenib on patient QoL was also not captured for the same reason. This would give patients hope that they can live a somewhat normal life for longer than currently possible. Hope is a factor that does not come into consideration in traditional drug appraisals.[29]

## **4b) Glossary of terms** 

**Adverse event (AE)** – An undesired effect of a drug or other treatment. AEs can range from mild to life-threatening 

**Alopecia** – Loss of hair from parts of the body where hair normally grows 

**Best supportive care (BSC)** – Care that focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life, rather than treating the cancer itself 

**Biopsy** – Removing a small sample of tissue so a specialist can examine it under a microscope **Clinical trial** – A research study in which people volunteer to test a new treatment to see how safe and effective it is 

**Double-blind study** – A type of clinical trial in which neither the participants nor the study doctors know who is getting the new treatment or the comparison treatment until the study ends **EORTC QLQ-C30** – A questionnaire that asks people with cancer about their symptoms, daily activities and overall quality of life 

**EQ-5D-5L** – A short questionnaire that measures general health in five areas 

**EQ-VAS** – A 0-to-100 scale on which patients mark how good or bad their health feels that day **Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)** – A rare cancer that starts in the digestive system, most often in the stomach or small intestine 

**Histologic confirmation** – Laboratory examination of tissue (from a biopsy) to confirm exactly what type of cells are present 

**HRQoL (health-related quality of life)** – How a person’s health affects their everyday life and wellbeing 

**Imatinib** – A medicine that blocks specific proteins inside cancer cells to slow or stop the growth of GIST; usually the first treatment given 

**INVICTUS** – The name of the main clinical trial that tested ripretinib in people with advanced GIST **KIT –** A gene, specifically, proto-oncogene c-KIT, that commonly becomes mutated in GIST 

**Metastatic** – Describes cancer that has spread from where it started to other parts of the body **Molecular analysis** – Lab tests that look for genetic changes (mutations) in tumour cells. 

**Mutation** – Any change in a cell’s DNA; some mutations help tumours grow 

**Objective response rate (ORR)** – The percentage of patients whose tumours shrink or disappear after treatment 

**Overall survival (OS)** –  The length of time from diagnosis or start of treatment that patients are still alive 

**Palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (PPES)** – Soreness, redness or blisters on the palms of the hands or soles of the feet; also called “hand-foot syndrome” 

**Patient-reported outcome (PRO)** – Information patients give directly about their symptoms, feelings, or daily functioning 

**PDGFRA** – A gene, specifically the platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha gene, that commonly becomes mutated in GIST 



<!-- page 201 -->

**Phase III** – A late stage of clinical testing that compares a new treatment with the current standard or a placebo in a larger group of patients **Placebo** – An inactive substance or other intervention that looks the same as, and is given the same way as, an active drug or treatment being tested. The effects of the active drug or other intervention are compared to the effects of the placebo. **Progression-free survival (PFS)** – The length of time during and after treatment that the cancer does not grow or spread **Quality-adjusted life year (QALY)** – A combined measure of quantity and quality of life; one QALY equals one year in perfect health **Regorafenib** – A targeted treatment used after imatinib and sunitinib stop working **Ripretinib** – A newer targeted treatment designed to work even when GIST has become resistant to earlier drugs **Sarcoma** – A group of cancers that start in bone or soft tissues such as muscle, fat or blood vessels **Statistical significance** – Evidence from a study showing the result is unlikely to have happened by chance **Sunitinib** – A medicine given when imatinib no longer keeps GIST under control **Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)** – A substance that blocks enzymes called tyrosine kinases, which help cancer cells grow; TKIs are a form of targeted therapy **Unresectable** – A tumour that cannot be removed completely with surgery

## **Section A: Clarification on effectiveness data** 

## _**SLR for clinical evidence**_ 

**A1. Company’s submission (CS) Appendix B, Section 2, pages 34-50. With reference to the systematic literature review (SLR) of clinical effectiveness evidence, please provide details of the number of reviewers involved and the methods used for screening citations and full-text articles, extracting data, and assessing study quality.** 

Publications identified through the systematic review were evaluated in a three-step process to assess whether they should be included in data extraction. The inclusion/exclusion criteria used against the publications were developed using the (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design) PICOS format (for inclusion/exclusion criteria see CS appendices, Appendix E, Table 9).[1] The search strategy is presented in CS Appendix B, Table 4, and details the points at which duplicates were removed from the search outputs. This procedure complies with stringent Health Technology Assessment (HTA) guidelines surrounding the methodology of systematic reviews.[2-4 ] 

## _**Title/abstract review**_ 

All publications were independently reviewed against the inclusion/exclusion criteria based on their abstract and title. All abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers, with a third party available to resolve discrepancies; all publications included by the reviewer at the end of this stage were retained for full-text review. For publications excluded at the abstract review stage, the reason for rejection was documented for use in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence Decision Support Unit (NICE DSU) guidance.[3,5] 

All publications included in the title/abstract review are presented in the accompanying Excel SLR Report, with the title, source, authors, and abstract provided.[6] 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 206 -->

## _**Full-text review**_ 

Publications included after title/abstract review underwent full review of the text. A record was kept of publications excluded at this stage along with clear justification for their exclusion as per NICE DSU guidance.[3,6] All publications excluded during full-text review are presented in the accompanying Excel SLR Report, tab “Clin FT Review”, with the title, source, authors, abstract and reason for rejection provided for review.[6 ] 

Two independent reviewers screened all citations and full-text articles and any discrepancies in their decisions were resolved by a third independent reviewer. 

## _**Data extraction**_ 

Data from studies still included after full-text review were extracted into a pre-defined Microsoft Excel[®] -based template, ensuring that data were extracted uniformly and extraction was comparable for all studies. Two analysts independently extracted data, which were then checked and reconciled by a third independent analyst. 

To ensure process consistency, researchers performing data extraction underwent specific training.[2] Additional follow-up was implemented to address any issues identified that related to data extraction. 

## _**Quality assessment**_ 

An assessment of quality was performed on abstracts, posters, or full-text articles of relevant Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) using the NICE checklist.[7] Two reviewers independently ranked each included study and then discussed their quality assessments as required to resolve any disagreements. 

A quality assessment was conducted for relevant RCTs published in four studies, comprising INVICTUS, VOYAGER, NCT02880020 and CHAPTER-GIST-301. Results of the quality assessment are presented in the SLR Excel Report, tab “QA RCT”.[6] 

Full details of the methods used are presented in the SLR write-up report.[1]

**A4. CS, Section 2.62, page 75. The CS states that health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in INVICTUS was assessed using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ C30) role and physical functioning domains, the Euroqol 5-Dimensions 5- Level (EQ-5D-5L) and the Euroqol Visual Analogue Scale (EQ VAS) from baseline to only Cycle 2 Day 1 and that this was due to the small number of patients after this time point. Please clarify why only a small number of patients were evaluated for HRQoL at later cycles.** 

The small number of patients evaluated for HRQoL at later cycles is particularly related to patients randomised to placebo. The number of patients in the placebo arm was low after Cycle 2 Day 1 due to rapid disease progression, meaning that any statistical comparison across study arms after this time point would be highly uncertain. Specifically, the patient-reported outcome (PRO) evaluable population in the placebo arm fell from 32 patients at Cycle 2 Day 1 to 13 patients at Cycle 3 Day 1 (Figure 1).[8,9] 

The rapid decline in the number of patients in the placebo arm was expected due to the severity of their fourth-line advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST). As a result, comparative statistical analysis across study arms was only pre-specified up to Cycle 2 Day 1.[10]

## **A6. PRIORITY. CS, Section 2.3.3, Table 8, page 38. Despite randomisation being stratified by ECOG PS in INVICTUS, the placebo group had slightly worse PS scores and older age. Please comment on the potential implications of this imbalance.** 

As a rare oncology indication, clinical trials in advanced GIST have relatively small patient populations, which makes stratifying patients by baseline parameters more difficult.[12] 

Multiple sources agree that both age and ECOG PS are key prognostic factors for survival in advanced GIST, where lower ECOG PS score and a younger age favour longer survival.[13-15] However, clinicians consider ECOG PS, the presence of secondary resistance mutations, and disease burden to be more important treatment effect modifiers than age.[16] 

Subgroup analyses were conducted for progression-free survival (PFS) (prespecified), overall survival (OS) and overall response rate (ORR), to assess the impact of age, ECOG PS and other factors on the findings. Ripretinib showed benefit (hazard ratio [HR<1]) across all subgroups assessed. None of the subgroup analyses showed that age or ECOG PS had a statistically significant impact on ripretinib benefit (for PFS see CS Section 2.8.1 Figure 21, for ORR see CS Appendix C Figure 5, and for OS see INVICTUS Clinical study report, Figure 14.2.4.1, page 569).[11] 

Similar subgroup analyses as conducted for the pivotal trials considering tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) use at earlier treatment lines for advanced GIST, were also investigated. In general, these trials also showed that age and ECOG PS were not statistically significant treatment effect modifiers (Table 4).[17,18]

**A7. CS, Section 2.8.1, Figure 21, page 88. The subgroup analysis of progressionfree survival (PFS) in INVICTUS suggests that patients with ECOG PS 0 had a worse treatment effect of ripretinib compared to those with ECOG PS 1–2. Also, older patients appear to have a greater treatment effect. These results appear counterintuitive, please comment on these findings.** 

As previously mentioned, due to the rarity of ≥4[th] line advanced GIST and therefore relatively small size of the INVICTUS trial, the subgroups analysed were small. The findings of the subgroup analysis suggest that ripretinib provides benefit across all subgroups; however, the subgroups analysed were not large enough to support any further conclusions.[19] 

Additionally, subgroup analyses consider a single variable in isolation and there may be other imbalances in baseline characteristics between subgroups that drive these counterintuitive results, particularly given the small patient numbers in each subgroup. Therefore, we explored the baseline characteristics between the ECOG PS and age subgroups. 

Interestingly, there was an imbalance between the ECOG PS and age subgroups in KIT exon 11 mutations for the ripretinib arm (Table 5). KIT exon 11 mutations are known treatment effect modifiers for TKIs in advanced GIST. Analysis of the UK compassionate use cohort showed that the presence of a primary KIT exon 11 mutation was consistently associated with significantly longer PFS, time-todiscontinuation (TTD) and OS.[20] This has also been demonstrated by subgroup analyses of the INTRIGUE trial, an open-label, phase 3 study in patients with second-line advanced GIST who were randomized to either ripretinib or sunitinib.[21] The ongoing INSIGHT trial aims to further explore the favourable response to ripretinib in patients with primary KIT exon 11 and secondary KIT exon 17/18 mutations.[21] In summary, being mindful of small numbers and limitations of this approach, the higher proportion of patients with KIT exon 11 mutations in the ECOG PS 1-2 and older subgroups vs the ECOG PS 0 and younger subgroup may have contributed to the counterintuitive results for the PFS subgroup analyses (Table 9).[22]

## **Section B: Clarification on cost-effectiveness data** 

## _**Survival analysis**_ 

**B1. PRIORITY. CS, Section 3.3, pages 108-128. The data for TTD, PFS and OS used in the economic model reflect the January 2021 DCO of INVICTUS. Please clarify whether more recent data-cuts are available, and if so, why these have not been used.** 

There is a later data cut-off (DCO) from INVICTUS dated May 2022. However, preparation and analysis for the NICE submission began before the 2022 DCO analysis became available. Therefore, the original model was built using data from the 2021 DCO. When the May 2022 DCO became available, the feasibility and possible impact of the final OS data on cost-effectiveness was investigated. 

Overall, the median OS for each treatment arm using the May 2022 DCO is the same as for the January 2021 DCO. The small difference in HR seen between the two sets of data could be explained by random variation, given the small sample size and/or prolonged OS seen for participants in the placebo arm who survived beyond the median OS which was primarily driven by treatment crossover. All patients randomised to placebo who continued into the open-label period (N=30) were receiving ripretinib during the January 2021 to May 2022 data collection period and many had dose escalated (N=16/30). 

Though the results were similar, we consider the 2022 data cut to be less robust than that for 2021. Prespecified end of study analyses only included OS and safety. PFS and HRQoL data had already been finalised from a statistical perspective and so further formal analyses were not appropriate. As such, a model incorporating 2022 data would be heterogenous with regards to clinical inputs for PFS, composite TTD, OS and HRQoL. 

In addition, use of the 2022 DCO would increase the risk of bias and confounding. Moving further into the post-unblinding, post-treatment switch/IPDE period increases the potential risk due to informative drop-out and other biases associated with data collection in the open-label setting. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 215 -->

As the January 2021 data were mature, with OS data out to 24 months, it was considered that there was no value in integrating the new potentially less robust data cut into the model. 

A summary of data from the 2022 DCO for patient disposition is presented in Table 6 and Table 7, OS data are presented in Table 8 and the Kaplan-Meier plot for OS is presented in Figure 2.[24]

## **B2. PRIORITY. CS, Section 3.3.3, page 127. Time to treatment discontinuation (TTD) is modelled as a composite endpoint including treatment discontinuation on either QD or BID dosing and disease progression as events.** 

- _**(a) Please include further details about how the composite endpoint of PFS+TTD was calculated, including details of what was counted as an event and how censoring rules were applied.**_ 

- _**(b) Please clarify why it was necessary to include PFS in the composite endpoint – why was time to treatment discontinuation not instead analysed as the time from study entry through to discontinuation on the last received dose of ripretinib in either the double-blind or open-label periods of INVICTUS?**_ 

- _**(c) Section 2.4.1 on page 47 of the CS describes a post hoc TTD analysis, including any dose discontinuation during both the double-blind and**_ 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 220 -->

_**open-label periods. The TTD definitions and calculations appear inconsistent between Sections 2.4.1 and 3.3.3. Why was the analysis in Section 2.4.1 not used as the base case? If these are separate analyses, please clarify the differences and explain which estimates were used in the model.**_ 

(a) TTD was considered a composite endpoint, when it was combined with PFS and treatment discontinuation into a single outcome, calculated as follows: 

1. Time from randomisation to a composite endpoint of PFS plus treatment discontinuation (QD or BD) over the double blind (DB) and open-label (OL) periods. 

2. The event time was measured from the date of randomisation to the latest of PFS and treatment discontinuation, calculated in weeks. Due to the PFS censoring rules pertaining to two or more missing assessments (refer to INVICTUS SAP)[10] , patients who: 

   - a. [did not either discontinue treatment, and/or 

   - b. who were considered as censored for PFS], and 

   - c. who died 

were assumed to have had the composite endpoint event at the time of their death. 

3. Patients without the above composite event (i.e. as described in step 2 above) were considered as censored. 

4. The censoring time was measured from date of randomisation to the latest of the two component times (PFS or last treatment), regardless of the event/censoring of each component. 

Randomisation was chosen as the start date in order to align with calculation of time to PFS and OS as defined for analyses described in the clinical study report. 

No subjects had missing TTD data. 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 221 -->

(b and c) PFS was included in the composite TTD endpoint because the economic model uses four partitions, explicitly separating progressed patients who remain on ripretinib from those who progressed but discontinued ripretinib. This approach was adopted to specifically address the effects of post-progression ripretinib use, in response to committee and ERG feedback on the proposed stopping rule in TA881 and to ensure the model reflected UK clinical practice.[16,25] An analysis based exclusively on TTD (as presented in section 2.4.1) would stratify all patients into either on- or off-treatment partitions regardless of progression status and would not correctly distinguish between PD-on-treatment and PD-off-treatment states; this was considered particularly important for capturing the effect of post-progression treatment on quality of life. Incorporating PFS into the composite ensures the model allocates patients to the appropriate post-progression partition. 

**B3. PRIORITY. CS, Section 2.6.2, Figure 10, page 65. For non-escalating patients in INVICTUS, the EAG understands that they either remained on ripretinib 150mg QD post-progression or received no further treatment and that the survival of these patients is calculated from the start of the trial. For those who escalated to ripretinib 150mg BID, survival appears to be measured from the first BID dose post-progression. Such comparisons are based on survival from different baselines (time of study entry and time of progression, respectively). This likely leads to immortal time bias, which cannot be corrected through statistical methods alone. Please clarify the following:** 

- _**(a) Is this analysis limited to patients randomised to the ripretinib treatment arm?**_ 

- _**(b) Given the risk of immortal time bias, how should this analysis be interpreted?**_ 

- _**(c) Please perform an updated analysis of post-progression survival from the first QD vs. BID dose among patients in the ripretinib arm after progression (assuming similar time from progression to next treatment in both cases), and report patient characteristics at the secondary baseline for the naïve comparison (at a minimum, report the covariates at secondary baseline used in the two-stage IPDE adjustment, including:**_ 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 222 -->

## _**time to progression, ECOG performance status at progression, EQ-5D VAS score at progression, and age at baseline), if feasible.**_ 

(a) Yes, the analysis is limited to patients who were randomised to the ripretinib treatment arm in INVICTUS. 

(b) We acknowledge the risk of immortal time bias in CS, Figure 10. Figure 3 presents Kaplan-Meier estimates of time from study randomisation to death, incorporating left truncation in the ripretinib 150 mg BID arm. Patients in this treatment arm, therefore, have delayed entry into the OS risk set. This analysis was conducted to account for the differing time origins between treatment dose groups, specifically addressing the risk of immortal time bias in the escalating (BID) population, although the presence of any treatment selection bias has not been adjusted for in Figure 3. The analysis incorporates the time post randomisation that patients started BID treatment, so they are not considered in the risk set prior to that time. Compared with the original analysis, patients who dose escalated had a slightly poorer survival probability compared with those who remained on the same dose, but this was not statistically significant. As such, this data adds to the other analyses included in CS, Section 2.6.2, page 63, by demonstrating the uncertainty surrounding the impact of ripretinib dose escalation on OS in INVICTUS given the considerable variability in the magnitude of and the positive/negative nature of the effect.

Initially, there was a survival advantage for patients who dose escalated versus those who remained on QD dosing; however, the curves converged at around 50 weeks post-progression. This initial benefit was likely to be due to imbalances in positive prognostic factors across the two populations since randomisation was broken at disease progression.

Table 9 presents a summary of patient demographic data and disease status, comparing patients who continued with 150 mg QD dosing vs those who dose -escalated to 150 mg BID. The data suggest that those who underwent IPDE were generally fitter and better able to tolerate dose escalation. Patients who continued with QD dosing were more likely to have ECOG PS ≥1 at baseline (62.5% vs 53.7% who dose escalated to BID) and were more likely to have ≥4 prior lines of therapy (41.7% for QD vs 31.7% for BID). This was also seen at the point of progression, where a much lower proportion of patients who stayed on QD post progression had ECOG score of 0 (16.7%) compared with those who dose escalated to BID (51.2%). Patients who dose escalated also had a better Euroqol Visual Analogue Scale (EQ-5D VAS) score at the point of progression vs those who did not dose escalate (Table 9).[22 ]

A UK clinical advisory board supported these findings, with clinicians stating that patients who did not dose escalate were more likely to be of ECOG PS ≥1 at the point of progression.[16] ECOG PS was also identified as a key prognostic factor / treatment effect modifier; it was perceived that a difference in performance status could account 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 226 -->

for a difference in OS between the two patient groups.[16] Higher ECOG PS for those not dose escalating is likely to explains the rapid decline over the ~10 weeks post-progression for patients who remained on QD dosing; after 10 weeks the rate of decline plateaued for these patients over the long-term. 

Eventual plateauing of survival curves aligns with comments by the advisory board that patients that reach the end of the survival curve probably have biologically better disease that would progress slowly whether on QD or BID dosing.[16] Additionally, as stated in the response to B12, depending on the commissioning route for BID, only a select few patients would likely dose escalate to 150 mg BID in clinical practice. Therefore, any potential bias seen in the analysis is unlikely to be relevant to real world practice.

**B5. PRIORITY. CS, Section 2.6.2, pages 63 to 72. Given that 97% of patients (63/65) who progressed received continued ripretinib (i.e., much higher than the 80% suggested by the clinicians consulted by the company), please also clarify whether post-progression QD ripretinib would alter the shape of the survival curve compared to those who received no further treatment.** 

Clinicians at the 2025 advisory board estimated that 80% of patients who initiate treatment with ripretinib would be likely to continue to receive ripretinib after disease progression.[26] The 97% quoted in the question, is the proportion of patients with disease progression who continued treatment beyond progression rather than the proportion of those who initiated treatment. 

In INVICTUS, the proportion of patients who initiated treatment with ripretinib and continued treatment after disease progression was 74% (63/85), slightly lower than would be expected in clinical practice.[27] As such, the survival curves are likely to reflect what would occur in clinical practice. 

**B6. PRIORITY. CS, Section 2.6.2, Figure 12, page 68. Is the analysis illustrated in Figure 12 related to the analysis described on page 122 of the CS (“Censored BID-dosing analysis”)? If not, please clarify how the analyses differ from one another and explain which analysis is included in the scenario analyses in CS Table 60.** 

Yes, these analyses are the same. CS Figure 12 presents the survival curves to which the parametric models were fitted (p122). The results of this were then included as 2 scenarios in the model ‘Open label BID vs QD OS analysis (non-progressors + IPDE progressors; log logistic)’ and ‘Open label BID vs QD OS analysis (non-progressors + QD progressors; log logistic)’. 

**B7. PRIORITY. CS, Section 2.6.2, page 68. Please clarify whether the Cox proportional hazards time-varying analysis for ripretinib 150mg QD includes only the QD period after progression. If not, please explain what data were included in the analysis (including any reprocessing of those data).** 

The Cox proportional hazards time-varying analysis includes ripretinib 150 mg QD treatment (and any subsequent ripretinib 150 mg BID treatment) from randomisation 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 230 -->

(rather than progression) until death/censoring (last known alive). The time from randomisation to death/censoring was split into periods (via a counting process which factored in changes in patient progression status, other time-varying variables, and treatment switch) giving start and stop times on ripretinib QD and ripretinib BID between randomisation, the date of escalation to ripretinib BID and death as appropriate. For example, for patients who dose-escalated from ripretinib QD to ripretinib BID, the assigned ripretinib QD period ended one day prior to the date of dose-escalation to ripretinib BID. The assigned ripretinib BID period, for the same patients, started on the date of the first ripretinib BID dose and ended at the date of death/censoring. 

A small error in the allocation of death during these periods was identified, in which 13 patients were assigned a death event in multiple periods; this error was corrected. Updated comparison of ripretinib BID vs QD resulted in a HR of 1.50 (95% confidence ‑ interval [CI] 0.70 to 3.22; p=0.300) indicating a 50% increase in the risk of death after dose escalation. This did not affect interpretation of the analysis.

**B10. PRIORITY. CS, Section 3.3.2, Table 34, page 122. Within the censored BIDdosing analysis, OS is assessed in two sub-populations based on postprogression treatment (IPDE vs. QD). Since this comparison is non-randomised and the groups differ in size, there is a risk of selection bias. Please comment on the potential impact of this selection bias on the interpretation of OS results.** Although the censored BID -dosing analysis can introduce selection bias due to informative censoring and loss of data over time, it is still thought to be of value as a comparison with other approaches that attempt to adjust the data for selection bias. 

The imbalance of ECOG PS between those who escalated vs those who did not is likely to be a major factor that introduces uncertainty. Clinicians and multiple research papers indicate ECOG PS as a key prognostic factor for survival and a treatment effect modifier in patients with GIST.[13-16] At the time of disease progression, patients 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 234 -->

undergoing ripretinib IPDE had a better ECOG PS score than those not undergoing dose escalation (ECOG PS 0, 51% vs. 18%, respectively).[28] This aligns with clinician opinion, that expected patients who continued with ripretinib QD at the point of progression to be less fit or experiencing poor treatment tolerability.[16] This suggests potential for selection bias in favor of BID dosing. Other unknown confounding factors are likely to exist as demonstrated by the variable results from the multiple analyses that aimed to quantify the effect of BID dosing while adjusting for potentially confounding variables (CS, Section 2.6.2, page 63). 

Though there is a likelihood of selection bias, primarily due to the imbalance in ECOG PS at the point of progression, this scenario avoids introduction of other uncertainties resulting from attempts to adjust for this bias. Additionally, adjusted scenarios are presented in the form of the two-stage analysis and Cox proportional hazards time-varying analysis.

## **provide further justification for the selection of the log-logistic OS model.** 

Several steps were taken during selection of the OS model for ripretinib, in line with NICE DSU Technical Support Document 14. The resulting choice was a balance of the different factors considered. Firstly, independent parametric curves fitted the data and produced good visual predictions for ripretinib and best supportive care (BSC) within the observed period. Combined Akaike Information Criterion (AICs) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BICs) were calculated across treatment arms, yielding total values that were very closely matched for the best performing models and did not, therefore, meaningfully differentiate between models in terms of statistical fit. However, the fitted curves clustered into two groups in terms of estimated 10-year survival; whilst the Weibull and exponential curves estimated a 10-year survival of 1 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 235 -->

to 2%, the other curves (log-logistic, log-normal, Gompertz and generalised gamma) all predicted a higher 10-year survival of around 8%. 

We subsequently reviewed published data and sought expert opinion to validate whether 10-year survival with ripretinib was more likely to be aligned with the lower or higher curves: 

- The 10-year survival rate for patients with advanced GIST who initiated previous lines of therapy is 10 to 23%.[13-15,29] In patients treated with second-line sunitinib, 10-year survival was approximately 10%.[29] Patients typically progress quickly on sunitinib and regorafenib, with each line of therapy providing only 6 to 9 months of benefit.[30-32] As such, if the survival rate for patients treated with second-line sunitinib has been observed at 10% by 10 years then 10% at 9 years for ripretinib (as modelled in the base case) would be plausible.[29 ] 

- Clinicians (N = 7) in an advisory board were asked to estimate 10-year survival for ripretinib; however, responses were not aligned. One advisor commented that 8% survival at 10 years is plausible as treatments are improving and new options are being developed. Another thought that 10% at 10 years would be an over estimation. Four advisors provided estimates after the meeting of 1%, 2%, 2.5% and ≤5%.[16 ] 

- Previous NICE TAs for advanced GIST indicate that clinicians repeatedly underestimate long-term survival associated with TKI treatment: 

   - Imatinib: During the NICE appraisal [TA86] the Committee concluded that cost-effectiveness estimates based on a 10-year time horizon were sufficient to encompass key costs and benefits suggesting that no patients would remain alive at this timepoint. However, recent observational studies show PFS rates of nearly 10% at 10 years for first-line patients with advanced GIST treated with imatinib.[33 ] 

   - Sunitinib: For TA179 clinical experts estimated 10% survival at 6 years. However, a recent study has shown that median OS for second-line 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 236 -->

treatment with sunitinib is 63.4 months (i.e. 50% of patients are alive at 5.3 years) with ~10% of patients surviving to 10 years.[18] 

- A naïve comparison of clinical data for other TKIs used to treat advanced GIST vs ripretinib show that, although ripretinib is used in more heavily pre-treated patients who are more likely to harbour secondary drug-resistance mutations, it provides a higher magnitude of benefit than previous lines of therapy (Table 12). This is likely to be due to its novel ‘switch-control’ mechanism of action. 

**Table 12: Pivotal trial outcomes for treatments indicated for advanced GIST**

|---|---|---|---|
|Sunitinib(trial comparator)32|6.8(0)|5.6(1.5)|17.0(14.9)|
|Regorafenib (trial<br>comparator)17,30,31,34|4.5 (1.5)|4.8 (0.9)|17.4 (11.9)|

Considering these real-world 10-year survival estimates for advanced GIST with earlier lines of therapy, coupled with the higher magnitude of benefit ripretinib provides vs other TKIs and the uncertainty surrounding clinical predictions, it was decided that 1-2% survival at 10 years was too low and that 8% survival at 10 years was plausible as modelled by log-logistic extrapolation.

**B14. PRIORITY. CS, Section 3.4.5, pages 134 to 136. With respect to the mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) analysis of the utility data in INVICTUS:** 

- _**Please clarify how switching in the control arm and dose escalation in the treatment arm were handled in the analysis of utilities for progressed disease (PD) for, BSC, PD on treatment, and PD off treatment?**_ 

- _**Please also provide the full model specification of the MMRM (ideally as a formula) and report the relevant coefficients.**_ 

- _**Please justify the preferred MMRM regression model specification, particularly the selection of regression covariates and how the model fit was assessed.**_ 

- _**Please clarify the number of data points available for progression-free (PF), PD (BSC), PD on treatment and PD off treatment to inform the MMRM analysis.**_ 

a) Subjects could transition from one state to another, across potentially multiple states during the DB and OL study periods. The MMRM analysed patient-visit level data, where the progression and treatment status of each patient was determined on an empirical (time-varying) basis. Placebo switch was formally incorporated in the model but dose escalation was not (i.e. utility measures were not separately assessed during ripretinib BID treatment). 

b) The model statement is as follows: 

EQ-5D3LUK = TRTARM  STATUS  PHASE    TRTARM*STATUS TRTARM*PHASE   STATUS*PHASE    TRTARM*STATUS*PHASE 

## Where: 

## EQ-5D3LUK = utility (Hernandez-Alava) 

TRTARM = last study treatment received prior to visit (Ripretinib OD or BID/ placebo) 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 239 -->

STATUS = subject on study treatment at visit (on / off) 

PHASE = subject progressed on or prior to visit (PF / PD) 

To account for intra-subject correlations, a compound symmetry covariance structure was employed. In addition, the model allowed for differences in underlying (co-)variance across the eight possible treatment-progression states. The Kenward-Roger method for calculating the denominator degrees of freedom was employed for inference. Observed marginals were used in calculation of mean utilities per health state. 

The SAS code used for this analysis is approximately as follows: 

proc mixed data = AD1; 

class USUBJID TRTARM STATUS PHASE; 

model EQ-5D3LUK = TRTARM STATUS PHASE TRTARM*STATUS TRTARM*PHASE STATUS*PHASE TRTARM*STATUS*PHASE / ddfm=kr; 

repeated / subject=USUBJID type=CS  group=TRTARM*STATUS*PHASE; 

lsmeans   STATUS*PHASE                /* for Total (marginalised over treatment) */ TRTARM*STATUS*PHASE  /* for individual treatment group estimates */ 

run;

c) The model was chosen to allow for mean utility estimation in the eight (=2*2*2) possible health states, hence the inclusion of all main effects as well as all two- and three-way interactions. The model also allowed for the (co-)variance of each of the 8 health states to vary. 

This was essentially the most parsimonious MMRM model that would allow for full flexibility in health-state utility estimations, whilst avoiding the potential risk of over-fitting. Hence, no other baseline or time-varying covariates were adjusted for.

**B18. CS, Section 3.5.2, Table 46 and model trace worksheets, columns AD:AG in the ripretinib trace and AD:AE in the BSC trace. Please justify the assumption that patients would receive palliative interventions (palliative resection and radiotherapy) at treatment initiation (in the progression free (PF) state in the first model cycle) or/and when they progress. Why are these costs applied twice instead of once only at model entry?** 

Palliative intervention costs are only incurred in the proportions of patients input in cells N110:N113 on the Cost Inputs worksheet (for ripretinib) and cells N119:N122 on the Cost Inputs worksheet (for BSC). In the base case analysis, these proportions are set to 10% for palliative surgical resection and 20% for palliative radiotherapy. The same proportions are used in the first model cycle and in a proportion of the cohort that can unambiguously be assigned to be ‘entering’ the PD partition (i.e. in model cycles in which the PD partition is growing). Overall, given this scaling of costs, total costs are not being incurred twice but would instead effectively be incurred for a maximum of 20% of patients for palliative surgical resection or 40% of patients for palliative radiotherapy.

## _**Uncertainty analysis**_ 

‑ **B21. CS, Section 3.11.2, page 160 and Figure 36. The deterministic one way sensitivity analysis (OWSA) presented in the CS identified the “PDOff” health state utility value as the parameter in the model with the greatest impact on the ICER. However, the EAG notes that in this analysis, the PDOff and PD (BSC) utility parameters are varied independently, although they are assumed to have the same value. Please explain why PDoff and PD were considered as independent parameters in the model, why they were varied/sampled separately, and the reason that varying the PDoff parameter has a large impact on the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) whilst varying the PD (BSC) parameter has a much smaller effect.** 

The PD utility parameter applies to all patients in the BSC arm with disease progression, while the PDOff parameter applies to patients in the ripretinib arm who have experienced both disease progression and discontinued treatment. In the base case analysis, these were assumed to have the same value as patients are ostensibly in similar positions with regard to treatment options. Clinical advisors felt that patients no longer receiving active treatment after progression (PD off-treatment), independent of which arm they were originally randomised to and whether they received post-progression ripretinib, would be likely to have similar quality of life.[26] However, we would contend that the option to vary these parameters is useful as the treatment trajectory taken to reach the two states is different. In the revised model, we have included an option in the one-way sensitivity analysis (OWSA) to enable these parameters to be varied simultaneously in the OWSA worksheet. 

That the variation in the PDOff utility parameter has a substantially larger impact on the ICER than the PD parameter is simply a function of the relative time spent in each state; in the submitted base case, patients accrued XXX QALYs in the PDOff partition in the ripretinib arm versus XXX QALYs in the PD partition in the BSC arm. 

## _**Model implementation**_ 

**B22. CS, Section 3.3.2, page 121 and executable model, worksheet “Data Store”, cells D120:E220. The CS states that the general population mortality estimates** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 254 -->

**have been updated to use life tables for the UK. These life table risks appear to be contained in the worksheet “Data Store.” However, the life tables applied in the live model calculations are contained in worksheet “ERG_WeightedGenPopModel.” Please amend the model to use life tables for England only and ensure that they are linked to the live model calculations.** 

General population mortality estimates have been revised to include life tables specific to England and specifically using the said life table data as stored in the Data Store worksheet in cells D120:E220. 

**B23. PRIORITY. CS, Section 3.4.4., page 134, Executable model, worksheet “Trace (Ripretinib)”, column BU and worksheet “Trace (BSC)”, column BU. The CS states that** _**“All AEs were assumed to occur in the first cycle of the model.”**_ **However, the QALY calculations in column BU are subject to several problems:** 

- _**(i) The disutility values are applied in every model cycle (rather than the first cycle only);**_ 

- _**(ii) The use of brackets means that the AE disutility is not scaled up by the population size (amending the cohort size from 1000 to 1 in worksheet “Settings” leads to very different mean QALYs in each treatment group);**_ 

- _**(iii)The AE disutility is applied only to people in the PF state after half-cycle correction (rather than all patients who start treatment with ripretinib or BSC);**_ 

- _**(iv)The AE disutility is divided by 13, instead of (“cycles/time”), meaning that any changes to the cycle length are not automatically applied.**_ 

_**Please confirm that these are errors and correct the model.**_ The formulae have been amended in light of all feedback. The original assumptions reflected by these formulae, particularly the assumption of ongoing utility decrements after occurrence of the initial AE, were conservative from the ripretinib perspective given the higher incidence of hypertension and abdominal pain seen versus the BSC arm. 

**B24. PRIORITY. Executable model, worksheet “Clinical Inputs”, columns C, G:L and M:O. The EAG understands that the calculations contained in column L are intended to reflect the adjusted cumulative probability of OS based on the loglogistic OS model fitted to data from INVICTUS including a constraint to ensure** 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 255 -->

**that the per-cycle risk of death must be as least as high as that for the age- and sex-matched general population. This constrained OS model feeds directly into the partitioned survival model trace. However, the life table constraint in column L has been implemented incorrectly. This can be seen by calculating the percycle risks of death from column L and comparing these risks against the general population risks in column C – the per-cycle adjusted modelled risk (from column L) is lower than the life table risk after cycle 285. An accompanying spreadsheet has been provided by the EAG to illustrate the issue. Please confirm that this is an error and correct the model.** 

The age- and sex-matched general population constraint was indeed not applied in the HR-adjusted OS column (column L in the “Clinical Inputs” worksheet in the submitted model). This has been addressed in the revised version of the model, which introduces an “HR adjusted mort. constrained to general population mort.” column (column L in the “Clinical Inputs” worksheet in the revised model). This column is then used as the basis of the constraint in column M in the “Clinical Inputs” worksheet in the revised model and in turn drives the calculations in the Trace worksheets. 

**B25. PRIORITY. Executable model, worksheet “Trace (Ripretinib)”, column V. The calculations in column V apply the cost of a new pack of 30 ripretinib tablets in every 9 model cycles, with no additional pack required in every 10th model cycle (due to the accumulated tablets in each 28-day cycle). These calculations: (a) are applied to the half-cycle corrected model trace and (b) do not account for any wastage in the base case analysis. Please amend the model to calculate acquisition costs from the uncorrected model trace and include an assumption that each patient initiating treatment with ripretinib will waste on average 0.25 packs, as was accepted by the Appraisal Committee in Technology Appraisal (TA) 881.** 

Relative to a simple per tablet-based approach, the adoption of an integer pack-based cost calculation approach for ripretinib resulted in analyses that show an additional cost of approximately 0.47 packs of ripretinib versus the previous approach of modelling tablet-based costs; this reflects tablet wastage with tablets remaining at the end of a pack. However, when the pack-based calculation approach is active, the model does not explicitly report wastage on the Results worksheet, but wastage is 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 256 -->

captured implicitly. We have, however, reverted the revised model to use a flat wastage rate of 0.25 packs of ripretinib. The impact of these scenarios on the ICER are presented in Table 21. 

**B26. CS, Section 3.5.1, page 137 and executable model, worksheet “Trace (Ripretinib)”, columns Q, V, X and Y. The model includes a relative dose intensity (RDI) estimate of 96.5%, based on the double-blind period of INVICTUS. Please clarify why RDI estimates for post-progression ripretinib use from INVICTUS were not included in the model, given that the company is now also seeking a positive recommendation which includes the use of ripretinib post-progression** 

**(i.e., the original stopping rule proposed in TA881 has been removed).** 

In routine practice, post-progression use may include patients receiving both the QD and BID doses of ripretinib, which complicates derivation of an RDI across the two populations. Exclusion of the RDI from the ripretinib pack-based price calculation was a conservative assumption from the ripretinib perspective. An option has now been incorporated into the model to also capture RDI in the post-progression period. 

**B27. Executable model, worksheets “Trace (Ripretinib)” and “Trace (BSC)”, columns V to Z. Regarding the costs of pre-treatment for patients receiving ripretinib and BSC, please confirm that these are errors and correct the model, as necessary:** 

- _**The pre-treatment cost applied to the PF state is not scaled up by the population size (the cost is included outside of the brackets in the formula which multiplies the drug treatment costs by the probabilities/numbers from the trace).**_ 

- _**The pre-treatment cost is also applied to the PD states (PDon and PDoff for patients receiving ripretinib and PD for patients receiving BSC) in the first cycle of the model, based on the half-cycle corrected model trace. This contradicts the information in CS, Section 3.5.2, Table 46, whereby the text suggests that the pre-treatment costs are applied as a lump-sum cost in the first model cycle to all patients starting ripretinib or BSC in the PFS state in the first model cycle.**_ 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 257 -->

Pre-treatment costs in the PF state are now multiplied by the patient number specified on the Settings worksheet. The pre-treatment costs cover CT scans, MRI scans, full blood count, and liver function tests. Some, but not all of these, may be performed either at the time of treatment initiation or dose escalation and could therefore be explored in sensitivity or scenario analysis. However, the model has been aligned with the caption for Table 46 in the CS and pre-treatment costs are captured only in the first cycle of the model, in the PF partition, and based on the model trace prior to half-cycle correction. 

## **B28. Executable model, worksheet “Trace (Ripretinib)”, columns V, X and Y. The formulae in column V include BSC costs for patients who are progression-free, but the formulae in columns X and Y exclude BSC costs for patients who have progressed. Please confirm that these are errors and correct the model.** 

In the submitted model, BSC costs in the ripretinib arm were captured at two ‘intensities’ covering progression-free patients and patients with progressed disease. Progressed disease BSC costs were only captured for progressed disease off-treatment patients in the base case analysis as data were not available on BSC treatment costs associated with the post-progression on-treatment state. However, formulae in columns X and Y have been amended to capture the same post-progression BSC costs as the post-progression off-treatment partition state (column Z in the “Trace (Ripretinib)” worksheet). 

**B29. Worksheet “Trace (Ripretinib)” columns AD:AG and worksheet “Trace (BSC)”, columns AD:AE. The palliative care (palliative resection and palliative radiotherapy) cost for the PF state is based on the half-cycle corrected model trace, but the cost in the PD state is based on the uncorrected trace. This applies to both the ripretinib and BSC traces. Please confirm that these are errors and correct the model.** 

The initial rationale for palliative care costs in the PD state being based on the uncorrected trace was driven by the notion that such costs would be incurred immediately at the start of each model cycle as patients ‘transition’ into the PD partitions. However, we accept that the PF and PD states should be aligned in this regard to avoid a half-cycle of double counting of palliative care costs. The model has, 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 258 -->

therefore, been amended to base all palliative care costs on the half-cycle corrected model traces. 

**B30. Worksheet “Trace (Ripretinib)”, column AB. The formula which calculates the total treatment costs for ripretinib does not include the values in column Y (costs of treatment in PDOn (BID Dosing)), which leads to the total treatment costs to decrease if the proportion of PD on-treatment patients requiring BID dosing is included in ‘Cost inputs’ cell F24. Please confirm that this is an error and correct the model.** 

The formulae in column AB of the “Trace (Ripretinib)” worksheet do not drive the calculation of the overall cost of ripretinib or the calculation of the ICER, and are only used for the purpose of calculating a subtotal that is not used in any downstream calculations. However, this did previously only reflect the costs of ripretinib QD and so the formulae in column AB have been updated accordingly. 

**B31. PRIORITY. Executable model, worksheet “Model Parameters”, cells D51:54. The probabilistic sampling routine does not account for logical ordering of the health states and the sampled utility value for the PD off treatment states can be higher than that for the sampled utility value for the PF states. Ren** _**et al.**_ **(** _**Pharmacoeconomics**_ **, 2018, vol. 36[3]) have proposed a method for sampling ordered parameters, including utility values. Please apply this method in the model using the variance-covariance matrix from the MMRM.** 

We have implemented the Ren _et al._ methodology for ensuring the logical ordering of the PD state utilities relative to the PF state utility.[36] We have followed the approach outlined in the Ren _et al._ manuscript and supplementary materials, which utilises the logit transformed central estimates of the utility value (and the variance around the central estimate) to inform the difference distribution.[36] We have assumed, as in Ren _et al._ , that the difference distribution follows a gamma distribution, while the reference distribution follows a beta distribution, with the latter in line with the submitted base case.[36] 

Clarification questions 




<!-- page 259 -->

**B32. Executable model, worksheet “Cost Inputs”, cell F127 and H129. The endof-life care cost in cell H129 does not update when alternative cost sources are selected from the drop-down menu in cell F127. Please correct this error.** 

The formulae in the model have been updated such that the drop-down menu for end-of-life care updates the value in cell H129 (scenario provided in Table 21). 

**B33. Executable model, worksheets “Trace (Ripretinib)” and “Trace (BSC)”, column C. Each cycle is assumed to be 1/13 years in duration. The calculations in this column assume that there are 52 weeks in a year. However, there are approximately 52.17 weeks in a year. Please correct the model, if possible.** 

It is acknowledged that the 28-day cycle length results in a ~0.34% (1.25 day) mismatch between model year length and calendar year length (assuming an average of 365.25 days per year). However, given the time constraints and structural changes that would be required to address this, no changes have been made to the model to address this discrepancy.

Hazard ratio less (greater) than one indicates a reduction (increase) in the risk of death following a switch to ripretinib BID. Variance of log (Hazard ratio) from a robust sandwich estimator to account for within-subject paired survival times. Abbreviations: BID - Twice-daily; CF - Counter-factual; CI - Confidence interval; HR – Hazard ratio; QD - Oncedaily. 

- c) For each set of (counterfactual) ripretinib 150mg QD survival times, the empirical unsmoothed hazard, a smoothed hazard, and the modelled hazards are plotted. These are presented in the reference pack of this response (file name “CONFIDENTIAL_os_itt_all_aft_km_fit_dcc2_all_f”).[2] 

- d) The time ratios in CS Table 36 and Table 1 can be considered as a comparison of BID vs QD post-progression survival in patients randomised to ripretinib 150mg QD who progressed. The time ratios range between approximately 2 to 4. A time ratio of 2 can be interpreted as an increase in survival time post progression due to BID (vs QD) by a factor of 2. The time ratio is the inverse of the acceleration factor (see part e) response below. 

- e) It should be noted that switching from QD to BID is an inherently different challenge compared with the switch from placebo to QD. Estimation of the potential impact of IPDE involves consideration of the transition from one treatment (QD) to two (i.e. remaining on QD or dose escalating to BID). Estimation of the potential impact of placebo switch involves consideration of the transition from placebo to one of two treatments (placebo, QD). An important statistical consideration is that in the latter scenario we are trying to estimate the effect of the first treatment (i.e. placebo), whereas in the former the aim is to estimate the effect of the second treatment (i.e. 



<!-- page 274 -->

BID). As such, many typical treatment switching adjustment methods, especially those that rely on randomisation, are not appropriate (e.g. RPSFTM) or readily interpretable for this latter IPDE scenario. For example, we cannot reliably estimate the effect of BID on overall survival under the assumption that patients were randomised to BID at study start. However, the 2-stage estimation method has been applied to the ripretinib 150mg QD arm to determine counterfactual ripretinib 150mg QD survival times in a similar manner to the placebo switching 2-stage adjustment. All of these parametric models are now incorporated into the model and can be run using the “Scenario analyses” and “BID OS analyses” menus on the Settings worksheet. The “Two-stage adjusted BID models” option must be selected from the “Scenario analyses” menu, and the individual two-stage adjustment models can then be selected from the “Two-stage adjusted BID models” menu. 

In the first stage, accelerated failure time models (exponential, Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic, generalised Gamma and Gompertz, including simple and complex covariate adjustment measured at the time of progression and including a covariate indicating treatment switch to BID) were fitted to the post-progression survival time in patients randomised to ripretinib 150mg QD in order to estimate the treatment effect in patients who switched compared to those who did not. The resulting acceleration factors were then used to shrink the post-progression survival times in patients who switched in order to estimate counterfactual OS times (i.e. unaffected by switching to BID). 

Stage 1 model fit was assessed via AICs and clinical plausibility (the complex generalised gamma had convergence problems so was not considered). The model considered to have the best fit was the simple, log-normal, with re-censoring and was subsequently used in the updated cost-effectiveness model as a sensitivity case. Parametric models have now been fitted to each set of counterfactual OS times as described in part a) above.

- _**(iv)The AE disutility is divided by 13, instead of (“cycles/time”), meaning that any changes to the cycle length are not automatically applied.**_ 

## _**Please confirm that these are errors and correct the model.**_ 

[Answer provided in responses delivered on 30[th] June 2025] 

**B24. PRIORITY. Executable model, worksheet “Clinical Inputs”, columns C, G:L and M:O. The EAG understands that the calculations contained in column L are intended to reflect the adjusted cumulative probability of OS based on the loglogistic OS model fitted to data from INVICTUS including a constraint to ensure that the per-cycle risk of death must be as least as high as that for the age- and sex-matched general population. This constrained OS model feeds directly into the partitioned survival model trace. However, the life table constraint in column L has been implemented incorrectly. This can be seen by calculating the percycle risks of death from column L and comparing these risks against the general population risks in column C – the per-cycle adjusted modelled risk (from column L) is lower than the life table risk after cycle 285. An accompanying spreadsheet has been provided by the EAG to illustrate the issue. Please confirm that this is an error and correct the model.** 

[Answer provided in responses delivered on 30[th] June 2025] 



<!-- page 280 -->

**B25. PRIORITY. Executable model, worksheet “Trace (Ripretinib)”, column V. The calculations in column V apply the cost of a new pack of 30 ripretinib tablets in every 9 model cycles, with no additional pack required in every 10th model cycle (due to the accumulated tablets in each 28-day cycle). These calculations: (a) are applied to the half-cycle corrected model trace and (b) do not account for any wastage in the base case analysis. Please amend the model to calculate acquisition costs from the uncorrected model trace and include an assumption that each patient initiating treatment with ripretinib will waste on average 0.25 packs, as was accepted by the Appraisal Committee in Technology Appraisal (TA) 881.** 

[Answer provided in responses delivered on 30[th] June 2025]

[Answer provided in responses delivered on 30[th] June 2025]

- _**The pre-treatment cost is also applied to the PD states (PDon and PDoff for patients receiving ripretinib and PD for patients receiving BSC) in the first cycle of the model, based on the half-cycle corrected model trace. This contradicts the information in CS, Section 3.5.2, Table 46, whereby**_

## Company rationale for revised base case regarding recensoring 

The Company base case prefers a without re-censoring approach whereas the EAG’s preferred base case includes a with re-censoring approach. The Company has adopted its position because re-censoring can introduce undue uncertainty when the intention is to extrapolate survival beyond the period of the trial due to loss of data. The company has explored both censoring and non-censoring approaches and notes that TSD24 does not state a preference for either approach. TSD24 states that “The loss of follow up information and the early truncation of the survival curves, due to re-censoring, may have an impact in terms of increased uncertainty when the intention is to extrapolate survival beyond the period of the trial”. With re-censoring, survival follow-up for patients receiving ripretinib is much shorter; for example, there are 20 patients left at risk at 87 weeks in the without re-censoring analysis vs 37 weeks in the with re-censoring analysis. Additionally, when plotted as Kaplan-Meier OS curves, the early truncation of the curve is immediately followed by a sharp drop in survival probability, which has a significant impact on the long-term extrapolations, largely driven by a drop in the number of patients at risk (53 to 10) (Figure 1).

|**10. What do patients or**<br>**carers think are the**<br>**disadvantages of the**<br>**technology?**|The frustration of a postcode lottery in treatment availability is a significant challenge for patients who rely on<br>these life-extending therapies. I don’t<br>know how long sunitinib will work for me but I’m very aware that after this there is currently only one more ‘line of<br>defence’ in the form of Regorafenib. It feels a bit like a “postcode lottery” on a worldwide scale at the moment, with the UK being<br>excluded.   Having a 4th line of defence (Ripretinib) available, for those of us for whom surgery is not an option,<br>would make an enormous difference and give us hope.<br>After imatinib, the drugs have more significant side effects and, in some cases, become intolerable for some<br>people to continue. For example, it is proven sunitinib<br>works better for Exon 9 or for mutations 13 and 14. However, Regorafenib works better for people from Exon 11 to<br>mutations 17 and 18. This needs to be considered when prescribing for patients to give them the best outcomes.<br>Considering personalized treatment approaches based on mutation type is also important. Access Programme, which provided Ripretinib to UK patients with disease progression, also suggests that many benefited from its availability. The question many patients are asking is: why was this international trial data sufficient for approval in other regions but not the UK? 

The cost of Ripretinib remains a major barrier—$32,000 per month is difficult to justify under NHS budgets. However, patients rightly question how a committee evaluates the worth of a life when such treatments could significantly extend survival and maintain quality of life for those who currently have no other options. Beyond the financial concerns, there’s also an urgent need for treatment personalization—rather than rigid 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th line drug sequences, prescribing based on mutation type could provide better outcomes for individual patients. These voices matter in shaping policy decisions. 

A patient said, ‘As I understand it, Ripretinib was approved by the US Food & Drug Administration (FDA) in 2020 and by the European Medicines Agency in 2021, for the treatment of patients with advanced GIST who have already had treatment with at least 3 TKIs.  Approval was based on the findings of the Phase 3 INVICTUS clinical trial, a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study, which showed a statistically significant improvement in progression-free survival with Ripretinib, in GIST patients who had received prior treatment with 3 or more TKIs.  Following this trial, an international Expanded Access Programme was initiated to provide Ripretinib to UK patients who had disease progression after at least 2 lines of approved therapies. In the INTRIGUE trial comparing Ripretinib with sunitinib (2024) the safety profile was consistently more favourable for Ripretinib.’ A further commented, ‘In the light of these findings, I very much hope that NICE will feel able to recommend the use of Ripretinib in the NHS to allow patients access to the most appropriate evidence-based care, which can prolong their lives and give hope to them and their loved ones.’ 

Another patient said, ‘This appraisal will assess the clinical and cost effectiveness of Ripretinib. Last time I checked the cost of Ripretinib was $32,000 per month. In all honesty, the life of any of us would not be seen, by the taxpayer, to be worth that amount. What criteria will the "committee" use to assess the worth of a person's life?’ 

Another commented, ‘Ripretinib has been approved for use in the USA and Europe, using the same trial data that led to NICE previously not approving it for use in the UK. This seems very strange and unfair to us as patients in the UK. It makes the NHS an outlier and suggests something went wrong in the first appraisal. A further comment, ‘There should always be new drugs being trailed and hopefully available to all when approved by NICE. Keep fighting, living a full life and stay positive as there are new and innovative ways to treat cancer.’ 

Ripretinib is not only offering another treatment level but also a more effective treatment for some GIST types post Imatinib. 

A final comment, ‘Due to the varying types of GIST, not all of the current available treatments work for patients, therefore it is important for patients to have all known affective treatments available to them to have the best quality of life with loved ones whilst living with this incurable disease.’ ‘On a separate note, I would also like to add it would be beneficial for once a patient is diagnosed with GIST, it is mandatory that the patient gets referred to a GIST specialist.’ 

We would also point out that the numbers likely to benefit from Ripretinib if approved would be small so costs would be limited. 

Patients with GISTs harbouring _KIT_ exon 9 mutation benefit more from sunitinib than do those with exon 11 mutation, because Sunitinib is better at targeting this KI _T_ ‐ independent oncogenic pathway activation. Ripretinib on the other hand has a different mechanism of action and can overcome all known primary mutations and secondary mutations associated with GIST progression and imatinib resistance, especially those in _KIT_ exons 13, 14, 17, and 18. This is particularly relevant for Exon 11 patients, where secondary mutations are a much more common cause of imatinib resistance. 

In the  INVICTUS trial, Ripretinib significantly improved mPFS in 129 patients with advanced or metastatic GISTs, including those with _KIT_ and _PDGFRA_ mutations that progressed following treatment with imatinib (first ‐ ‐ ‐ line therapy), sunitinib (second line therapy), regorafenib (fourth line therapy and beyond) and/or other drugs relative to placebo (6.3 months vs 1.0 month, _P_ < 0.0001). Ripretinib significantly prolonged the median OS (18.2 months vs 6.3 months) in this population. But, in the INTRIGUE study, patients with advanced GISTs who ‐ had been treated with imatinib received 6 weeks of Ripretinib or sunitinib as a second line therapy. The median PFS was similar between the Ripretinib and sunitinib groups (8.0 and 8.3 months, respectively). 

Patient organisation submission Ripretinib for treating advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours after 3 or more treatments (review of TA881) [ID6496]

However, looking deeper into this data, among patients with exon 11 _KIT_ mutations, the mPFS was better in the Ripretinib group (n = 163, 72.12%) than in the sunitinib group (n = 164, 72.25%; 8.3 months vs 7.0 months, HR 0.88, _P_ = 0.36)/ 

‐ Importantly, the incidence of treatment emergent adverse events (AEs) of grade ≥3 was significantly lower with Ripretinib than with sunitinib (24% vs 51%). Compared with the sunitinib group, the Ripretinib group ‐ experienced significantly fewer grades 3 and 4 treatment emergent AEs (65.6% vs 41.3%), specifically ‐ neutropenia (6.3% vs 0%), hand foot syndrome (10.0% vs 1.3%), and hypertension (26.7% vs 8.5%), and significantly fewer AEs such as diarrhoea and fatigue. 

There are two issues- one is whether NICE should fund Ripretinib as a fourth line therapy for everyone who's run out of other options; two is whether NICE should fund it earlier in treatment for specific patients with exon 11 mutations. 

1. After the three licenced TKIs there are no further treatment options in the UK, and this is out of line with treatment offers in Europe and USA. Whilst Ripretinib is not necessarily better than sunitinib head-tohead in the INTRIGUE trial, If you don't have sunitinib anymore because you've become resistant to it, INVICTUS shows that Ripretinib works well. The median overall survival was 18.2 months versus just 6.3 in the patients who got nothing. If they are going to fund 3 lines of treatment, what on earth justification do they have for stopping arbitrarily at the fourth when it's shown to prolong life? 

2. Overall, Ripretinib can as much as triple overall survival in advanced or metastatic GIST according to Invictus; INTRIGUE was less convincing but certainly showed no harm in ripritenib over sunitinib. Importantly, it has a much better side effect profile so that people can get on with their lives whilst on treatment- hand and foot syndrome is awful to live with and means people can't walk/type/support themselves, which has a major cost to society 

3. In exon 11 patients Ripretinib significantly improves progression free survival in all the major trials. Within this, patients with KIT exon 11 mutations and exon 17/18 secondary mutations had 9 times better overall survival with Ripretinib. At the very least NICE should fund Ripritenib in exon 11 patients.
