## **Living with the condition** 

|**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|GIST cancer is a Sarcoma which differs in many ways from the more commonly understood carcinoma cancers.<br>Treatment often involves surgery in addition to tablets taken orally rather than chemotherapy administered<br>intravenously.<br>Those GIST patients who are fortunate enough to be diagnosed very early while it is possible to surgically<br>remove all of the tumour before it has spread, can go on to lead cancer free lives under surveillance.<br>While a GIST cancer diagnosis is a terrible shock to patients and their families complete surgical removal is the<br>best outcome aside from the negative impact on their mental health of a cancer diagnosis.<br>For those GIST patients whose disease has already metastasized (spread to other parts of the body) at<br>diagnosis or whose disease returns after surgery the focus and all of their hopes rely upon the existence of drugs<br>that will stop / slow the growth of the tumour(s) and enable them to continue living.<br>Luckily the first, second- and third-line drugs that are available to GIST patients are very effective for the more<br>commonly found GIST mutations and as a result many patients are able to “live with GIST cancer” and continue<br>their lives as they have done previously as regards to studying, working and engaging with their families and in<br>society. There are undoubtedly side effects with all of the therapies but with guidance from oncologists, specialist<br>nurses and other patients these are in the main manageable.<br>Carers experience significant stress and distress watching the person they love battling to survive and searching<br>for treatments that will target their type of GIST.<br>Seeing other GIST patients respond to treatments designed specifically to target the mutation driving their GIST<br>cancer makes the drive to seek effective treatments for a loved ones’ type of GIST even greater.<br>Being a rare cancer, GIST patient carers often find themselves very involved in advocating for the patient to<br>ensure they are receiving the best treatment available.<br>Being a GIST cancer patient or carer is not a way of life that anyone would choose.|

## **Living with the condition** 

|**6. What is it like to live**<br>**with the condition? What**<br>**do carers experience**<br>**when caring for someone**<br>**with the condition?**|GISTs are the most common soft tissue sarcoma. An average of 795 cases of GIST are diagnosed every year in<br>England. GIST makes up 20.16% of all soft tissue sarcomas, about 0.26% of all cancers. They develop in the<br>gastrointestinal (GI) tract which runs from the oesophagus to the anus and includes the stomach and intestines.<br>Most GISTs are found in the stomach and small bowel but can occur anywhere along the GI tract. The median<br>age at diagnosis is 68 years old (Sarcoma UK,_Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)_).<br>•<br>An analysis of people diagnosed with one of 84 soft tissue sarcoma sub-types in England between 2013 and<br>2017, found that people diagnosed with GIST in England have a 5-year survival of 86%. (Source: Andrew<br>Bacon, Kwok Wong, Malee S. Fernando, Brian Rous, Roger J. W. Hill, Shane D. Collins, John Broggio,<br>Sandra J. Strauss,_Incidence and survival of soft tissue sarcoma in England between 2013 and 2017, an_<br>_analysis from the National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service_ (December 2022).<br>•<br>GIST symptoms vary depending on the tumour’s size and location. They may include blood in your poo or<br>vomit; anaemia; fatigue; fever and sweating at night; discomfort or pain in your stomach; painless lump in the<br>stomach; feeling sick and vomiting; or weight loss. The most common symptoms and side effects reported by<br>GIST patients to our 2020 and 2025_National Sarcoma Surveys_, were: fatigue, diarrhoea, changes to hair,<br>skin and nails, nausea or vomiting. Fatigue has the greatest impact on their lives, during and after treatment.<br>•<br>Many GIST respondents to our National Sarcoma Surveys reported that diagnosis and treatment negatively<br>affected their overall mental health/ wellbeing: 48% in 2020 and 50% in 2025 said “to some extent”; 9% in<br>2020 and 24% in 2025 said “severely”. 40% of GIST respondents in 2020 and over 50% in 2025, said they<br>would have liked to have received more emotional support from hospital staff during their treatment. <br>•<br>GIST patients, overall, manage to work whilst managing treatment side effects. In both surveys, according to<br>carers, around half of patients either often, sometimes, or always have trouble taking care of themselves.<br>Living with a GIST can mean relying on loved ones, impacting mentally, financially and socially on patients<br>and carers. Carers provide patients with emotional support; accompany them on trips and appointments;<br>transport and travel with the patient; and may communicate on their behalf. Carer respondents to both<br>surveys spent between a few hours or up to at least 35 hours a week giving care and support. Over half of<br>carers had to stop working or studying, either temporarily or permanently. 71% of carers in 2020 and 100% in<br>2025 said they had experienced a negative financial impact due to a patient’s sarcoma diagnosis. At least<br>80% of carers said they had felt either more often or constantly depressed or anxious since the diagnosis.|
|---|---|

|**7. What do patients or**<br>**carers think of current**<br>**treatments and care**<br>**available on the NHS?**|Three main treatment-lines exist for GIST patients with advanced disease. (1) Imatinib is effective for around<br>80% of patients and on average will control the disease for about two years. (2) Sunitinib is used if the tumour<br>becomes resistant to imatinib. (3) Regorafenib is used if a GIST cannot be operated on, has become metastatic,<br>the patient has already received Imatinib and Sunitinib but it has not worked or has had bad side effects.<br>•<br>Some treatments are more or less effective dependent on mutations within the tumour. The efficacy of<br>different treatments also partly depends on the age of the patient, any co-morbidities, and if they can tolerate<br>side-effects. Imatinib is considered to be the most-effective. Sunitib and Regorafenib can also be effective for<br>some patients; but compared to Imatinib, may have diminishing results generally and are more toxic. For a<br>very small handful of patients with Neurotrophic Tyrosine Receptor Kinase (NTRK) positive tumours including<br>sarcomas, Larotrectinib was approved in England under the _Cancer Drugs Fund_ in 2020.<br>•<br>However, there is a significant population who do not have an effective treatment because the treatment<br>does not target their mutation, or progression renders the treatment ineffective. It is common for GIST<br>patients to stop responding to treatments as they develop resistance after a certain length of time. Of the 24<br>GIST patients who responded to our_State of the Nation review_that said they had received Imatinib, Sunitinib<br>or Regorafinib: some said they were effective; others said they had significant side-effects, had to be given<br>reduced doses, or had to discontinue treatment on them. One respondent received Ripretinib on<br>compassionate grounds after becoming resistant to Regorafinib.<br>•<br>NHS England (NHSE) aims to have 75% of all cancers diagnosed at stages I or II by 2028. However, it is<br>difficult to understand the stage at which sarcoma patients are diagnosed as there is incomplete data for<br>sarcoma – on average just over 50% of sarcomas had staging data reported over the four quarters of 2024<br>(NHS England,_National Disease Registration Service, _(2024)). Many respondents to our_State of the Nation_<br>_review_, including GIST-patients, received a late diagnosis, often having to see their GP or another health<br>professional multiple times before receiving an onward referral for further scans or assessment.<br>•<br>NHS England’s_Sarcoma Service Specification_ stipulates thatallGIST patients should be treated by a<br>specialist sarcoma cancer team; but only 64% of GIST respondents in 2020 and 61% in 2025 to our national<br>surveys, said this was the case. Many GIST-patients that responded to our_State of the Nation_review<br>reported difficulties in getting the correct referral to a sarcoma specialist centre. Another national charity told<br>us that many GIST patients are unaware that they should be treated in a specialist centre and could only rely<br>on the advice given by healthcare professionals as they have little or no awareness of the current referral<br>pathway.<br>•<br>42% of GIST respondents to our 2020_National Sarcoma Survey (_and 50% in 2025 to our Survey), said they<br>were not given any information at diagnosis. 51% in 2020 and 57% in 2025 had a named clinical nurse<br>specialist. Many said that diagnosis and treatment negatively their overall mental wellbeing: 48% in 2020 and|

Is there an unmet need**<br>**for patients with this**<br>**condition?**|•<br>There is a significant population who do not have an effective treatment either because the treatment does<br>not target their mutation, or progression renders the treatment ineffective. It is common for GIST patients to<br>stop responding to treatments as they develop resistance after a certain length of time. Therefore, there is a continuing and ongoing unmet need in this population.<br>•<br>This ongoing unmet need for GIST patients, is symptomatic of inadequate support for research into<br>sarcomas, including GIST, which was highlighted by patients and healthcare professionals that responded to<br>our_State of the Nation review_. It is clear that the development of a wider range of new treatments, is due to<br>systemic barriers, due to market failure (i.e. lack of profitability), lack of funding, lack of clinical trials or<br>inequitable access to those that are being run, which hold back the development of new treatments.|

## **Disadvantages of the technology** 

|**10. What do patients or**<br>**carers think are the**<br>**disadvantages of the**<br>**technology?**|The current first three lines of treatment for GIST patients - Imatinib, Sunitinib and Regorafenib - can be more or<br>less effective dependent on mutations within the tumour. However, there is a significant population who do not<br>have an effective treatment either because the treatment does not target their mutation, or progression renders<br>the treatment ineffective. Further to this, it is common for patients to stop responding to treatments. And there are<br>currently no treatments for GIST patients after three lines of therapy. Studies have shown that following these<br>three treatments, patients have on average six weeks of life remaining.<br>By comparison, Sarcoma UK is not aware of Ripretinib having any disadvantages compared to the above current<br>standard treatments, as we understand that it may:<br>(a) Potentially extend patients' lives after three lines of therapy with reduced side-effects compared to having on<br>average only six weeks of life remaining.<br>(b) Provide an improved quality of life by mitigating: -<br>(i) Some of the physical symptoms experienced by GIST patients, including fatigue which has the greatest<br>impact, both during and after treatment, as reported to our 2020 and 2025_National Sarcoma Surveys_. As well<br>as other reported symptoms of diarrhoea; changes to hair, skin and nails; and nausea or vomiting.<br>(ii) The impact on mental wellbeing, following a diagnosis and treatment.<br>(c) Extend patients’ lives, reduce side-effects and improve quality of life, it may also mitigate the physical and<br>emotional burden on family and carers.|
|---|---|

GIST patients in **considering this condition** England diagnosed from 2013-2017 in the fifth deprivation quintile were 24% more likely to die of their disease **and the technology?** 

- Analysis of routinely collected NHS data shows that social deprivation has an impact on survival. GIST patients in England diagnosed from 2013-2017 in the fifth deprivation quintile were 24% more likely to die of their disease than those in the least deprived group (p<0.1, weak evidence). The same trend is seen with greater significance across all soft tissue sarcomas, and the findings for sarcomas appear more pronounced than for more common cancers. 

- There was also an increasing likelihood for patients to present through an emergency route as deprivation increases; although cases of soft tissue sarcoma were less common in more deprived areas for male patients. (Source: Andrew Bacon, Kwok Wong, Malee S. Fernando, Brian Rous, Roger J. W. Hill, Shane D. Collins, John Broggio, Sandra J. Strauss, _Incidence and survival of soft tissue sarcoma in England between 2013 and 2017, an analysis from the National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service_ , (December 2022). 

## **GIST patients are also affected by health inequalities related to how the NHS responds to their needs:** 

- Whilst NHSE aims to have 75% of all cancers diagnosed at stages I or II by 2028; it is difficult to understand the stage at which sarcoma patients are diagnosed as there is incomplete data for sarcoma – on average just over 50% of sarcomas had staging data reported over the four quarters of 2024 (NHS England, _National Disease Registration Service,_ (2024)). Many respondents to our _State of the Nation review_ , including GIST-patients, received a late diagnosis, often having to see their GP or another health professional multiple times before receiving an onward referral for further scans or assessment. 

- NHS England’s _Sarcoma Service Specification_ stipulates that all GIST patients should be treated by a specialist sarcoma cancer team; but only 64% of GIST respondents in 2020 and 61% in 2025 to our national surveys, said this was the case. Similarly, many people with GISTs that responded to our _State of the Nation_ review, often reported difficulties in getting the correct referral to a sarcoma specialist centre. Another national charity also told us that many GIST patients are often unaware that they should be treated in a specialist centre and could only rely on the advice given by healthcare professionals as they have little or no awareness of the current referral pathway.

## **Key messages** 

|**15. In up to 5 bullet**<br>**points, please summarise**<br>**the key messages of your**<br>**submission.**|•<br>**For people diagnosed with a GIST, fatigue has the biggest impact**, during and after treatment. As well as<br>other reported symptoms of diarrhoea; changes to hair, skin and nails; and nausea or vomiting. 48% of GIST<br>respondents in 2020 and 50% in 2025 to our_National Sarcoma Surveys_said, their mental wellbeing was<br>impacted “to some extent”; 9% in 2020 and 24% in 2025 said “severely”.<br>•<br>GIST patients work whilst dealing with treatment side effects; but according to carers in both surveys, around<br>half of patients either often, sometimes, or always have trouble taking care of themselves. Carers may have<br>to stop working or studying and have elevated levels of depression or anxiety following the diagnosis.<br>•<br>**No effective treatments exist for many GIST-patients as they do not target their mutation.**Current<br>treatments have severe side-effects – so patients may require a lower and less effective dose. They may<br>stop responding to treatment as resistance grows over time, or progression of the disease renders treatment<br>ineffective. Patients are frustrated by a lack of effective treatment options after three lines of therapy; after<br>which they may have on average six weeks of life remaining. There is a continuing and ongoing unmet need<br>for many GIST patients in this population. People in the fifth deprivation quintile are almost 25% more likely<br>to die of their disease than those in the least deprived group.<br>•<br>**Ripretinib’s benefits:**potentially extending GIST patients’ lives after three lines of therapy with reduced<br>side-effects compared to only on average only six weeks of life remaining. And provide a better quality of life<br>by mitigating symptoms experienced by GIST patients, during and after treatment, including fatigue which<br>has the greatest impact, both during and after treatment. Extending patients’ lives, reduced side-effects and<br>improved quality of life, may mitigate the physical and emotional burden on family and carers.|

- Is taken orally 

- Is life extending – allowing time to access further specifically targeted treatment options

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

## Ripretinib: 

- Inhibits the mutations that are resistant to first, second- and third-line GIST therapies. 

- Has a manageable side effect profile 

- Is taken orally 

- Is life extending – allowing time to access further specifically targeted treatment options 

- Will provide treatment equality for UK GIST patients. 

Thank you for your time.

|**6. What is your experience of living with**<br>**gastrointestinal stromal tumours?**<br>**If you are a carer (for someone with gastrointestinal**<br>**stromal tumours) please share your experience of**<br>**caring for them**|I was initially diagnosed with a gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) in 2014 after<br>collapsing on holiday with internal bleeding. I underwent a major operation to remove<br>the tumour from my duodenum, followed by 3 years of adjuvant drug therapy with<br>Imatinib. During my time on Imatinib my only significant side effect was fatigue, so I<br>was able to continue working part time in the NHS and look after my children who<br>were 7 and 11 at the time of diagnosis. Unfortunately, in 2019 the GIST returned, this<br>time to my liver, and I underwent another major operation. Although the operation<br>was successful, the GIST returned to one of my ribs 6 months later, and so I was put<br>back on Imatinib indefinitely. As well as the drug therapy, the last 5 years have seen<br>2 further operations and 6 weeks of radiotherapy which have all taken their toll,<br>physically and mentally, but I was able to sustain a fairly normal life continuing to<br>work part-time, look after my family, and do things that I enjoy like walking, eating<br>out, going to shows and concerts, and going on holiday. Imatinib has been the key<br>stone in my survival over the last 10 years, but sadly this has now stopped working<br>for me, as my GIST has mutated to Exon 17 and is no longer sensitive to the drug. I<br>am now taking part in a clinical trial for a 2ndline drug and will then continue onto<br>Sunitinib and Regorafenib in due course. This has been really difficult to cope with<br>mentally as the clinical trial has uncertain outcomes by its very nature, and Sunitinib<br>is not particularly effective against Exon 17. I could therefore potentially be in an<br>extremely life limiting situation. Ripretinib offers real hope for a patient in my situation<br>because it is proven to be effective against my particular mutation and it is<br>documented to be well tolerated, which would preserve my quality of life, possibly for<br>a year or more which is a huge difference when you are living with terminal illness. It<br>is my dearest wish to see my daughter graduate from university in 3 years – hope is<br>what keeps me going.|

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

- Ripretinib is particularly effective for GIST patients with Exon 17/18 mutations. 

- Ripretinib is well tolerated by patients in terms of side effects and biological toxicities. 

- Ripretinib will in some cases be a vital 2[nd] or 3[rd] line treatment if other TKIs have failed to work or are intolerable. 

- Ripretinib offers a level of certainty for an extended period of ‘qualtiy’ life in which valuable preparations can be made. 

- GIST is rare with few breakthroughs – access to Ripretinib would help to redress the inequality of treatment options. 

Thank you for your time.

## **1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY** 

This report assesses ripretinib for the treatment of advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) after at least three prior treatments, including imatinib. This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the External Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision-making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental costeffectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 provides an overview of key model outcomes and the modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER. Sections 1.3 to 1.5 explain the key issues in more detail. The results of the EAG’s preferred analysis are summarised in Section 1.6. Background information on the condition, technology and evidence and information on non-key issues are detailed in the main EAG report. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). 

## **1.1 Overview of the EAG’s key issues** 

The key issues identified by the EAG are summarised in Table 1. 

## **Table 1: Summary of the EAG’s key issues** 

|**Table 1:**|**Summary of the EAG’s key issues**||
|---|---|---|
|**ID3805**|**Summary of issue**|**Report sections**|
|Issue 1|Concerns regarding the exclusion of a later data-cut of<br>INVICTUS from the company’s model|4.3.5,critical appraisal<br>point 2|
|Issue 2|<br>Uncertainty surrounding the long-term benefits of ripretinib<br>on OS, including the effects of BID dosing|<br>4.3.5,critical appraisal<br>points 3 and 5|
|Issue 3|<br>Inconsistency between the health outcomes and costs<br>associated with BID dosing in the company’s model|<br>4.3.5,critical appraisal<br>point 4|



_EAG - External Assessment Group; OS - overall survival; BID - twice daily_ 

The company’s economic model is informed by analyses of overall survival (OS) data from the INVICTUS trial (in which some patients dose-escalated to ripretinib 150mg twice daily [BID] after disease progression) but includes the costs of ripretinib 150mg once daily (QD) dosing only. The key difference between the company’s base case model and the EAG’s preferred analysis relates to how OS is modelled. The company’s model applies log-logistic distributions fitted to OS data which have been adjusted for treatment switching in the best supportive care (BSC) group and OS data which have not been adjusted for the effects of BID dosing in the ripretinib group. The EAG’s preferred model includes adjustment of the ripretinib OS data to remove the effects of BID dosing using the two-stage estimation method and applies a log-logistic model fitted to the BID-adjusted OS data. The EAG’s preferred model also applies a generalised gamma distribution to the switching-adjusted OS data in the BSC group. 

12 



<!-- page 364 -->

## **1.2 Overview of key model outcomes** 

NICE technology appraisals (TAs) compare how much a new technology improves length of life (OS) and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

Compared with BSC alone, ripretinib is assumed to impact on QALYs by: 

- Extending progression-free survival (PFS) 

- Extending OS 

- Slightly reducing HRQoL due to a higher burden of adverse events (AEs). 

Compared with BSC alone, ripretinib is assumed to affect costs by: 

- Increasing overall costs due to the acquisition cost of ripretinib (including use of the drug after disease progression) 

- Increasing overall disease management costs due to extended OS 

- Increasing the costs associated with managing AEs. 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER for ripretinib versus BSC are: 

- Whether OS data in the ripretinib group are adjusted to account for the effect of postprogression ripretinib 150mg BID dosing in the INVICTUS trial. Adjustment using the twostage estimation method with re-censoring leads to higher ICERs compared with the equivalent adjustment models excluding re-censoring. 

- The choice of parametric survival model fitted to the adjusted/unadjusted ripretinib OS data. 

- Whether the OS data in the BSC group are adjusted to account for confounding due to treatment switching in the placebo group of INVICTUS. 

## **1.3 The decision problem: Summary of the EAG’s key issues** 

The company’s submission (CS) describes the current treatment pathway for patients with advanced GIST as being comprised of first-line imatinib, second-line sunitinib, third-line regorafenib and BSC. The evidence in the CS relates to the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of fourth- and subsequent-line (4L+) ripretinib (plus BSC) versus BSC alone for the treatment of patients with advanced GIST. The decision problem addressed in the CS is generally in line with the final NICE scope. The value proposition presented in the CS reflects the use of ripretinib within its marketing authorisation i.e., at a dose of 150mg once daily (QD). However, the CS also presents an economic scenario analysis in which the costs of BID dosing are included. 

In the previous NICE appraisal of ripretinib for GIST (TA881), clinical advisors to the Evidence Review Group (ERG) explained that a large proportion (50% or more) of patients who receive third-line regorafenib continue to receive this treatment after progression. The clinical advisors commented that if ripretinib was recommended for use in the NHS, they would discontinue regorafenib at the point of 

13 



<!-- page 365 -->

progression; this indicates that continued post-progression regorafenib may be considered as a relevant comparator for ripretinib. However, in this previous appraisal, the company concluded that insufficient data exist to inform a reliable indirect treatment comparison (ITC). The EAG believes that data to inform this ITC are still lacking. 

## **1.4 The clinical effectiveness evidence: Summary of the EAG’s key issues** 

The CS presents data from the INVICTUS randomised controlled trial (RCT) of ripretinib 150mg QD (once a day) plus BSC versus placebo plus BSC in 129 patients with advanced GIST who had progressed on, or were intolerant to, (at least) imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib. Upon progression, patients randomised to ripretinib could discontinue ripretinib, continue their current dose of 150mg QD, or double their dose to 150mg BID, whilst patients randomised to placebo who progressed could discontinue the study or switch to ripretinib 150mg QD. At the May 2019 data cut-off (DCO), median PFS was 6.3 months for ripretinib versus 1.0 months for placebo (hazard ratio [HR] 0.15, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.09 to 0.25, _p_ <0.0001). Median OS was 15.1 months for ripretinib versus 6.6 months for placebo (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.62, _p_ =not reported [NR]), 11.6 months in placebo crossover patients, and 1.8 months in placebo non-crossover patients. At the January 2021 DCO, the most common Grade 3/4 treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) with ripretinib (vs. placebo) were: anaemia (11% vs. 14%); abdominal pain (7% vs. 5%); hypertension (7% vs. 0%); increased lipase (5% vs. 0%) and hypophosphataemia (5% vs. 0%). At the May 2019 DCO, treatment-related Grade 3/4 TEAEs were reported in xxx of patients in the ripretinib arm and xxx of patients in the placebo arm. TEAEs of special interest included squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the skin xxx xxxx xx xxx and actinic keratosis xxxxxx xx xxxx. 

The EAG’s clinical advisors considered the population of enrolled in INVICTUS to be broadly representative of those who would be seen in NHS practice. At the factual accuracy check (FAC) stage of the appraisal, the company clarified that its proposed positioning of ripretinib is as a fourth- and subsequent-line (4L+) therapy, which is aligned with the patient population enrolled in INVICTUS. 

The clinical evidence presented in the CS also includes Real World Evidence (RWE) from the Royal Marsden expanded access cohort study of ripretinib for treating GIST. Forty-two percent of patients included in this study had received only two prior lines of treatment before initiating ripretinib. As this is not consistent with the licensed indication for ripretinib, these patients fall outside the scope of the appraisal. This limits the relevance of this study. 

## **1.5 The cost-effectiveness evidence: Summary of the EAG’s key issues** 

The company’s economic model assesses the cost-effectiveness of ripretinib plus BSC versus BSC alone for the 4L+ treatment of patients with advanced GIST. The model adopts a partitioned survival approach which includes four health states: (i) progression-free; (ii) progressed disease (on treatment); 

14 



<!-- page 366 -->

(iii) progressed disease (off treatment/BSC), and (iv) dead. The analysis adopts an NHS and Personal Social Services (PSS) perspective, including QALYs accrued by GIST patients; caregiver effects are not included. Clinical outcomes for both treatment groups are based on parametric survival models fitted to data on PFS and OS from INVICTUS, including adjustment of OS in the BSC group to account for treatment switching which occurred in the placebo arm of the trial. The company’s base case analysis applies the costs of ripretinib 150mg QD dosing only and does not include any statistical adjustment of OS in the ripretinib group to account for the effects of post-progression ripretinib 150mg BID dose escalation on OS in the intervention arm of the trial. Health state utility values are based on Euroqol 5- Dimensions 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) data from INVICTUS (mapped to the 3-level version) based on a mixed model for repeat measures (MMRM) analysis. Resource use and cost parameters were taken from a clinical expert survey used in NICE TA488, standard costing sources and other literature. 

A Patient Access Scheme (PAS) has been proposed for ripretinib; this takes the form of a simple price discount of xxx (PAS price = xxxxxx for 30 days’ supply). All ICERs presented in this EAG report include this PAS. The company’s base case model applies a decision modifier of 1.7 which is consistent with estimates obtained from the York QALY Shortfall Calculator. Following the clarification round, the company submitted a revised version of the model which included the correction of errors and additional functionality to address several issues raised in the EAG’s clarification letter. The probabilistic version of the company’s updated model suggests that compared with BSC, ripretinib generates an additional xxxx QALYs at an additional cost of xxxxxxx; including the decision modifier of 1.7, the ICER is expected to be £28,576 per QALY gained. The deterministic version of the model suggests a slightly higher ICER of £28,730 per QALY gained. 

The EAG critically appraised the company’s health economic analysis and double-programmed the deterministic version of the company’s original model. The EAG also checked the amendments applied in the company’s updated model. The EAG’s critical appraisal identified three key issues: the exclusion of a later data-cut of OS from INVICTUS from the company’s model (Issue 1); uncertainty surrounding the long-term benefits of ripretinib on OS, including the effects of BID dosing (Issue 2), and inconsistency between the health outcomes and costs associated with BID dosing in the company’s model (Issue 3).

## **1.6 Summary of EAG’s preferred model and sensitivity analysis results** 

The results of the EAG’s preferred model and additional sensitivity analyses are summarised in Table 

2. Exploratory analysis 1 (EA1) reflects the EAG-corrected version of the company’s model (deterministic). EAs 2-4 also include these corrections. EA4 is the EAG’s preferred model. 

18 



<!-- page 370 -->

The company’s updated base case model suggests that the deterministic ICER for ripretinib versus BSC is £28,730 per QALY gained. The EAG’s preferred model suggests a higher ICER of £52,822 per QALY gained. The main driver for this higher ICER is the adjustment of the ripretinib OS data to account for the effects of ripretinib 150mg BID dosing using the two-stage method. The EAG’s additional sensitivity analyses indicate that the ICER for ripretinib is likely to be lower when the OS data are not adjusted for BID dosing and instead the costs of BID dosing are included in the analysis. The EAG’s other sensitivity analyses indicate that the ICER for ripretinib is sensitive to: the choice of parametric survival model for OS; whether the BID-adjustment of OS includes re-censoring; whether the BSC OS data are adjusted for treatment switching and the choice of parametric survival model selected for TTD.

## **2. BACKGROUND** 

This report evaluates ripretinib for the treatment of adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors, including imatinib. This assessment has been conducted to inform the re-appraisal of NICE Technology Appraisal (TA) 881.[1] As with TA881, the main evidence to inform the clinical effectiveness of ripretinib comes from the INVICTUS randomised controlled trial (RCT).[2] The main difference between the company’s submission (CS) presented in TA881 and the submission for the current appraisal relates to the company’s proposed use of ripretinib, which now includes the use of ripretinib prior to and following disease progression for patients who are still deriving benefit from treatment (i.e., the proposed treatment stopping rule in TA881 no longer forms part of the company’s value proposition). As the clinical evidence informing the economic model for this appraisal remains unchanged from TA881, some sections of this EAG report are based on the same content contained in the Evidence Review Group (ERG) report which was produced to inform the earlier appraisal. This EAG report also includes reference to clinical input received by the ERG in TA881. 

This chapter presents a brief summary and critique of the company’s description of the disease, the company’s overview of the current treatment pathway and its intended positioning of ripretinib, and a summary and critique of the decision problem addressed in the CS.[3] 

## **2.1 Company’s description of the underlying health problem** 

## _2.1.1 Overview of GIST_ 

The company’s description of the disease (Section 1.4 of the CS[3] ) is summarised briefly here together with additional information from the previous ERG report for TA881[4] as well as further input from the EAG's clinical advisors. The EAG’s clinical advisors agree that the company’s description of GIST is broadly accurate. 

Soft tissue sarcomas account for 1% of malignancies in adults, and GISTs account for approximately 7% of all soft tissue sarcomas.[5] GIST is a mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. GIST most frequently develops in the stomach (60-70% of cases) or small intestine (25-35% of cases), or in the colon, rectum or other rare sites (4-5% of cases).[3] The median age at presentation is between 60 and 65 years. GIST is not commonly diagnosed in people aged under 40 years (<10%).[6] 

The majority of patients present with symptoms at diagnosis and approximately half have acute or chronic GI bleeding.[7-9] Symptoms of GIST are often non-specific and include GI pain, nausea, early satiety, abdominal bloating, anaemia, detection of an abdominal mass, gastric discomfort or ulcer-like symptoms.[7, 8, 10-12] Common sites of GIST metastases include the liver (65%) and the peritoneum (21%), whilst less than 10% of tumours metastasise to the lungs or bone.[13] Disease progression to advanced 

21 



<!-- page 373 -->

stages often has a negative impact on the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of patients as well as a reduction in cognitive and social functioning. Patients with advanced GIST are often also functionally impaired, with 19% having a baseline Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 2 or 3.[14, 15] Section 1.4 of the CS[3] states that clinical experts consulted by the company suggested that the expected survival of patients who have received four or more therapies for advanced GIST and who are treated with best supportive care (BSC) is two to three months. The EAG’s clinical advisors agreed that the prognosis for these patients is very poor, with few patients receiving BSC alone expected to remain alive after 12 months. 

## _2.1.2 Genetics of GIST_ 

The CS[3] (Section 1.1) states that GIST is generally driven by mutations in the KIT (also referred to as CD117) or platelet derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRA) receptor tyrosine kinases. These mutations often lead to constitutively activated KIT or PDGFRA (i.e., their cellular signalling activity is permanently “turned on”). Approximately 80% of GISTs have primary mutations in KIT, and 5-10% have a mutation in PDGFRA. Around 10% of GISTs lack mutations in KIT or PDGFRA genes and are referred to as wild-type; these cases often have mutations in other genes.[16] Most primary KIT mutations involve a single mutation at diagnosis; however, secondary acquired mutations can also occur over time in response to treatment with targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapies, leading to treatment resistance. Primary and secondary mutations are a known issue in GIST, and patients may have multiple mutations. 

## **2.2 Company’s overview of current service provision** 

## _2.2.1 Primary localised GIST: surgery and adjuvant imatinib_ 

Surgery is the recommended approach for primary and localised GIST and is the only potentially curative option. Around one-third of patients have an intermediate to high risk of disease progression and approximately 50% have disease recurrence within 2 to 3 years following resection.[8, 17] Patients who are at high risk of recurrence can receive adjuvant imatinib for up to 3 years. 

## _2.2.2 Current treatment pathway and proposed positioning of ripretinib_ 

The company’s view of the current treatment pathway for advanced GIST and its proposed positioning of ripretinib is shown in Figure 1. Whilst not shown in the diagram, each TKI would be given alongside BSC. The CS[3] (Section 1.4.2) states that approximately 50% of patients present with metastatic or unresectable GIST at diagnosis and around 40-90% of surgical patients develop subsequent recurrence or metastasis.[18, 19] Targeted therapy with TKIs is the standard of care for metastatic or unresectable GIST due to their anti-KIT and anti-PDGFRA properties. Imatinib is the standard first-line treatment in England. Disease progression after imatinib treatment occurs mostly due to primary resistance, secondary KIT mutation or inadequate drug exposure. If progression or imatinib intolerance is 

22 



<!-- page 374 -->

confirmed, the standard second-line treatment is sunitinib. Most patients will experience relapse again within 6 months to 1 year due to additional or alternative secondary mutations in KIT, or due to multiple different KIT mutations occurring in different areas of the tumour. In addition, some imatinib-resistant patients have primary resistance to sunitinib due to the specific secondary mutation(s) that arise during imatinib treatment. Regorafenib is regarded as standard therapy for the third-line treatment of patients who progress on or fail to respond to imatinib and sunitinib. 

The CS[3] (Section 1.4.2) states that there is no established standard care for GIST patients in the UK who have received prior treatment with three or more TKIs, including imatinib, other than BSC. The CS highlights that some patients may be enrolled into clinical trials or, as a last resort, they may be offered continued post-progression regorafenib. The company’s proposed positioning in the treatment pathway for advanced GIST is shown in Figure 1. The CS describes the proposed positioning of ripretinib is as a 4L therapy; however, at the factual accuracy check (FAC) stage of the appraisal, the company clarified that the proposed positioning of ripretinib is as a fourth- and subsequent-line (4L+) therapy.  Whilst not explicitly shown in Figure 1, the company is seeking a positive recommendation from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) for ripretinib treatment prior to and following disease progression (for patients who are still obtaining benefit from treatment).

_2.2.3 EAG’s critique of the company’s treatment pathway and positioning of ripretinib_ The EAG’s clinical advisors agreed that the company’s description of the current treatment pathway is accurate. The company’s proposed positioning of ripretinib within the pathway is consistent with the final NICE scope[20] and the marketing authorisation for ripretinib.[21] 

In TA881,[1] the EAG’s clinical advisors commented that a large proportion of patients (50% or more) who progress on third-line regorafenib will continue to receive this treatment after disease progression if they are still tolerating and deriving clinical benefit from it and there are no other alternative treatment options, whilst the remainder will receive BSC alone. The relevance of regorafenib as a comparator for ripretinib is discussed briefly in Section 2.3.3. One of the EAG’s clinical advisors stated that in the 

23 



<!-- page 375 -->

absence of other therapies beyond third-line, they may sometimes consider rechallenging using imatinib, but that this approach does not reflect standard of care. 

The EAG’s clinical advisors agreed with the company’s proposed use of ripretinib beyond disease progression and commented that the continued use of TKI therapy in patients with active disease progression is consistent with clinical recommendations on the use of TKIs in patients with advanced and progressed GIST published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network [NCCN] Task Force[22] and UK clinical practice guidelines for the management of GIST.[23] The 2022 update to the NCCN guidelines[24] does not mention the use of continued regorafenib following progression on third-line therapy as it instead recommends ripretinib as 4L therapy. The 2024 update to the British Sarcoma Group guideline mentions that post-progression regorafenib is sometimes used, but places greater emphasis on the need to recruit patients into clinical trials, when available.[25]

## _2.3.1  Population_ 

The final NICE scope[20] specifies the relevant population as adults with advanced GIST who have received prior treatment with three or more TKIs, including imatinib. The main clinical evidence for ripretinib included in the CS[3] comes from the INVICTUS RCT.[2] Patients enrolled in INVICTUS were adults with advanced GIST with progression on at least imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib or documented intolerance to any of these treatments despite dose modifications. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) and Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) marketing authorisation for ripretinib relates to _“adult patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) who have received prior treatment with three or more kinase inhibitors, including imatinib.”_[21] As such, the populations defined in the NICE scope, the key clinical evidence and the marketing authorisation for ripretinib are all broadly aligned. 

## _2.3.2 Intervention_ 

The intervention described in the CS[3] is consistent with the final NICE scope.[20] The intervention under consideration is ripretinib (Qinlock[®] ). Ripretinib is a novel TKI which inhibits KIT proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase and PDGFRA kinase, including wild-type, primary, and secondary mutations. Ripretinib also inhibits other kinases _in vitro_ , such as PDGFRB, TIE2, VEGFR2, and BRAF.[21] 

A full marketing authorisation for ripretinib was issued by the MHRA in December 2021. According to the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) for ripretinib,[21] the recommended dose is 150mg ripretinib (three 50mg tablets) taken once daily (QD) at the same time each day with or without food. Ripretinib is administered orally in tablet form. The list price per pack of 90 x 50mg ripretinib tablets (30 days’ supply) is £18,400.[26] The CS[3] states that a Patient Access Scheme (PAS) has been proposed for ripretinib: this takes the form of a simple price discount of xxx. The price per pack of ripretinib including the PAS is xxxxxx. 

The INVICTUS trial[2] allowed patients in the ripretinib group to continue to receive the study drug after disease progression. The SmPC for ripretinib[21] states that treatment with ripretinib should continue as long as benefit is observed or until unacceptable toxicity; as such, treatment beyond disease progression is permitted within the marketing authorisation. The EAG’s clinical advisors commented that if ripretinib was recommended by NICE, they would want to be able to continue to offer treatment with ripretinib beyond disease progression if patients were still deriving clinical benefit from it. The clinical experts consulted by the EAG and the company commented that they expected continued ripretinib given after disease progression to improve OS.[27] In contrast to the company’s earlier submission in TA881,[1] the proposed use of ripretinib within the CS for the current appraisal includes the use of postprogression ripretinib. 

27 



<!-- page 379 -->

The INVICTUS trial[2] also permitted the use of intra-patient dose escalation (IPDE) to ripretinib 150mg BID (twice daily) following disease progression on ripretinib 150mg QD in both treatment groups. Clinical experts consulted by the company commented that the 150mg BID dosing regimen is expected to have led to a _“non-negligible”_ impact on OS. The EAG’s clinical advisors stated that they would expect BID dosing to improve OS but that the magnitude of the benefit is uncertain. The 150mg BID dosing regimen is not mentioned in the ripretinib SmPC,[21] except in the situation whereby ripretinib is co-administered alongside strong or moderate CYP3A inducers, and therefore represents an off-label use of the drug. The EAG’s clinical advisors stated that they would want to be able to use 150mg BID dosing post-progression, if permitted and where clinically appropriate. The company’s proposed use of ripretinib in the CS[3] is limited to the use of the 150mg QD (once daily) dose. The company’s base case economic model applies the outcomes observed in INVICTUS[2] (including IPDE to the ripretinib 150mg BID dose in some patients) with ripretinib costs restricted to the 150mg QD dose (see Section 4.3.5). 

The CS[3] states that additional testing is required for people prior to and during treatment with ripretinib. This includes: (i) monitoring for people with a history of high blood pressure which may require blood pressure medication, as clinically indicated; (ii) ejection fraction assessment using an echocardiogram or multiple gated acquisition (MUGA) scan prior to initiating and during treatment with ripretinib, as clinically indicated, and (iii) dermatological evaluations due to the increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). 

## _2.3.3  Comparators_ 

The final NICE scope[20] includes a single comparator - established clinical management. The INVICTUS trial[2] was placebo-controlled (given  alongside BSC), and the comparator considered in the CS[3] and the company’s economic model is BSC alone. Patients who were randomised to the placebo group of INVICTUS were permitted to switch treatment to receive ripretinib after disease progression; the company’s economic model includes statistical adjustment of the OS data to account for potential confounding caused by treatment switching onto ripretinib in the placebo arm of the trial; these methods are described in Section 4.2.4. 

In TA881,[1] the ERG’s clinical advisors commented that a large proportion of patients who have progressed on third-line regorafenib (after previously failing earlier treatment with both sunitinib and imatinib) continue to receive regorafenib if they are still obtaining benefit from it. The clinical advisors also stated that if ripretinib received a positive NICE recommendation, they would switch patients onto 4L ripretinib as soon as they progress on third-line regorafenib. On this basis, continued postprogression regorafenib may be considered as a relevant comparator to ripretinib. However, in TA881, the company was unable to identify sufficient evidence to inform a reliable indirect treatment comparison (ITC) between ripretinib and regorafenib. The Appraisal Committee acknowledged that the 

28 



<!-- page 380 -->

absence of such a comparison introduced uncertainty, but concluded that BSC is likely the most appropriate comparator for the appraisal, given the available evidence.[1] The EAG believes that evidence on PFS and OS outcomes for continued post-progression regorafenib is still lacking and therefore this issue is not discussed in detail in this EAG report. 

## _2.3.4  Outcomes_ 

The following outcomes are listed in the final NICE scope:[20] 

- Progression-free survival (PFS) 

- Overall survival (OS) 

- Response rate (including partial response rate and duration of response) 

- Stable disease 

- Adverse effects of treatment 

- Health-related quality of life (HRQoL). 

The CS[3] reports on all of these outcomes for the ITT population of INVICTUS.[2] The company’s economic model is informed by data on PFS, time to treatment discontinuation (TTD), OS, adverse events (AEs) and HRQoL from INVICTUS (see Section 3.2.4). 

## _2.3.5  Other relevant factors_ 

Section 1.5 of the CS[3] states that there are no known equality issues relating to the use of ripretinib for treating advanced GIST after three or more therapies. 

29 



<!-- page 381 -->

## **3. CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS** 

The clinical evidence contained in the CS[3] is comprised of: 

- A systematic literature review (SLR) 

- Summary and results of the INVICTUS[2] trial of ripretinib. 

- Summary and results of real-world evidence (RWE) from the Royal Marsden expanded access cohort study.[28] 

This chapter summarises and critiques the company’s review methods and the clinical effectiveness data contained in the CS.[3] Full details are presented in Section 2 of the CS and CS Appendices B, C, and D.[29] 

## **3.1 Critique of the methods of review** 

## _3.1.1 Searches_ 

The company performed an SLR to identify all clinical effectiveness and safety studies of ripretinib or comparator treatments for advanced, unresectable, or metastatic patients with 4L+ GIST.  The company performed an initial SLR in July 2020 followed by five updates in July 2021, March 2022, May 2023, April 2024 and March 2025 (CS, Appendix D).[29] 

The EAG identified two main limitations in the clinical effectiveness searches: 

- Restricted terms and fields to search for prior treatments (4L+ studies) 

- The absence of intervention and comparator terms from the searches. 

The company searched a single Ovid host platform that comprises a suite of databases including: MEDLINE; Embase; Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR); Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL); ACP Journal Club; Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE); Cochrane Clinical Answers; Cochrane Methodology Register; Health Technology Assessment (HTA); NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED) and EconLit. The company hand searched the bibliographies of relevant SLRs to identify other new studies for inclusion. 

Three conference abstract websites were also searched for the last five years (2021-2025): American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) and ASCO Gastrointestinal Cancers Symposium. The company searched clinicaltrials.gov for ongoing, completed or unpublished trials. Four HTA agency websites were also searched: NICE; Scottish Medicines Consortium (SMC); Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC); and Canada’s Drug Agency (CDA-AMC). 

30 



<!-- page 382 -->

The company applied multiple concept combinations to the search for the population (disease GIST AND “metastatic/advanced/unresectable” AND relapsed/refractory/resistant). The company’s searches also applied a limit to patients who have had prior treatment by searching for the drugs imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib (see CS Appendix B,[29] statement 19 in Table 4: Search strategy: Clinical SLR). The EAG would have recommended either the inclusion of the synonyms/drug trade names in statement 19 of the electronic search strategy (Table 4 of CS Appendix B[29] ) such as those listed on page 34 of CS Appendix B, i.e., _"gleevec OR glivec OR sti571 OR stivarga OR bay 73-4506 OR sutent OR su011248"_ , or the use of “multi-purpose” field as opposed to title and abstract searching (which will search for drug trade names, registry number and chemical name of the drugs). Omitting drug name synonyms results in a lower search recall (i.e., finds fewer relevant studies) which will impact the comprehensiveness of the search. In addition, according to Chapter 4 of the Technical Supplement of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions,[30] _.mp_ field searching is preferred over title and abstract field searching for interventions as it increases the sensitivity of the search because the relevant terms could be found elsewhere such as the subject headings. 

The company restricted the database searches to English language publications. According to the Cochrane Handbook,[30] applying language filters to restrict the search may lead to publication language bias, where relevant studies published in other languages are excluded. 

The EAG suggests that the drug term ripretinib should have been included in the ‘prior therapy’ concept search statement, as there will invariably be studies where the prior therapies are not mentioned in the title and abstracts. The EAG repeated the company’s MEDLINE and Embase search which showed that only 26 out of 39 included studies would be retrieved in the RCT search. However, if the term ripretinib was included in the strategy, this would find a further four of the included studies: Becker _et al._ , 2021;[31] Zalcberg _et al._ , 2021;[32] von Mehren _et al._ , 2019;[33] and Janku _et al._ , 2020.[34] 

The EAG also recommends the inclusion of the comparator terms listed in the SLR eligibility criteria, and the ‘approved interventions’ and ‘other interventions’ listed in the included studies (Tables 5 and Table 6 of CS Appendix B[29] ). 

Given the limitations mentioned above, the EAG believes that the company’s electronic search strategy alone is not sufficient to find all relevant studies. The company’s supplementary searches, which include reference tracking and grey literature searches, may have mitigated the impact of the limitations described above. 

## _3.1.2 Inclusion criteria for the SLR_ 

The clinical SLR described in the CS[3] is broader than the decision problem defined in the NICE scope.[20] The SLR included RCTs and single-arm interventional studies of patients with advanced GIST 

31 



<!-- page 383 -->

receiving 4L+ therapy, published from the year 2000 onwards. The included interventions were: ripretinib; imatinib; regorafenib; sunitinib; BSC and other interventions for 4L+ GIST. The EAG considers the inclusion criteria to be appropriate to identify RCTs of ripretinib for the 4L+ treatment of GIST. 

## _3.1.3 Critique of study selection, data extraction and quality assessment_ 

The CS[3] does not report details about the process used for study selection, data extraction or quality assessment. Following a request for clarification from the EAG[35] (question A1), the company confirmed that screening, data extraction and quality assessment were undertaken by two independent reviewers, and checked by a third independent analyst. The EAG considers these methods to be appropriate. The company assessed the quality of the included INVICTUS RCT[2] using the NICE quality assessment checklist (CS Appendix B1.3).[29] However, the CS did not include a quality assessment of the Royal Marsden expanded access cohort study.[28] Following a request from the EAG[35] (question A8) the company quality assessed this study using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) Cohort Study Checklist. The EAG considers the use of these quality assessment tools to be appropriate. 

## _3.1.4 EAG’s view on the company’s review methods_ 

Overall, the EAG considers that the majority of the company’s review methods were appropriate, with the exception of the limitations in the search methods described in Section 3.1.1. 

## _3.1.5 Results of the company’s SLR_ 

The company’s clinical SLR identified 39 publications, 15 of which assessed ripretinib and were relevant to this submission (see CS,[3] Section 2.2, Table 3). Of these, 10 publications related to the INVICTUS trial of ripretinib, the primary references being the INVICTUS Clinical Study Report (CSR)[2] and Blay _et al._ (2020).[36] Two publications[37, 38] were related to a Phase 2 single-arm, open-label study of ripretinib (NCT04282980) and a further two publications[34, 39] related to a Phase 1 nonrandomised dose escalation study of ripretinib (NCT02571036). These publications are not discussed further in the CS[3] or in this EAG report. Therefore, the SLR identified only one relevant study: the INVICTUS RCT of ripretinib.[2] Although outside the remit of the SLR for the clinical effectiveness, the CS presents details of the methods and results of an RWE study undertaken at the Royal Marsden Hospital in London (UK) as part of an expanded access programme.[28] The CS[3] notes that this study was not used to inform the company’s economic model due to its retrospective nature, shorter follow-up period and smaller sample size compared with INVICTUS.[2] In addition, the CS[3] also included insights from three advisory board meetings with oncologists based in the UK; these meetings were held in August 2022, July 2024 and April 2025.[27, 40, 41 ] 

32

## **3.2 Characteristics of INVICTUS study of ripretinib** 

## _3.2.1 Study design: INVICTUS_ 

The company’s SLR identified one relevant RCT of ripretinib.[2] INVICTUS is an international, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial in patients with advanced GIST after at least three prior anticancer therapies. INVICTUS compared the efficacy of ripretinib plus BSC versus placebo plus BSC (CS,[3] Section 2.3). The study was conducted at 29 specialised hospitals across 12 countries across North America, Europe, and Asia. The design of the INVICTUS RCT is summarised in Table 4 and Figure 2.

## _Population in INVICTUS_ 

The INVICTUS trial[2] included 129 patients with advanced GIST who had received at least three prior anticancer therapies including (at least) imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib. The inclusion criteria for INVICTUS are slightly more restrictive than the final NICE scope[20] and the SmPC for ripretinib,[21] both of which specify the population as patients who have received at least three prior kinase inhibitors, including imatinib. Approximately 37% of patients in INVICTUS had received more than three prior therapies at enrolment (i.e., they were at fifth-line or later). 

## _Intervention in INVICTUS_ 

Patients were randomised 2:1 to ripretinib plus BSC versus placebo plus BSC. In total, 85 patients were randomised to ripretinib and 44 to placebo. The ripretinib dose was 150mg QD (once a day) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. 

34 



<!-- page 386 -->

Upon progression, patients and investigators were unblinded, and patients randomised to ripretinib could either discontinue ripretinib, continue their current dose of ripretinib 150mg QD, or double their dose to 150mg BID (twice per day). Patients randomised to placebo could discontinue the study or cross over to receive ripretinib 150mg QD. Patients who crossed over to ripretinib and then experienced a second disease progression were given the option to continue treatment at an increased dose of 150mg BID, to continue their current dose of 150mg QD, or to discontinue treatment with ripretinib. Ripretinib dose interruption or dose reduction was permitted at the discretion of the investigators at any time due to adverse events (AEs). The company’s clarification response in TA881[42] (question A4) states that the rationale for permitting patients in the ripretinib group to double their dose was because this higher dose was well-tolerated in the Phase 1 study (NCT02571036)[34, 39] and so BID dosing was offered to patients with disease progression in INVICTUS[2] due to the lack of alternative treatments, even though 150mg QD was established as the recommended dose based on safety, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics data. The EAG notes that the recommended dose in the SmPC for ripretinib[21] is 150mg QD, and the company’s base case economic model applies the outcomes for the ITT population (including post-progression BID dosing in some patients) and only the costs of QD dose (see Section 4.2). 

## _Comparator in INVICTUS_ 

The comparator in INVICTUS[2] was placebo plus BSC. The EAG’s clinical advisors consider that it was reasonable to compare against placebo plus BSC because there are no further recommended 4L+ therapies in England. 

## _Outcomes in INVICTUS_ 

Outcomes included: PFS; PFS1 (time from randomisation until progressed disease [PD] in patients who received IPDE in the ripretinib arm); PFS2 (time from the first dose of ripretinib 150mg BID to PD or death in patients who received IPDE in the ripretinib arm); OS; time to progression (TTP); response rates; TTD; AEs and HRQoL measured using the 5-level Euroqol 5 dimensions (EQ-5D-5L) questionnaire, the Euroqol visual analogue scale (EQ-VAS) and the physical and role functioning domains of the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire for Cancer 30-item questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30). 

## _Study quality of INVICTUS_ 

Quality assessment of INVICTUS[2] is presented in CS Appendix B1.3.[29] The CS[3] reports that the study is of high methodological quality in terms of: randomisation; baseline comparability of groups; blinding of patients and staff; no unexpected imbalances in drop-outs; no selective outcome reporting and use of ITT analysis. The EAG largely agrees with the company’s quality assessment. However, the EAG notes the following points regarding study design: 

35 



<!-- page 387 -->

- a) There were some differences in baseline characteristics between the groups (see Section 3.2.3) 

- b) The study was unblinded on progression, and patients were permitted to continue or change treatment (including dose-escalating to ripretinib 150mg BID) on progression. These factors may have impacted on OS, which was measured until the patient died. 

- c) No attempt has been made in the CS[3] to integrate the assessment of study quality into the findings reported. 

## _Analysis populations and data cut-offs in INVICTUS_ 

The data cut-offs (DCOs) for INVICTUS[2] were as follows (CS,[3] Section 2.3): 

- Primary data cut-off: 31[st] May 2019 (Blay _et al._ , 2020)[36] 

- Additional analysis with extra 9 months of follow-up: DCO 9[th] March 2020 (Zalcberg _et al._ 2020 abstract)[43] 

- Additional analysis with extra 14 months of follow-up: DCO 10[th] August 2020 (Zalcberg _et al._ 2021)[32] 

- Additional analysis with extra 19 months of follow-up: DCO 15[th] January 2021 (von Mehren _et al._ , 2021 abstract).[44] 

In addition, the company’s response to clarification question B1[35] states that a further DCO of May 2022 was available for OS and safety. However, data relating to this later DCO were not included in the CS and have not been used to inform the company’s economic model. 

The analysis populations were as follows: 

- Primary efficacy analyses were based on the ITT population, defined as all randomised patients (n=129). The period analysed was the double-blind period for all outcomes except OS, which followed up patients until they died. 

- Safety population, which included all randomised patients who received at least one dose of study drug (n=128). 

## _3.2.2 Participant flow in INVICTUS_ 

Participant flow for the May 2019 DCO is shown in Figure 3 and Table 5. In total, 129 patients were randomised: 85 to ripretinib and 44 to placebo (one placebo patient did not receive treatment). In the placebo group, 29 of 44 patients (66%) crossed over to ripretinib 150mg QD upon progression, whilst 15 of 44 patients (34%) did not cross over (CS,[3] Section 2.6.2). Patient withdrawals in the ripretinib and placebo groups were very similar (2.4% vs 2.3%) in the double-blind period (ITT population) and no patient was lost to follow up. 

In the ripretinib group, at the May 2019 DCO, 26 of 85 patients (31%) were still on double-blind ripretinib, 17 of 85 patients (20%) had discontinued double-blind treatment, and 42 of 85 patients (49%) 

36 



<!-- page 388 -->

had moved to open-label ripretinib after progression, some of whom later discontinued. One patient remained in the placebo double-blind group and 13 of 44 patients (30.2%) discontinued treatment in the double-blind period. Reasons for withdrawal included clinical progression (ripretinib n=4 [4.7%] vs placebo n=3 [7.0%]) and death (ripretinib n=3 [3.5%] vs placebo n=4 [9.3%]). The proportions of patients still receiving ripretinib (either double-blind or open-label) at the May 2019 DCO were: 36 of 85 patients (42%) in the ripretinib group and 11 of 44 patients (25%) in the placebo group.

At the August 2020 DCO, 65 patients in the ripretinib group had progressed, of whom 43 dose-escalated to ripretinib 150mg BID (i.e., IPDE) and 22 did not dose-escalate (see Figure 4). Of these 22 patients, 16 continued ripretinib 150mg QD and 6 discontinued ripretinib (see clarification response,[35] question A2). The median duration of treatment with ripretinib 150mg BID was 3.7 months (range: 1 day to 18.6 months) and 11 of 43 patients (26%) received ripretinib 150mg BID for 6 months or longer. Amongst patients who were randomised to the placebo group, 29 of 44 patients (66%) switched to ripretinib after disease progression. Of these, 10 patients continued 150mg QD, 10 had their dose escalated to ripretinib 150mg BID following a second disease progression and 9 discontinued treatment.

As of January 2021, 63 of 85 patients (74%) originally randomised to ripretinib had entered the openlabel period following disease progression based on independent radiological review. Of these, 19 patients continued to receive 150mg QD and 44 underwent IPDE to 150mg BID. The company’s clarification response[35] (question A3) states that 65 patients had progressed at the January 2021 DCO. However, the EAG identified a discrepancy between these figures and those relating to the August 2020 DCO. Specifically, it appears that only 2 patients in the ripretinib group who progressed did not enter the open-label period (65 progressed vs. 63 entered open-label period), which is fewer than the 6 patients previously reported. This discrepancy raises some concerns about the reliability of the company’s analyses, particularly those evaluating the impact of post-progression treatment during the open-label period in the ripretinib arm (i.e., the ripretinib arm OS _post hoc_ analysis described in Section 3.3.2.1). However, the EAG also notes that the company’s response to clarification question A3[35] states that the definition of progression used for the aforementioned 65 patients was based on the TTP rule and subsequent treatment received. That is, four patients censored in the TTP analysis but who entered the open-label phase were not included in the 65, while six patients who progressed but did not enter the open-label phase were included. This suggests a total of 69 patients (i.e., 65 + 4) who either progressed and/or entered the open-label phase in the ripretinib arm. If accurate, the difference (69 - 63 = 6 patients) representing those who progressed but did not enter the open-label phase appears reasonable, as this number should technically be equal to or greater than the six patients reported in the August 2020 DCO. Nonetheless, the EAG remains cautious in its interpretation. 

39 



<!-- page 391 -->

At the FAC stage of the appraisal, the company noted the following additional information: 

- _2021 DCO (CS description):_ 63 patients entered the open-label phase. The company also noted in the FAC form that patients could enter the open-label period prior to BICR-confirmed progression. It should be noted the protocol of the INVICTUS trial specified that _“the open-label portion occur after study treatment unblinding at the time of disease progression based on the independent radiologic review”_ . 

- _2021 DCO (clarification response, question A3):_ 65 patients progressed = 63 patients entered the open-label phase – 4 censored in the PFS analysis but entered the open-label phase + 6 progressed but did not enter the open-label phase. 

Given the company’s inconsistent terminology around progression (e.g., whether BICR-confirmed or not) across documents, the EAG remains cautious in interpreting these figures. The acronym TTP was used inconsistently across the CS, the clarification questions, and the protocol. In the INVICTUS protocol, “time-to-progression” and “time-to-tumour progression” seem to be used interchangeably, but it was unclear whether the company’s references to “time-to-progression” sometimes referred instead to the primary PFS analysis (e.g., in reference to clarification question A3 in the company’s FAC form), which was defined slightly differently. These inconsistencies raise concerns about the consistent application of censoring rules across analyses, which the EAG cannot verify. 

A final total of 30 of 44 participants (68%) who received placebo in the double-blind period crossed over to receive ripretinib 150mg QD in the open-label period; 16 subsequently dose escalated to 150mg BID following progression with QD dosing. 

In response to clarification question A3,[35] the company provided data on the duration of postprogression ripretinib treatment for patients randomised to ripretinib who experienced disease progression (see Table 6). The company stated that the data were based on the 65 patients defined as having progressed according to the TTP rules and subsequent treatment received, as described above. Based on the definition provided, the EAG considers that the “QD only group” in Table 6 included the six patients who progressed (BICR-confirmed) but did not enter the open-label phase. Thus, the duration of post-progression ripretinib treatment for patients labelled as “QD only” label should be interpreted with caution, as it contains six patients with post-progression duration of zero, lowering the group mean. The company defined “QD before IPDE” as the time from progression to the start of BID treatment. However, according to the trial design (Figure 2), all patients were expected to switch to BID immediately after progression. The EAG is therefore unclear why any post-progression QD period exists, but considers that this may be due to delays in assessment scheduling. The number of patients in the QD only vs. BID groups in Table 6 also appears to be slightly different from earlier figures reported for this DCO in the CS (19 received post-progression QD; 44 received post-progression BID). At the 

40 



<!-- page 392 -->

FAC stage of the appraisal, the company explained that the values reported in Table 6 were derived from the definition of BICR-confirmed progression used in response to clarification question A3, and were therefore slightly different, as described earlier. 

Nevertheless, the EAG considers the mean, minimum, and maximum durations of post-progression ripretinib treatment reported in Table 6 to be reasonable. These data were considered descriptive only and were not used in the company’s economic analysis.

The CS[3] reports that clinicians who attended the UK 2025 advisory board meeting[41] estimated that approximately 80% of all patients receiving ripretinib 150mg QD (as stated in the company’s response to clarification question B5[35] ) would be expected to continue ripretinib post-progression in UK clinical practice. Of those on post progression ripretinib, clinicians estimated that around 50% (i.e., 40% of the total population) would dose-escalate if BID dosing was routinely commissioned.[41] At the January 2021 DCO, 63 of 85 (74%) patients had continued ripretinib post-progression, which is comparable to clinical estimates obtained by the company, whilst a higher proportion, 44 of 63 patients (70%), underwent dose escalation in INVICTUS.[2] The EAG’s clinical advisors commented that they would continue to offer treatment with ripretinib beyond disease progression if patients were still deriving clinical benefit from it. They also stated that they would escalate to BID dosing in patients who are fit enough to tolerate it, if permitted. The company’s response to clarification question B3[35] reflected the clinicians’ statement regarding dose escalation in fit patients. Specifically, the company noted that a higher proportion of patients who received an escalated dose of ripretinib after progression had ECOG PS 0 at progression (51.2%) compared to just 16.7% among those who did not escalate.

## **3.3 Effectiveness of ripretinib - INVICTUS** 

Effectiveness data for ripretinib based on the INVICTUS trial[2] are summarised in this section. Full details are provided in Section 2.6 of the CS[3] and CS Appendix C.[29] The statistical methods used for the analysis of INVICTUS are reported in CS,[3] Section 2.4. Primary efficacy analyses were based on the ITT population, defined as all randomised patients (n=129). The safety population was used for safety analyses and included all patients who received at least one dose of study drug (n=128). 

44 



<!-- page 396 -->

## _3.3.1 Progression-free survival (PFS)_ 

At the May 2019 DCO, the median follow-up time in the double-blind period was 6.3 months (interquartile range [IQR] 3.2 to 8.2 months) for the ripretinib group and 1.6 months (IQR 1.1 to 2.7 months) for the placebo group.[36] As shown in Table 9 and Figure 5, median PFS was 6.3 months for ripretinib versus 1.0 months for placebo. PFS was statistically significantly longer in the ripretinib group than the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.15, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.09 to 0.25, _p_ <0.0001). Disease progression or death occurred in 60% of patients in the ripretinib group (34 patients [40%] were censored) and in 84% in the placebo group (7 patients [16%] were censored).[36] PFS was very similar at the March 2020 and January 2021 DCOs (Table 9). 

## _PFS2 for patients crossing over from placebo to ripretinib_ 

PFS2 refers to the time from ripretinib initiation after crossover to second disease progression or death (CS,[3] Section 2.6). In an exploratory analysis of PFS2 in the open-label period for the 29 (of 44) patients crossing over from placebo to ripretinib 150mg QD at their first disease progression (Table 9 and CS,[3] Figure 6), median PFS2 was 4.6 months. Of these 29 patients, 45% (n=13) had a PFS event and 55% (n=16) were censored. 

## _PFS for patients dose escalating on progression - PFS after IPDE to ripretinib 150mg BID_ 

At the 10[th] August 2020 DCO, amongst 43 (of 85) patients originally randomised to the ripretinib group who dose-escalated to ripretinib 150mg BID upon progression, median PFS1 (time from randomisation to progression in patients who received IPDE in the ripretinib arm) was 4.6 months, and median PFS2 (time from first dose at 150mg BID to progression or death in patients who received IPDE in the ripretinib arm) was 3.7 months (Table 9). The median PFS2/PFS1 ratio was 80% (CS,[3] Section 2.6 and CS[3] Figure 7). 

The CS[3] states that the clinical experts who attended the advisory board meetings in 2024 and 2025[40, ] 41 confirmed that the proportion of patients who remained on treatment with ripretinib beyond progression in INVICTUS[2] reflects anticipated clinical practice in the UK. The analysis for PFS1 and PFS2 (CS[3] Figure 7) only includes patients who dose-escalated to 150mg BID, and the efficacy of continuing ripretinib 150mg QD after progressive disease could not be assessed given the limited number of patients and multiple reasons for continuing ripretinib 150mg QD (not reported during the study) after disease progression. A comparison of PFS for patients who dose escalated to ripretinib 150mg BID versus those continuing 150mg QD was therefore not possible.[32]

## _3.3.2 Overall survival (OS)_ 

None of the OS analyses presented in this section include adjustment for treatment switching in the placebo group. The company’s methods for adjusting for treatment switching in the placebo group are described separately in Section 4.2.4. 

At the May 2019 DCO,  31% of patients in the ripretinib group (69% censored), and 59% in the placebo group (41% censored) had died (see Table 10 and Figure 6). Median OS was 15.1 months for ripretinib versus 6.6 months for placebo. The HR for OS for ripretinib versus placebo was 0.36 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.62, _p_ =not reported [NR]). 

As noted in Section 3.2.2, at the May 2019 DCO, 42 of 85 patients (49%) in the ripretinib group and 29 of 44 patients (66%) in the placebo group had received open-label ripretinib after progression. The EAG’s clinical advisors stated that continued ripretinib use beyond progression is likely to have extended OS. 

From the analysis of more mature OS data (January 2021 DCO; see Table 10), the estimated median OS for the ripretinib group was 18.2 months (95% CI: 13.1 to 30.7) (Figure 8). The median OS for the placebo group remained at 6.3 months (95% CI: 4.1 to 10.0). The HR for OS was 0.41 (95% CI: 0.26 to 0.65). Given that the January 2021 DCO is used to inform survival outcomes informing the company’s economic analysis, further details are summarised in Section 4.4.3.3.
