## _3.3.2.1 OS post hoc analyses: OS after IPDE to ripretinib 150mg BID_ 

The company conducted a series of _post hoc_ analyses and consulted UK clinical experts at advisory board meetings to assess whether dose-escalating ripretinib from 150mg QD to 150mg BID after progression would affect OS (CS,[3] Section 2.6.2: OS _post hoc_ analyses: OS after IPDE to ripretinib 150mg BID). All of these analyses focused on patients who were randomised to the ripretinib arm of INVICTUS.[2] 

Four analytic approaches were undertaken: 

1. Open-label BID vs QD OS analysis 

2. Censored BID-dosing analyses 

3. Cox proportional hazards time-varying analysis 

4. Two-stage adjustment. 

Of the four analytic approaches, the open-label BID vs QD OS analysis was a naïve comparison of OS between mutually exclusive subgroups (i.e., patients who did versus did not receive dose escalation in the ripretinib arm) and was not included in the company’s economic scenario analyses. In contrast, the remaining approaches employed various adjustment methods to estimate the direction and magnitude of the effect of post-progression dose escalation on OS, and their results were included in scenario 

49 



<!-- page 401 -->

analyses using the company’s economic model (see Section 4.2.5, Table 41). The company conducted several variations of each of the four approaches. The EAG has summarised these analyses in Table 11, based on CS,[3] Section 2.6.2 and Table 15, and the company’s responses to clarification questions B4 and B9.[35] 

Across the four analytic approaches, the evidence on the effect of post-progression dose escalation on OS was inconclusive. The advice received by the company from its clinical advisory board meetings suggested that the effect on OS is likely positive but not quantifiable. This broadly aligns with input received from the EAG’s clinical advisors, who noted that dose escalation would typically be used in patients who are more likely to benefit and tolerate it. 

Since these _post hoc_ analyses ultimately aim to estimate (counterfactual) OS as if no dose escalation occurred – adjusting for subsequent treatments that would affect OS but are not expected to be used in practice (i.e., ripretinib 150mg BID, assuming this dosing regimen is not routinely commissioned) – the methods should align with those for treatment switching outlined in NICE Decision Support Unit (DSU) Technical Support Document (TSD) 16,[47, 48] with causal inference in mind. Specifically, methods such as inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) and the two-stage estimation approach are better suited for adjusting for subsequent treatments that fall outside the original randomised treatments. For instance, adjusting the subsequent treatment from ripretinib 150mg BID to 150mg QD falls outside the original randomised comparison of ripretinib 150mg QD versus placebo. Other commonly used methods for treatment switching adjustment, such as the rank-preserving structural failure time model (RPSFTM) rely on the treatment effect between groups in the original randomised comparison. Hence, RPSFTM was deemed unsuitable in this context, and the EAG agrees that it was appropriate for the company not to explore this method for the IPDE adjustment in the ripretinib arm. 

The EAG therefore considers the results from the company’s two-stage approach to be the most appropriate among all of the _post hoc_ analyses related to IPDE, which suggested that post-progression survival would likely “shrink” without dose escalation (CS[3] Section 2.6.2, page 69 and clarification response,[35] question B9). This finding aligns with the views of the clinicians consulted by the company and the EAG. The IPCW adjustment was not pursued due to the small sample size in the INVICTUS trial; the EAG considers the company’s decision not to apply this method to be reasonable. 

The EAG provides a detailed critique of the _post hoc_ analyses related to IPDE adjustment that were used to inform the company’s economic scenario analyses (Analyses 2-4 in Table 11) in Section 4.2.5. It summarises all models fitted using the two-stage approach (Analysis 4 in Table 11) and explains why alternative methods (Analysis 2-3 in Table 11) are considered unsuitable. Analysis 1 ("Open-label BID 

50 



<!-- page 402 -->

vs QD OS analysis") was not applied in the company’s economic scenario analyses and is therefore described separately below. 

A naïve comparison of OS between patients who received dose escalation and those who did not (Analysis 1(a) in Table 11; CS,[3] Figure 9) showed a higher median OS of 18.4 months (95% CI 14.5 months to not estimable [NE]) for patients with IPDE versus 14.2 months (95% CI 7.2 months to NE) for those without IPDE. However, these results are not directly comparable because patients were not randomised to receive or not receive dose escalation. Additionally, selecting patients based on postbaseline characteristics introduces immortal time bias (i.e., patients who received dose escalation needed to survive long enough to receive it, whereas patients who did not could be receiving subsequent ripretinib 150mg QD treatment or discontinue treatment either before or after progression). 

The company presented an additional naïve comparison (Analysis 1(b) in Table 11) which evaluated the time from first BID dosing to death for patients receiving dose escalation versus the time from first QD dosing (i.e., approximately at randomisation) to death for patients who did not receive dose escalation. This analysis suggested slightly better survival with QD dosing compared to BID dosing (CS,[3] Figure 10). However, this comparison is misleading due to the use of different starting points: BID dosing can only begin at a later disease stage (after progression), which artificially disadvantages this group in the analysis. 

Following concerns raised in the EAG’s clarification letter[35] (question B3), the company conducted an updated naïve comparison (Analysis 1(c) in Table 11). This analysis compares post-progression survival (i.e., time from disease progression to death) between patients who received dose escalation and those who did not, which showed a non-statistically significant improvement in post-progression survival for patients receiving BID dosing. This finding may be partly explained by the higher proportion of patients with ECOG PS 0 at the time of progression among those who received dose escalation within the ripretinib arm (see clarification response,[35] Table 9). This is consistent with the EAG’s clinical advisors’ view that BID dosing would typically be offered to fitter patients who are more likely to tolerate and benefit from it. Nevertheless, since post-progression treatments were not randomised, the analysis cannot reliably estimate the causal effect of dose escalation among patients with comparable characteristics upon disease progression. 

In summary, the company’s naïve comparisons in Analyses 1(a)–1(c) (Table 11) provide insights into unadjusted survival among patients who underwent IPDE but cannot support causal conclusions due to the presence of important biases, including the lack of randomisation, differing treatment start times, and immortal time bias.

## _3.3.3 Response rates_ 

Objective responses in the double-blind period occurred in 8 of 85 patients (9%) in the ripretinib group and 0% of patients in the placebo group, at the May 2019 DCO (see Table 12). All responses were partial; there were no complete responses (CRs). Compared with placebo, a higher proportion of ripretinib patients had stable disease (SD) at 6 weeks (66% versus 20%) and 12 weeks (47% vs 5%).[15] Fewer patients in the ripretinib group had disease progression (19% versus 64%) compared with the placebo group. At the March 2020 and January 2021 DCOs, objective response rates (ORRs) were 11.8% for ripretinib and 0% for placebo. The August 2020 DCO (reported in the SmPC[21] ) reports the same ORR results as those observed in March 2020 and January 2021.

## _3.3.4 Other secondary endpoints_ 

Duration of response (DoR), TTP, and time to best response are descriptive endpoints which were not tested for statistical significance due to insufficient power. 

## _Time to best response_ 

Median time to best response in the ripretinib group at the May 2019 DCO was 1.9 months (IQR 1.0 to 2.7 months). No patients in the placebo group achieved a response. 

## _DOR_ 

Median DOR in the ripretinib group was not reached at the May 2019 DCO and was 14.5 months at the January 2021 DCO. 

## _TTP_ 

At the May 2019 DCO, median TTP was longer in the ripretinib group than the placebo group: 6.4 months (95% CI 4.6 to 8.4 months) vs 1.0 month (95% CI 0.9 to 1.7 months).[36] A TTP event occurred in 54.1% of patients (46/85, 39 censored) in the ripretinib group compared with 72.7% (32/44; 12 censored) in the placebo group.[49]

## _3.3.5 Subgroup analyses for PFS, OS and ORR_ 

_PFS:_ Subgroup analyses for PFS are reported in CS[3] Section 2.8 and CS Appendix C;[29] these are reproduced in Figure 10. These analyses were pre-specified. Results were generally consistent across subgroups, though the small number of patients in some subgroups limits the interpretation of these analyses. The CS[3] states that the UK advisory board 2024[40] did not consider age or line of therapy to be treatment effect modifiers. The EAG’s clinical advisors agreed with this view. In addition, the CS[3]

<!-- page 407 -->

also stated that the PFS subgroup analyses for the January 2021 DCO showed consistent results with the May 2019 DCO.  However, data from January 2021 DCO were not provided in the CS.

_BICR - blinded independent central review; CI - confidence interval; ECOG - Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group; PS - Performance Status; ITT - intention-to-treat; PFS - progression-free survival; QD - once daily. Note: The number (% of total patients) of patients in each treatment group along with the number of events for each subgroup is presented. Source: Blay et al. 2020.[36]_ 

The EAG notes that the subgroup analyses of PFS in INVICTUS suggests that the treatment effect for ripretinib in patients with ECOG PS 0 was less than that in patients with ECOG PS 1–2 (see Figure 10). In addition, older patients appear to have experienced a greater treatment effect. These results appear counterintuitive, and they contrast with the views of the UK advisory board. The company’s clarification response[35] (question A7) states that: “ _the findings of the subgroup analysis suggest that ripretinib provides benefit across all subgroups; however, the subgroups analysed were not large enough to support any further conclusions. Additionally, subgroup analyses consider a single variable in isolation and there may be other imbalances in baseline characteristics between subgroups that drive these counterintuitive results._ The company’s response also states _“….the higher proportion of patients with KIT exon 11 mutations in the ECOG PS 1-2 and older subgroups vs the ECOG PS 0 and younger subgroup may have contributed to the counterintuitive results for the PFS subgroup analyses”_ (see Table 13). 

The EAG’s clinical advisors considered this to be a plausible explanation. Specifically, KIT exon 11 mutations are the most common mutation type in the GIST population, whereas KIT exon 9 mutations tend to be more aggressive and are more frequently observed in younger patients, possibly because patients with exon 9 mutations have a lower likelihood of surviving to older age.[50] In contrast, older 

56 



<!-- page 408 -->

patients, who are typically more frail and more likely to have an ECOG PS of 1-2, tend to have a lower prevalence of exon 9 mutations. This is indirectly reflected in the INVICTUS population shown in Table 13, whereby a higher percentage of KIT exon 11 mutations is observed among older patients and those with ECOG PS 1-2, suggesting a likely lower proportion of exon 9 mutations in these subgroups. 

Given that ripretinib may be more effective in patients with exon 11 mutations than in those with exon 9 mutations, this imbalance in mutation prevalence may partly explain the greater PFS benefit observed in both the older and ECOG PS 1-2 subgroups. However, due to the small sample sizes and lack of randomisation in these subgroup analyses, the findings should be interpreted with caution.

## _3.3.6 Health-related quality of life (HRQoL)_ 

HRQoL in INVICTUS[2] was assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 role and physical functioning domains, the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire and the EQ-VAS from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1 (i.e., the first 29 days of treatment). On Cycle 2 Day 1, 71 patients were evaluable in the ripretinib arm and 32 patients were evaluable in the placebo arm (CS,[3] Section 2.6, page 74). The CS[3] states that later measurements are not reported due to the low number of evaluable patients in the placebo group after this time point. In response to clarification question A4,[35] the company stated that due to rapid disease progression, the number of patients in the placebo arm was very low after Cycle 2 Day 1; hence, any statistical comparison across study arms after this time point would be highly uncertain (see Figure 12).

The CS[3] states that patients in the ripretinib group reported an improvement in the physical and role functioning domains of the EORTC QLQ-C30 from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1 (see Figure 13), with an adjusted mean increase in scores (indicating improvement) of 1.6 and 3.5 points, respectively, compared with a decline of 8.9 and 17.1 points for patients in the placebo group. Patients likewise reported an improvement in HRQoL from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1, as assessed by an adjusted mean increase in EQ-VAS scores of 3.7 versus a decline of 8.9 with placebo. The CS[3] states that no minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for HRQoL has been established in GIST, but that assuming a MCID of 10% mean score change or score change of 5 points, the difference between ripretinib and placebo could be considered clinically meaningful. The CS[3] also reports the above HRQoL measures through to Cycle 10 in the ripretinib arm, but not the placebo arm. Patients treated with ripretinib appeared to remain stable on all scores for patient-reported outcome (PRO) measures through to Cycle 10 (see CS,[3] Figure 15 and Table 17). 

Patient demographic and baseline characteristics were generally well balanced between treatment arms in terms of stratification factors including ECOG PS and number of prior systemic anticancer treatments.[2] The adjusted mean change from baseline to Cycle 2 Day 1 in EQ-5D-5L utility score was -0.009 (standard error [SE] 0.020) for the ripretinib group and -0.06 (SE 0.028) for the placebo group (see CS,[3] Table 17).[2]

At the August 2020 DCO, time until definitive deterioration (TUDD), which was defined as a clinically meaningful decline in the PRO measure that does not recover,[31] was longer in patients receiving ripretinib compared with placebo.[31, 52 ] For overall health, the median TUDD for the placebo group was 7.7 weeks; however, it had not been reached in the ripretinib group by 56 weeks. For EORTC QLQ-C30 (physical and role function) and EQ-VAS score, median TUDD was 41.6 weeks in the ripretinib group vs 7.9 weeks in the placebo group. Median TUDD was longer than median PFS (6.3 months) and median TTD with ripretinib (8.8 months) (see CS,[3] Figures 16, 17 and 18). ## **3.4 Supporting evidence – the Royal Marsden expanded access study** 

As supporting evidence for the effectiveness of ripretinib, the CS[3] includes details of the Royal Marsden expanded access study, which was undertaken independently by The Royal Marsden Hospital, London, UK.[28 ] Full details are provided in CS[3] Section 2.3.4. 

60 



<!-- page 412 -->

## _3.4.1 Study design_ 

The Royal Marsden expanded access study is a single-arm retrospective observational study assessing the effectiveness and safety of ripretinib in a cohort of patients treated in a real-world setting. Study details are presented in Table 15. Study eligibility criteria are reported in Table 10 of the CS.[3] In summary, the study included patients with advanced (unresectable or metastatic) GIST who commenced ripretinib at the Royal Marsden Hospital between January 2020 and October 2021; patients had to have had imaging available for retrospective assessment of radiologic response according to mRECIST version 1.1, and had to have at least one measurable lesion. Radiological assessments were performed every 10–14 weeks or when clinically indicated. Patients remained on treatment until clinical benefit was no longer observed or until unacceptable toxicity was seen.[28] 

The EAG notes that the Royal Marsden expanded access study included patients who had received two or more prior lines of treatment; as such this study does not fully align with the population defined in the final NICE scope,[20] the MHRA marketing authorisation[21] or the population in the INVICTUS trial,[3] each of which relates to adults with advanced GIST who have received prior treatment with three or more TKIs, including imatinib.

Patients received a starting dose of ripretinib 150mg QD but were given the opportunity to dose-escalate to 150mg ripretinib BID at the time of disease progression, as determined by their treating physician. Patients were retrospectively assessed as two groups: (i) those receiving 150mg ripretinib QD and (ii) those with dose escalation to 150mg ripretinib BID upon tumour progression.[28] 

## _Outcomes_ 

The following outcomes were reported for the DCO of the 15[th] January 2023[28] 

- _PFS QD:_ The time from the date of the first 150mg ripretinib QD dose to the time of progression or death[28] (equivalent to PFS  in INVICTUS[2] ). 

61 



<!-- page 413 -->

- _PFS BID:_ The subgroup of patients undergoing IPDE, defined as the time from date of the first 150mg ripretinib BID dose to the time of progression or death (equivalent to PFS2 in INVICTUS). 

- _PFS ITT:_ The overall duration of ripretinib treatment regardless of dosage (no equivalent end point in INVICTUS). 

- _ORR:_ Confirmed CR or PR. 

- _TTD:_ Time from the first day of ripretinib treatment (at a specified dose) to the last day of ripretinib treatment (at a specified dose) regardless of the cause of treatment discontinuation. Defined for the same groups as PFS endpoints. 

- _TBP:_ Ripretinib treatment beyond disease progression. 

- _OS:_ Time from the date of the first 150mg ripretinib QD dose to the time of death from any cause. 

Retrospective mRECIST measurements were used to assess PFS, best ORR and time to best response. 

## _Study quality_ 

Following a request from the EAG, the company conducted a quality assessment of the Royal Marsden expanded access cohort study (see clarification response,[35] question A8) using the CASP Cohort Study Checklist. The CS[3] highlights that as a non-randomised, non-controlled retrospective study, the Royal Marsden study has inherent limitations affecting the statistical validity of its results. Such retrospective studies are prone to issues including limited or missing data, less rigorous data collection (due to the absence of a pre-specified analysis plan or study protocol) and potential recall bias. 

## _3.4.2 Patient baseline characteristics_ 

Of the 61 patients registered for the ripretinib expanded access programme at the Royal Marsden Hospital, 16 patients were excluded (see Figure 14). Overall, 45 patients with available clinical and radiological data were included in the study.[28]

Baseline patient characteristics are reported in Table 16. Information on primary mutational status was not available for 6 patients, and the small bowel was the most common primary tumour site (51.1%). All but one patient had metastatic disease. All patients had progressed after imatinib and 95.6% of patients had also progressed after sunitinib. Some baseline characteristics of patients in the Royal Marsden expanded access study[28] differed from those in INVICTUS.[2] Patients in the Royal Marsden cohort were older (median age 62 vs. 59 years), had higher prevalence of  KIT exon 11 mutation (73.3% vs. 64%), and had poorer PS at baseline with 98% having an ECOG score of 1 and 2 compared to 56% in INVICTUS. Additionally, 42% of patients in the Royal Marsden study had received only two prior lines of treatment before initiating ripretinib. The EAG requested that the company provide data that reflect the subgroup with three prior lines of treatment to enable a more appropriate comparison with

the population relevant to this appraisal (see clarification response,[35] question A9). The company’s response states that this re-analysis was not possible because the company does not hold relevant individual patient data (IPD) for the Royal Marsden study as it was investigator-led. However, the company’s response notes that in the univariate and multivariate Cox regression models, the number of previous lines of treatment (2 versus 3 or more) was not associated with a significant difference in PFS (QD or ITT) or OS (see CS,[3] Section 2.8.2). Despite the company’s clarification, the EAG notes that 42% of patients in the Royal Marsden Study are outside the scope of this appraisal; hence, the data should be interpreted with caution.

## _3.4.3 Summary of clinical effectiveness - Royal Marsden expanded access study_ 

3.4.3.1 Patient disposition 

The median follow-up time was 24.2 months (95% CI 19.7 to 29.7 months). At the January 2025 DCO, 5 (11.1%) patients were still receiving 150mg ripretinib QD and 40 (88.9%) patients discontinued ripretinib QD due to: mRECIST (radiological) PD in 21 (46.7%) cases, clinical  PD (defined as worsening patient-reported symptoms in the presence of radiological signs of PD that did not reach the level required for confirming mRECIST PD) in 17 (37.8%) cases, and toxicity in 2 (4.4%) cases. Of the 21 patients with mRECIST PD, 15 dose-escalated to ripretinib BID and 6 did not dose-escalate (2 received another TKI, and 4 declined IPDE and were referred back to their local team). Of the 17 patients with clinical PD, 10 were too unwell to continue treatment and 7 dose-escalated to ripretinib BID. In total, 22 (48.9%) patients had their dose escalated to ripretinib 150mg BID (see Figure 14). 

Of the 22 patients undergoing IPDE, 4 (18.2%) were still receiving ripretinib BID at the time of the DCO, 4 (18.2%) had clinical progression and 14 (63.6%) had mRECIST PD. Four patients went on to receive a further line of treatment after progression on ripretinib BID. At the time of the DCO, 20 (44.4%) patients were still alive and 25 (55.6%) had died.[28] 

## 3.4.3.2  Progression-free survival 

Median PFS for patients receiving ripretinib 150mg QD was 7.9 months (95% CI 5.6 to 19.3 months) (Figure 15A). Median PFS for patients receiving ripretinib 150mg BID (after initial disease progression) was 5.4 months (95% CI 2.8 to 9.3 months). The overall median PFS ITT was 9.7 months (95% CI 8.3 to 18.1 months) (see Figure 15). The CS[3] notes that the median PFS achieved in INVICTUS[2] (6.3 months; 95% CI 4.6 to 8.1 months) was shorter than that reported for patients receiving ripretinib 150mg QD in the expanded access program, potentially due to the lower frequency of radiological assessment in clinical practice.[40] The EAG’s clinical advisors considered this explanation to be plausible.

## 3.4.3.3 Overall survival 

Median OS was 14.0 months (95% CI 9.9 months to NE), including all patients, irrespective of postprogression ripretinib dosing (see Figure 16). This was lower than the median OS achieved in INVICTUS[2] (18.2; 95% CI 13.1 to 30.7 months) after a similar median follow-up period.[28, 36 ] The company stated that the OS achieved in clinical practice is often lower than that achieved in clinical trials due to the ‘controlled by protocol’ nature of a clinical trial, i.e., stringent recruitment criteria, intensive patient care with close monitoring and contact maintained throughout the study. 

Patients in the Royal Marsden study had poorer PS at baseline compared with those in INVICTUS (ECOG PS 1-2 98% vs 56%, respectively).[28, 36] The EAG’s clinical advisors and the UK clinical advisory panel confirmed that ECOG PS is a key treatment effect modifier in this patient population.[40, ] 53-55 However, it should also be noted that 42.2% of the patients received ripretinib as a third-line treatment (these patients are outside of the scope of the appraisal and the marketing authorisation for ripretinib).

## 3.4.3.4 Objective response rates 

The best responses to ripretinib 150mg QD were PR in 7 of 42 patients (16.7%) and SD in 29 of 42 patients (69.0%). Median time to best response was 2.6 months (IQR 1.9–3.3 months). Three patients did not undergo radiologic evaluation whilst receiving ripretinib QD due to rapid clinical deterioration. The best responses to ripretinib 150mg BID were PR in 2 of 20 patients (10.0%) and SD in 9 of 20 patients (45.0%). Three patients did not undergo radiologic evaluation whilst on ripretinib BID (2 patients due to rapid clinical deterioration and 1 patient was dose-escalated 2 weeks before the DCO).[28] 

## 3.4.3.5 Time to discontinuation and treatment beyond progression 

The CS[3] reports that median TTD was similar to median PFS in patients receiving ripretinib 150mg QD at 7.1 months (95% CI 5.8 to 11.0 months). Post-progression ripretinib 150mg QD was recorded for 14 patients (31.1%) and the median duration of treatment beyond progression (TBP) was 1.9 months (IQR 1.0 to 3.0 months). The CS[3] notes that patients with TBP generally showed no significant differences in baseline characteristics compared with patients without TBP, apart from site of disease and that this difference was most likely due to the small sample size. 

Median TTD in patients receiving ripretinib 150mg BID was 6.5 months (95% CI 4.6 to 10.7 months). Ripretinib BID TBP (treatment beyond second disease progression) was observed in 6 patients (27.3%). The median duration of TBP was 2.8 months (IQR 1.0 to 5.4 months).[28] 

67 



<!-- page 419 -->

## 3.4.3.6 Subgroup analyses 

The CS[3] reports that in multivariate Cox regression models, the absence of a KIT exon 11 mutation was associated with a statistically significant reduction in PFS QD (HR 4.67, 95% CI 1.53 to 14.29), PFS ITT (HR 3.06, 95% CI 1.08 to 8.67) and OS (HR 4.19, 95% CI 1.49 to 11.82) compared to when a KIT exon 11 mutation was present. Patients with three or more metastatic sites had statistically shorter PFS ITT compared with patients with less than two metastatic sites (HR 3.00, 95% CI 1.05 to 8.57). Other variables tested, including number of previous lines of treatment (2 vs 3 or more) and age, were not associated with significant differences in PFS (QD or ITT) or OS.[28] 

## **3.5 Safety of ripretinib** 

## _3.5.1 Studies providing safety data on ripretinib_ 

The CS[3] (Section 2.11) focuses on safety data from the INVICTUS RCT.[2] The reported safety data are for the double-blind period of INVICTUS (i.e., up to disease progression), therefore the EAG notes that these data should not be affected by treatment switching after progression. The safety population included all 85 patients randomised to ripretinib and 43 of 44 patients randomised to placebo (i.e., a total of 128 of 129 randomised patients). 

In terms of other sources of safety data on ripretinib, the company identified two studies; a Phase 1 single-arm study of GIST patients treated with ripretinib at a dose of 150mg either QD or BID (NCT02571036)[34, 39] and a Phase 2 single-arm study of adults with advanced GIST who had progressed on prior three or more TKIs (NCT04282980).[37, 38] The company provided no further details apart from stating in CS Appendix D[29] that the safety results of the Phase 2 and Phase 1 single-arm studies were broadly aligned with those of INVICTUS.[2] In addition, the company included safety data from the Royal Marsden expanded access study[29] and undertook a pooled safety analysis of the INVICTUS study and the Phase 1 single-arm study (NCT02571036).[34, 39]

## _3.5.3 Deaths_ 

Deaths during the double-blind period were less frequent for ripretinib than placebo (14% vs. 30%) and were stated in the CS[3] to be mainly due to disease progression (11 of 12 deaths in ripretinib arm);[36] see Table 17. AEs leading to death were less frequent for ripretinib than placebo (7% vs. 23%), whilst treatment-related AEs leading to death occurred in one patient in each group (1.2% vs. 2.3%). One death was due to unknown causes in the ripretinib group, and one death was due to septic shock and pulmonary oedema in the placebo group.

As part of its clarification response in TA881[42] (question A12), the company sought UK clinical opinion on the clinical significance of these events. The clinician consulted by the company stated that the rates of actinic keratosis should always monitored closely, but with an active and well-tolerated anticancer treatment, dealing with Grade 1-2 keratosis is not a major clinical problem. The clinician also stated that SCC is an important event which needs to be carefully monitored, but that in this population, the benefit of ripretinib is far greater than the disadvantage of SCC, given the low incidence. The company also noted that a dermatopathological review of cutaneous SCC (cuSCC) events in 10 ripretinib-treated GIST patients concluded that patients who developed cuSCC lesions whilst on ripretinib were elderly, with a median age of 76 years. The cuSCC lesions occurred in sun-exposed areas, did not show aggressive histopathological features, and were analogous to their lowest-risk ultraviolet-induced counterparts. Based on this analysis, the company stated that the low-risk cuSCC lesions in patients treated with ripretinib can generally be managed using local interventions without the need for dosing modifications or interruptions.

## **3.6 Ongoing studies** 

The CS[3] reports that there are currently no ongoing studies of ripretinib that are relevant to this appraisal. The EAG i **s** also unaware of any ongoing studies. 

## **3.7 Meta-analysis** 

The CS[3] does not contain any meta-analysis because only one study (the INVICTUS RCT[2] ) was identified in the company’s SLR as being relevant to the appraisal. The EAG agrees that meta-analysis is not required. 

## **3.8 Indirect comparison and/or mixed treatment comparison** 

The CS[3] states that no indirect or mixed treatment comparison was conducted because only one study (INVICTUS[2] ) was identified in the SLR as being relevant to the appraisal, and this study included the only comparator of interest (BSC). 

## **3.9 Additional work on clinical effectiveness undertaken by the EAG** 

No additional work was undertaken by the EAG. 

## **3.10 Conclusions of the clinical effectiveness section** 

_Methods of systematic review:_ The EAG considers the company’s SLR methods to be of a generally good standard. The literature search was subject to some limitations. The electronic search strategy was inadequate for finding all the included studies described in the CS SLR;[3, 29] however, given the company’s supplementary searches, it is unlikely that any relevant studies have been missed. 

_Clinical evidence:_ The CS[3] presents data from the INVICTUS RCT of ripretinib plus BSC versus placebo plus BSC in 129 patients with advanced GIST who had progressed on, or were intolerant to, (at least) imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib.[2] The EAG’s clinical advisors considered the patients 

74 



<!-- page 426 -->

enrolled in INVICTUS to be broadly representative of those who would be eligible for treatment in clinical practice in England. 

At the May 2019 DCO, median PFS was 6.3 months for ripretinib versus 1.0 months for placebo. The HR for PFS for ripretinib versus BSC was 0.15 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.25, _p_ <0.0001). Median OS was 15.1 months for ripretinib versus 6.6 months for placebo. The HR for OS for ripretinib versus placebo was 0.36 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.62, _p_ =NR). Median OS was 11.6 months in placebo crossover patients, and 1.8 months in placebo non-crossover patients. HRQoL was only reported for both groups during the first cycle (the first 29 days - due to attrition in the placebo arm, patient numbers were low after this point), during which there was improvement in the ripretinib group and worsening in the placebo group based on the EQ-VAS and the EORTC QLQ-C30 (physical and role functioning domains). The most common Grade 3/4 TEAEs with ripretinib (vs. placebo) were: anaemia (11% vs. 14%); abdominal pain (7% vs. 5%); hypertension (7% vs. 0%); increased lipase (5% vs. 0%) and hypophosphataemia (5% vs. 0%). Treatment-related Grade 3/4 TEAEs were reported in xxx of patients in the ripretinib arm and xxx of patients in the placebo arm. TEAEs of special interest included SCC of the skin xx x xxxx xxx xxxx and actinic keratosis xx xxxxxx xxx x xxxxxxx in the ripretinib and placebo arms, respectively. 

In addition, the CS[3] included  RWE from the Royal Marsden expanded access cohort study.[28] However, the EAG notes that 42% of patients included in this study had received only two prior lines of treatment before initiating ripretinib. As this is not consistent with the licensed indication for ripretinib, the relevance of this study to the current appraisal is limited. 

As part of the CS,[3] the company undertook multiple _post hoc_ OS analyses to assess the impact of IPDE in the ripretinib arm, The EAG considers the two-stage approach (provided in response to clarification question B9[35] ) to be the most appropriate among the four analytic approaches explored by the company (Section 3.3.2.1). This analysis suggested that adjusting the effect of dose escalation to reflect no escalation would likely shrink post-progression survival, and consequently, OS. Further details on the application of each method in the company’s economic scenario analyses are presented in Section 4.2.5 and critiqued in Section 4.3.5. The company also conducted treatment switching adjustment for OS in the placebo arm; full details are provided in Section 4.2.4. 

75

## **4. COST EFFECTIVENESS** 

This chapter presents a summary and critique of the company’s health economic analyses of ripretinib for the treatment of patients with advanced GIST after 3 prior therapies. Section 4.1 describes and critiques the company’s review of existing economic evaluations. Section 4.2 describes the original version of the company’s economic model and summarises its results. Section 4.3 presents the EAG’s critical appraisal of the company’s economic model. The results of the company’s updated (postclarification) model and the EAG’s exploratory analyses are presented separately in Chapter 5. 

## **4.1 Critique of company’s review of existing economic analyses** 

## _4.1.1 Summary and critique of company’s searches_ 

The company performed an initial SLR in July 2020 followed by four update searches in July 2021, March 2022, April 2024 and March 2025. The SLR two-in-one search was undertaken to identify literature for published cost-effectiveness studies (CS Appendix E[29] ) combined with cost and resource use studies (CS Appendix G) in patients who have advanced, unresectable, or metastatic patients with 4L+ GIST. 

The company searched all relevant electronic bibliographic databases in March 2025 (CS Appendix E,[56] Table 14) via the Ovid host platform, notably Medline, Embase, HTA, NHS EED and Econlit, as well as CDSR; CENTRAL, the ACP Journal Club, DARE, Cochrane Clinical Answers and the Cochrane Methodology Register. 

As with the clinical effectiveness SLR searches, three conference abstract websites were searched for the last five years (2021-2025): ASCO, ESMO, and ASCO Gastrointestinal Cancers Symposium. The company searched clinicaltrials.gov registry for ongoing or completed or unpublished trials. Four HTA agency websites were searched: NICE, SMC, PBAC and CDA-AMC. 

The company combined the search for the population (disease GIST) with the various economic outcomes, health care and resource use filters. The Cochrane Handbook refers to additional terms that could have been included in the burden of illness search filter (Aluko _et al._ ,[57] 2023). Other than the limitation of restricting the search to English language studies, there were no issues or errors in the search and the EAG considers that the search is comprehensive. 

For the review of HRQoL studies, an initial search was carried out in July 2020 followed by four updates in July 2021, March 2022, April 2024 and March 2025. The company searched the same sources as in the cost-effectiveness and health costs and resource use searches, i.e., electronic database and grey literature searches. The company combined the search for the population (GIST AND “metastatic/advanced/unresectable” AND relapsed/refractory/resistant) with an HRQoL outcomes 

76 



<!-- page 428 -->

search filter. There were no errors in the search and the EAG considers that the search is comprehensive and relevant studies are unlikely to have been missed. 

_4.1.2  Summary and critique of company’s review of existing economic evaluations_ 

The inclusion criteria for the company’s review of published economic evaluations are reported in Table 9 of CS Appendix E.[29] Studies were eligible for inclusion in the review if the population included in the analysis related to people with advanced, metastatic or unresectable GIST at any line of treatment. The inclusion criteria also specified that studies must be economic evaluations, budget impact analyses, or burden of illness studies, or must report measures of costs and/or health care resource use. No restrictions were applied to the interventions or comparators assessed within the studies. Editorials, reviews, comments, and letters were excluded, as were studies not published in the English language and studies published prior to 2000. Extracted data from the identified records were provided in a separate SLR Excel workbook provided as part of the CS references. 

Across the original and update searches, a total of 36 unique studies were included in the review. Twenty-four of the identified studies were cost-effectiveness/cost-utility analyses, three were budget impact analyses and nine were health care resource use studies. The company’s quality assessment of the included economic evaluations using the Drummond checklist[58] is provided in the SLR Excel workbook. The results of this quality assessment are presented in tabular form only; a narrative summary of the quality assessment is not provided in either the CS or the CS appendices.[3, 29] Table 12 of CS Appendix E summarises all included economic evaluation studies regardless of geographical setting; Table 27 of the main CS summarises the subset of UK economic evaluation studies. 

The economic analyses included in the company’s broader review used a variety of modelling approaches, including state transition, partitioned survival and simulation models. Treatments evaluated included: surgical resection; imatinib; sunitinib; regorafenib; ripretinib; pazopanib and standard care (including no treatment, BSC, palliative care and placebo). Studies were conducted in various settings including: Brazil; Canada; China; England; Germany; the Netherlands; France; Mexico; Singapore; Spain; Turkey; the UK and the US. None of the UK-based cost-effectiveness studies included ripretinib as an intervention. 

One non-UK study (Liao _et al._[59] ) evaluated ripretinib versus placebo as a 4L+ treatment for advanced GIST. Liao _et al._ reports the methods and results of a health economic model in which parametric survival models were fitted to replicated IPD from the INVICTUS trial.[2] The authors state that the model uses a Markov approach; however, the survival model parameters reported in the paper relate to the end points of PFS and OS, which indicates that the model is a partitioned survival analysis. The analysis did not include statistical adjustment of the OS data to account for confounding resulting from 

77 



<!-- page 429 -->

placebo group patients switching onto ripretinib; instead, the costs of post-progression ripretinib (after switching) were included in the total costs for the BSC group. In addition, the text indicates that the costs of continued post-progression ripretinib in INVICTUS were excluded from the total costs for the intervention group. Health state utility values were taken from analyses of EQ-5D-3L data collected in the GRID trial (regorafenib versus placebo in patients with metastatic/unresectable GIST who have progressed on or were intolerant to imatinib and who have progressed on sunitinib; PF utility = 0.767; PD utility = 0.647).[60] The authors report an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for ripretinib versus placebo of US $244,010 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. The EAG notes that the study by Liao _et al._ is limited due the absence of any statistical adjustment to account for confounding of the OS data due to placebo treatment switching in INVICTUS and the exclusion of post-progression ripretinib costs from the intervention group of the model. 

## **4.2 Summary of the company’s original submitted economic analysis** 

## _4.2.1 Scope of the company’s economic analyses_ 

As part of their submission to NICE,[3] the company submitted an executable health economic model programmed in Microsoft Excel. The scope of the company’s economic analysis is summarised in Table 24.

|---|---|

_GIST - gastrointestinal stromal tumour; mg - milligram; QD - once daily; QALY - quality-adjusted life year; NHS - National Health Service; PSS - Personal Social Services_ 

The company’s economic model assesses the cost-effectiveness of ripretinib (plus BSC) versus BSC alone for the treatment of patients with advanced GIST after at least three therapies, including imatinib. Cost-effectiveness is assessed in terms of the incremental cost per QALY gained from the perspective of the NHS and Personal Social Services (PSS) over a 40-year (lifetime) horizon. Unit costs are valued at 2023/2024 prices, except for drug acquisition costs which are valued at current prices. Health outcomes and costs are discounted at a rate of 3.5% per annum. 

78 



<!-- page 430 -->

## _Population_ 

The company’s economic analysis is intended to reflect the population of patients with advanced GIST who have received three or more prior therapies, including imatinib (i.e., the company intends to position ripretinib as a 4L+ therapy). Patient characteristics are based on the population enrolled in the INVICTUS trial.[2] At model entry, patients are assumed to be 60.1 years of age and 43.41% of patients are assumed to be female. 

As noted in Section 3.2.1, approximately 37% of patients in INVICTUS[2] had already received at least four prior lines of treatment at study entry (see Table 7). The EAG’s clinical advisors commented that the number of prior therapies received is likely to be a prognostic factor. 

## _Intervention_ 

The intervention included in the company’s economic analyses is ripretinib, administered orally at a dose of 150mg (taken as 3 x 50mg tablets) daily. This is in line with the final NICE scope[20] and the MHRA marketing authorisation for ripretinib.[49] The SmPC for ripretinib (page 2) states that _“treatment with QINLOCK should continue as long as benefit is observed or until unacceptable toxicity.”_ In contrast to the previous model used to inform TA881,[1] the model for the current appraisal includes the continued use of ripretinib treatment after disease progression (i.e., a progression-based stopping rule is no longer applied). As noted in Section 3.2.1, patients who experienced disease progression in INVICTUS[2] were allowed to continue on the current dose of ripretinib 150mg QD or dose-escalate to ripretinib 150mg BID; the higher dose of ripretinib is not in line with the marketing authorisation for ripretinib. The company’s base case model does not include any statistical adjustment of the OS data from INVICTUS[2] to account for the effects of ripretinib 150mg BID dosing and the post-progression ripretinib drug costs are based on the QD dosing regimen. This issue is discussed further in Section 4.3.5. The model assumes that patients do not receive any further active anticancer treatment after discontinuing ripretinib (i.e., they receive BSC alone). 

## _Comparator_ 

The company’s base case analysis includes a single comparator: BSC (no active therapy). The economic model includes costs associated with: pain management (analgesics); computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans; full blood counts (FBCs) and liver function tests (LFTs); outpatient appointments; palliative resection; palliative radiotherapy (RT); the management of AEs and end-of-life care (see Section 4.2.4). 

79 



<!-- page 431 -->

## _4.2.2 Model structure and logic_ 

The company’s economic model adopts a partitioned survival approach, including four health states: (i) progression-free; (ii) progressed disease (on treatment with ripretinib); (iii) progressed disease (off treatment with ripretinib/BSC), and (iv) dead (see Figure 17). 

## **Figure 17: Company’s model structure (drawn by the EAG)** 

**==> picture [452 x 141] intentionally omitted <==**

_BSC - best supportive care Dashed arrows and ellipses indicate parts of the model which are applicable to the ripretinib treatment group only_ 

The model logic operates as follows. Patients enter the model in the progression-free state and receive treatment with either ripretinib (plus BSC) or BSC alone. At any time _t_ , health state occupancy is determined by the cumulative probabilities of OS, PFS and TTD, whereby: 

- The probability of being alive and progression-free is given by the cumulative probability of PFS; 

- The probability of being alive following disease progression is calculated as the cumulative probability of OS minus the cumulative probability of PFS; 

- The probability of being on treatment following disease progression is calculated as the cumulative probability of having progressed and discontinued treatment minus the cumulative probability of PFS (this applies to the ripretinib group only); 

- The probability of being dead is calculated as one minus the cumulative probability of OS. 

The company’s model includes half-cycle correction. Patients in the ripretinib group are assumed to receive treatment during the entire PFS period and during part of the post-progression survival period. No further active anticancer treatments are assumed to be given after disease progression in the ripretinib group, or to any patient in either of the alive health states in the BSC group. 

The cumulative probabilities of OS and PFS for patients receiving ripretinib and BSC are modelled using parametric survival distributions fitted to time-to-event data from the INVICTUS trial.[2] The model applies a structural constraint whereby if the per-cycle risk of death from the parametric survival model is lower than that for the age- and sex-matched general population (based on Office for National Statistics [ONS] life tables[61] ) in any given cycle, the general population mortality risk is used, otherwise 

80 



<!-- page 432 -->

the unadjusted OS probability is used. This aspect of the model is subject to an error (see Section 5.3.5, critical appraisal point 1). In addition, the model includes a constraint which ensures that the PFS function cannot be higher than the adjusted OS function at any time point. No other structural constraints are included in the model. 

HRQoL is assumed to be determined by the presence/absence of disease progression and whether patients receive ripretinib treatment after progression. The utility values applied in the progression-free (PF) and progressed disease (PD) states are based on EQ-5D-5L data (mapped to the 3L version) collected in INVICTUS.[2, 3] Utility values are adjusted for increasing age. The model also includes shortterm QALY losses associated with Grade 3/4 TEAEs occurring in ≥5% of either group in the doubleblind period of INVICTUS, based on disutility values reported in other literature.[62, 63] Based on the description in the CS, all TEAEs are assumed to have a duration of one model cycle (approximately 28 days), although this part of the model is also subject to an error (see Section 4.3.5, critical appraisal point 1). 

The model includes costs associated with: (i) drug acquisition (ripretinib and BSC pain management drugs); (ii) health state management (scans, tests and outpatient visits); (iii) pre-treatment resource use (scans and tests); (iv) palliative treatments; (v) the management of AEs and (vi) end-of-life care costs. Drug acquisition costs for ripretinib are modelled as a function of the TTD distribution, relative dose intensity (RDI) and unit costs. BSC pain management costs and health state costs are applied in each model cycle. Palliative treatment costs are applied once in the first model cycle and once again at the point of disease progression. Other costs are applied once only at specific time points - either at model entry, on disease progression or at the point of death. 

The incremental health gains, costs and cost-effectiveness for ripretinib versus BSC are estimated over a 40-year time horizon using a 28.10-day cycle duration (1/13[th] of a year). No economic subgroup analyses are presented in the CS.[3] 

## _4.2.3 Key assumptions employed in the company’s base case model_ 

The company’s base case model employs the following key assumptions: 

- The modelled population is 60.10 years of age at model entry.[2] 

- The model assumes that patients receive ripretinib prior to disease progression and treatment may be continued beyond progression. Patients do not go on to receive further active treatments after discontinuing ripretinib or after progression on BSC. 

- BSC is the sole comparator for ripretinib. 

81 



<!-- page 433 -->

- TTD for ripretinib is modelled using an exponential distribution. PFS is modelled using independently fitted log-normal distributions in both treatment groups. OS is modelled using independently fitted log-logistic distributions in both treatment groups. 

- The model includes a structural constraint which should prevent the mortality risk for people with advanced GIST from being lower than that for the age- and sex-matched general population (although this has been implemented incorrectly; see Section 4.3.5). The model also assumes that the cumulative probability of PFS cannot be greater than the cumulative probability of OS at any time point. No other constraints are included. Given the use of a partitioned survival approach, the risks of progression and death are structurally unrelated. 

- Dose escalation to ripretinib 150mg BID in patients with disease progression in INVICTUS[2] is assumed not to have impacted on OS estimates relative to QD dosing. All post-progression ripretinib costs are based on the ripretinib 150mg QD dose. Taken together, the model assumes that the outcomes observed in INVICTUS (including the effects of post-progression ripretinib 150mg BID dosing in some patients) can be achieved by using the 150mg QD dose in all patients. 

- HRQoL is determined by the presence/absence of disease progression and whether patients receive ripretinib after disease progression. The same utility values for the PF and PD (off treatment) states are applied in each treatment group. The utility value applied to patients who remain on ripretinib treatment after progression lies between the values for the PF and PD (off treatment) states. Utility values are adjusted for increasing age. 

- AEs result in QALY losses and additional costs. The CS[3] indicates that AEs are assumed to be resolved within the first 28-day model cycle (although the model is subject to an error whereby AErelated QALY losses are applied in all cycles). 

- Prior to disease progression, pre-treatment and disease management costs are assumed to be higher for patients receiving ripretinib compared with those receiving BSC alone. The same costs per cycle/event for pain management, the management of progressed disease after ripretinib discontinuation, palliative treatments and end-of-life care are applied to the ripretinib and BSC groups.

_4.2.4.1 Time-to-event parameters_ 

_Statistical adjustment of OS data to account for treatment switching in the placebo group and intrapatient dose escalation (IPDE) dosing in the ripretinib group_ 

As discussed in Section 3.2.1, within both groups of the INVICTUS trial,[2] a change in treatment could occur following disease progression. Patients who were randomised to receive placebo had the option to commence treatment with ripretinib 150mg QD after progression and could increase their dose to 150mg BID on further progression. Patients who were randomised to receive ripretinib (plus BSC) could remain on treatment at their current dose (150mg QD), increase their dose (to 150mg BID) or discontinue ripretinib. The decision to remain on ripretinib (at either the current or increased dose) was informed by the investigator’s view of whether the patient was obtaining benefit from ripretinib, if dose escalation could be tolerated and whether or not they had access to additional therapies.[4] An overview of the treatment changes that occurred during the trial is provided in Section 3.2.2. The company’s base case economic model includes statistical adjustment for treatment switching onto ripretinib in the BSC group but does not include adjustment to account for IPDE to the 150mg BID dose in the ripretinib group. Six alternative approaches to adjusting for IPDE are considered in the company’s scenario analyses (see Table 41). Additional IPDE adjustment analyses were provided as part of the company’s clarification response.[35] The subsequent sections describe the methods and results of the company’s adjustment of OS to account for treatment switching in the placebo group and IPDE to ripretinib 150mg BID in the intervention group of INVICTUS. 

_Adjustment of OS data to account for treatment switching onto ripretinib in the placebo group (included in the base case model)_ 

The company’s adjustment of the placebo group OS data to account for placebo group patients switching onto ripretinib remains unchanged from the analysis presented in TA881.[1] At the 15[th] January 2021 DCO of INVICTUS,[2] 30 of the 44 (68%) patients in the placebo arm had crossed over to receive ripretinib following disease progression, with the majority of switches occurring less than four weeks (one model cycle) after disease progression (mean xxxx weeks).[4] NICE DSU TSD 16[48] details three main approaches which may be considered to adjust estimates of OS for treatment switching: (i) IPCW; (ii) RPSFTM; and (iii) two-stage estimation methods. All three approaches are discussed in the CS,[3] although IPCW was not considered for formal analysis by the company due to the small sample size and the large proportion of patients switching. The other two methods – the RPSFTM and two-stage estimation approaches – were both explored. An RPSFTM was implemented using the _rpsftm_ package in R. This approach relies on the ‘common treatment effect’ assumption, which in this case, assumes that the delay in receiving ripretinib observed in the subset of placebo group patients who switched to receive ripretinib in INVICTUS[2] (compared to the ripretinib arm) has not influenced OS outcomes. A plot of counterfactual event times provided in Figure 26 of the CS was used to assess this assumption; this plot suggests that the common treatment effect assumption is likely to be violated. 

84 



<!-- page 436 -->

The two-stage approach (with re-censoring) was used in the company’s base case economic model. This approach relies on there being an appropriate secondary baseline at the point of treatment switching, with no unmeasured confounding at this point. Time of disease progression was taken as the secondary baseline, with measurements of covariates that were closest to this time point being used in the analyses. Two models were considered for the two-stage approach: a ‘simple’ model in which the only covariate was time to progression, and a ‘complex’ model which also included age, HRQoL (measure not stated), and ECOG PS. Median switching-adjusted OS for the placebo arm was xxxx and xxxx weeks for the simple and complex models, respectively. The company used the simple two-stage model in its base case analysis on the basis that time to progression was the only statistically significant variable in the complex model and retaining additional variables would add to uncertainty. 

The CS[3] reports the results of several scenario analyses relating to the statistical adjustment of OS data to account for treatment switching from placebo to ripretinib. These included: unadjusted OS; the simple two-stage approach; the complex two-stage approach and the RPSFTM approach. Each adjustment approach was applied separately with and without re-censoring. In addition, two further RPSFTM analyses were conducted which relax the common treatment effect assumption (assuming _ki_ =0.50). The results of these scenario analyses are reproduced in Table 41 (Scenarios S19 to S26). Estimates of cost-effectiveness were not particularly sensitive to the adjustment method chosen, with the ICER for ripretinib versus BSC ranging from £27,470 to £31,104 per QALY gained (including QALY weighting). The company’s deterministic base case ICER is near the middle of this range (£28,836 per QALY gained). As expected, the ICER for ripretinib versus BSC was substantially higher when switching adjustment was excluded from the analysis (Scenario S19: ICER = £61,731 per QALY gained). 

In TA881,[1] the ERG requested further information from the company regarding the approach used to implement the two-stage estimation method. The analyses provided used a log-normal model to derive the counterfactual OS as if no crossover occurred in the placebo group; this model had the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) value of the five parametric survival models considered (the exponential, log-normal, log-logistic, Weibull, and generalised gamma distributions). Estimates of switchingadjusted median OS for placebo from the exponential model lacked face validity, whilst estimates from other models showed little variation: compared with the log-normal model estimate of xxxx weeks, estimates for the other models ranged from xxxx to xxxx weeks. The impact of these alternative models on the cost-effectiveness of ripretinib was not explored, but this is not expected to be a key driver.[4] 

Seven patients in the placebo group had censored times of disease progression. When performing the statistical adjustment of OS data to account for treatment switching in the placebo group, these patients were assumed to have an observed progression time equal to their censored progression time. The company stated that of these seven patients, three had crossed over to ripretinib treatment.[4] 

85 



<!-- page 437 -->

_Adjustment of OS data for IPDE in the ripretinib group (included in the company’s scenario analyses only)_ 

The adjustment of OS data in the ripretinib group to account for IPDE to post-progression ripretinib 150mg BID dosing was not a relevant consideration in TA881[1] because the company’s economic model included a stopping rule at the point of disease progression. The company’s model for the current appraisal allows for continued treatment with ripretinib following disease progression. As 150mg BID dosing represents an off-label use of ripretinib,[21] the company applied a variety of methods to adjust the OS data to attempt to estimate the counterfactual OS under ripretinib 150mg QD dosing - though only one approach (i.e., two-stage adjustment) is aligned with that intent. These methods were only applied in the company’s scenario analyses; the base case analysis does not include any adjustment of the OS data in the ripretinib group. 

Approaches for IPDE adjustment undertaken by the company are summarised in the clinical section of this EAG report (Section 3.3.2.1, Table 11). Of the four approaches listed in CS[3] Section 2.6.2 and CS Section 3.3.2, Approach 1 (Open-label BID vs QD OS analysis) included three variations (Approach 1(a) to 1(c) in Table 11). Approach 1(a) and 1(b) were presented in CS Figures 9 and 10, and Approach 1(c) was presented in response to clarification question B3.[35] These were descriptive analyses of OS in mutually exclusive subgroups within the ripretinib arm (i.e., with or without dose escalation), exploring the impact of IPDE. The company did not include these in scenario analyses, which the EAG considers reasonable given the key biases outlined in Section 3.3.2.1. 

The company’s scenario analyses included two variations of each of the remaining three approaches (as described in Table 11): 

- Approach 2: Censored BID-dosing analysis 

- Approach 3: Time-varying Cox proportional hazards model 

- Approach 4: Two-stage adjustment. 

Among the three approaches, only the two-stage estimation is recommended in NICE TSD24[70] for adjusting (i.e., removing) the effects of subsequent treatments that differ (ripretinib 150mg BID) from those in the original randomised arm (ripretinib 150mg QD). IPCW would be an appropriate alternative; however, the company did not apply this method due to the small sample size. 

The EAG provides a detailed summary and critique of the three approaches that informed the company’s scenario analyses in the subsequent sections. Please refer to Table 11 for the corresponding method numbers. 

86 



<!-- page 438 -->

## _Approach 2: Censored BID-dosing analysis_ 

Approach 2(a) compared OS in the ripretinib arm with and without censoring patients at the point at which they escalated to BID dosing (CS,[3] Figure 11). The censored analysis showed slightly improved OS, which suggests that excluding BID dosing leads to better outcomes. This contradicts the views of the clinicians who attended the company’s 2024 advisory board meeting[40] and the EAG’s clinical advisors. Nevertheless, since patients were not randomised to receive BID, this analysis is likely to be biased due to informative censoring and does not reflect a fair comparison. The company did not use this analysis for scenario analysis. 

In Approach 2(b), the company compared OS between two non-mutually exclusive subgroups: (i) patients with progressed disease who escalated to BID dosing combined with those whose disease did not progress versus (ii) patients with progressed disease who did not escalate to BID dosing combined with those whose disease did not progress (see Table 11 and CS, Figure 12). The first group showed OS similar to the unadjusted OS, while the second group had worse OS. These analyses aimed to “isolate” the effect of post-progression BID and QD dosing, respectively. However, as patients were not randomised to dose escalation, selecting subgroups based on post-randomisation characteristics introduces selection bias. In particular, attrition bias is apparent: the proportion of non-progressors in each of these analyses would not reflect the natural rate of progression and non-progression in the overall population. Consequently, these comparisons do not allow for reliable inferences about the causal effect of dose escalation. 

Six parametric models (exponential, generalised gamma, Gompertz, log-logistic, log-normal, and Weibull) were fitted to the adjusted OS for survival extrapolation, with the AIC and Bayesian information Criterion (BIC) statistics indicating the exponential model as the best fit for the "plus BID progressors" subgroup and the log-normal model for the "plus QD progressors" subgroup. However, the company selected the log-logistic model for both scenario analyses, referred to as "Open-label BID vs QD OS (non-progressors + IPDE progressors)" (Scenario S34 in Table 41) and "Open-label BID vs QD OS (non-progressors + QD progressors)" (Scenario S35 in Table 41). These scenario analyses resulted in slightly higher ICERs (£31,371 and £30,142 per QALY gained, respectively) than the company’s base case. 

The company did not provide further justification for selecting log-logistic models for survival extrapolation in these two IPDE-adjusted OS scenario analyses (Approach 2(b)(i) and 2(b)(i) in Table 11). This choice reflects the company’s use of log-logistic models as in its preferred base case with unadjusted ripretinib OS, and because the log-logistic models showed the lowest combined AIC values for the IPDE-adjusted ripretinib OS (CS, Table 34) and placebo OS (with two-stage adjustment) (CS, Table 33). 

87 



<!-- page 439 -->

## _Approach 3: Time-varying Cox proportional hazards model_ 

The company conducted three time-varying Cox proportional hazards models for dose escalation adjustment, each with a different set of time-varying covariates (Approach 3(a)-3(c) in Table 11; corresponding HRs are reported in CS,[3] Table 35): 

- Model 1 included only IPDE as a covariate 

- Model 2 included IPDE, progression status, ECOG score, EQ-5D VAS, lesion diameter (change from baseline) 

- Model 3 included all variables in Model 2, plus baseline lesion diameter sum, age, sex, race, region, baseline BMI, hepatic impairment, number of prior therapies, baseline creatinine clearance, and baseline renal impairment. 

Each model produced a HR estimating the effect of IPDE on OS, with all HRs > 1.0 and 95% CIs crossing 1.0, indicating a non-statistically significant association with reduced survival. The treatmentonly model (Model 1, HR=1.58; 95% CI: 0.85 to 2.95; Approach 3(a) in Table 11 and Scenario S32 in Table 41) and the full model (Model 3, HR=1.37; 95% CI: 0.66 to 2.84; Approach 3(c) in Table 11 and Scenario S33 in Table 41) were used in scenario analyses. For each analysis, a weighted average HR was applied to the base case OS curve in the ripretinib arm, with weights based on the proportion of patients in the on-treatment PD state, determined by the selected OS and TTD curves. The adjustment was implemented as: 

## Adjusted OS = OS^(1 + Proportion_PDOnRip × (HR – 1)). 

These analyses resulted in slightly higher ICERs compared with the company’s base case, at £29,347 and £29,162, respectively. In response to clarification question B7,[35] the company corrected an error in these analyses whereby 13 patients were assigned a death event in multiple periods. The updated analysis yielded a revised HR of 1.50 (95% CI: 0.70 to 3.22; _p_ =0.300). However, the company did not specify which time-varying Cox model was corrected, and no updated ICERs were provided following the correction. 

The EAG highlights two key concerns with the time-varying Cox model approach. First, the HR was estimated for the full OS dataset but is applied only to a subset of patients with progressed disease who remain on treatment – this leads to a mismatch between estimation and application. Second, because dose escalation was not randomised, simply including time-varying covariates (i.e., time-varying treatment exposure and time-varying confounders) in a Cox model, without causal inference methods, such as a marginal structural model, cannot address time-varying confounding and limits the ability to interpret the causal effect of IPDE on OS. This likely explains the counterintuitive HR that suggests that IPDE to ripretinib 150mg BID is harmful versus continued QD treatment, which contradicts clinicians’ expectations that dose escalation would be given to patients who are likely to benefit and can tolerate it. 

88 



<!-- page 440 -->

## _Approach 4: Two-stage adjustment_ 

In the two-stage estimation approach, the company used methods similar to those for crossover adjustment in the placebo arm. This involved estimating a time ratio to shorten or extend postprogression survival (the period during which ripretinib BID was received), aiming to derive the counterfactual OS had patients continued ripretinib 150mg QD instead of escalating to BID dosing after progression. This method requires establishing a suitable secondary baseline at the point of treatmentswitching (i.e., initiation of subsequent treatment) and assumes no unmeasured confounding at this point. The company defined disease progression as the secondary baseline, using covariate measurements closest to this event. 

A simple two-stage model (without g-estimation) is valid only if there is no time-varying confounding between progression and initiation of subsequent treatment, and if subsequent treatment consistently follows progression (i.e., occurs on the same date or close to it). Although the company did not provide evidence on the interval between progression and initiation of subsequent treatment, this gap is likely to be small, given the advanced stage of disease in this patient population. Therefore, the EAG considers the simple two-stage approach without g-estimation to be reasonable. 

In the first stage, two sets of models were considered for the two-stage approach to generate time ratios (Approach 4(a) and 4(b) in Table 11): the ‘simple’ model included only time to progression as a covariate, while the ‘complex model’ additionally incorporated age, EQ-5D VAS score at progression, and ECOG PS at progression. Each model was fitted using a range of parametric distributions, including the exponential, Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic and generalised gamma distributions. The Gompertz distribution was also added in response to clarification question B9.[35] 

In all cases, time ratios were greater than 1.0 (with some 95% CIs crossing 1.0), indicating prolonged survival for patients who received dose escalation dosing compared with those who remained on QD dosing (CS Table 36; response to clarification question B9[35] ). For the scenario analysis, the company selected the log-normal distribution for the simple model (time ratio = 3.45; 95% CI: 1.56 to 7.60; Scenario S30 in Table 41) and the generalised gamma distribution for the complex model (time ratio = 2.72; 95% CI: 1.57 to 4.74; Scenario S31 in Table 41), as these had the lowest AIC values within their respective model types (CS, Table 36). 

The second stage involved applying the time ratio to estimate counterfactual OS, as if patients had continued QD dosing without dose escalation. The company incorporated these time ratios through a ‘weighted average hazard adjustment’ to the OS base case parametric model for the ripretinib arm. Time ratios were treated as equivalent to inverse HRs and weighted by the proportion of patients in the ontreatment PD partition. The adjustment was implemented in the economic model using the following formula: 

Adjusted OS = OS^(1 + Proportion_PDOnRip × ([1 / SurvivalTimeRatio] − 1)) 

89 



<!-- page 441 -->

The EAG notes several concerns regarding this approach. First, time ratios should not be used to derive HRs, as these are conceptually distinct measures. Time ratios are calculated based on accelerated failure time (AFT) models, whereas HRs arise from proportional hazards (PH) models. Only the exponential and Weibull distributions can be directly expressed under both modelling frameworks. Even in those cases, the transformation HR = 1 / time ratio is only valid for the exponential distribution. Second, the company inappropriately applied a uniform time ratio adjustment to all patients who had progressed at each time point in the model, rather than restricting it to those who actually underwent dose escalation. This application is inconsistent with the derivation of the time ratio, which was based on patients who had progressed and remained on treatment at each time point. 

The approach to implementation in the economic analysis described above was further simplified by relying on a summary percentage rather than IPD, which undermines the validity of the analysis. Overall, the EAG recommended in clarification question B9[35] that the company instead conduct the two-stage adjustment using an approach similar to that employed for crossover adjustment in the placebo arm and to use the resulting counterfactual OS for survival extrapolation. 

In response to clarification question B9,[35] the company provided a comprehensive update, which the EAG considers to be reasonable. Specifically, counterfactual OS was derived using time ratios from each of the six distributions, following an approach similar to that used for crossover adjustment in the placebo arm. This was done with and without re-censoring, resulting in 12 counterfactual OS scenarios. Parametric survival models (the exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-normal, log-logistic, and generalised gamma distributions) were then fitted to each counterfactual OS dataset for extrapolation (i.e., 12*2*6 = 144 scenarios). 

The company did not provide updated ICERs for each of these scenarios but included functionality to apply each of these distributions and adjustments within their updated economic model. Among all scenarios, the complex model using the generalised gamma distribution to derive the time ratio had the lowest AIC, indicating the best statistical fit for estimating counterfactual OS, as if all patients had continued on ripretinib QD dosing without dose escalation. 

In summary, for the IPDE adjustment scenario analyses, the EAG considers the company’s updated two-stage adjustment approach, as outlined in their response to clarification question B9,[35] to be reasonable and in line with TSDs 16 and 24.[48, 70] In contrast, the EAG considers all other approaches applied by the company to be unsuitable for informing decision-making, as they fail to support a causal interpretation of the IPDE effect due to time-varying confounding and selection bias not being appropriately addressed, and/or because they suffer from questionable implementation within the company’s economic model. 

90 



<!-- page 442 -->

_Summary of parametric survival model fitting process and model selection_ 

The company fitted a series of standard parametric survival models to the time-to-event data on TTD+PFS (as a composite end point), PFS and OS (adjusted for treatment switching onto ripretinib in placebo group) from INVICTUS.[2] The DCO for TTD, PFS and OS was the 15[th] January 2021;[3] this is the same DCO applied in TA881.[1] The company’s base case model for the current appraisal does not include any adjustment of OS for ripretinib IPDE or the costs of ripretinib 150mg BID dosing following progression in the intervention group, although these factors are considered in the company’s scenario analyses (see Table 41). 

The same general survival modelling approach was applied to both the PFS data and the switchingadjusted OS data. For each end point, the company assessed the PH assumption to determine whether it is reasonable to fit models which include a treatment-indicating covariate (an HR). This was done by examining log-cumulative hazard plots, plotting Schoenfeld residuals and performing Schoenfeld global tests. There was evidence to suggest that the PH assumption was violated for PFS, but that it may be a reasonable assumption for OS. Quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots which can be used to assess the appropriateness of using jointly fitted AFT models are not presented in the CS.[3] The company elected not to use jointly fitted models and instead fitted models independently to the data for each treatment group. These considerations were not necessary for TTD as this end point is only relevant to the ripretinib group. The company fitted six standard parametric survival models to the PFS and OS data, including the exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-normal, log-logistic and generalised gamma distributions. For TTD, the company fitted the same six models as well as the gamma and generalised F models, although the latter two distributions are not included in the executable economic model. More flexible parametric survival distributions, such as restricted cubic spline (RCS) models, were not considered for TTD, PFS or OS. 

The CS[3] indicates that the company’s model selection process included consideration of: relative goodness-of-fit statistics using the AIC and BIC, visual inspection of the fitted models and plausibility based on expert opinion obtained from clinicians consulted during three advisory board meetings held by the company in 2022, 2024 and 2025.[27, 40, 41] The CS also mentions that the same parametric survival distributions were selected for both treatment groups. The CS does not present empirical or modelled hazard plots for OS or PFS; however, these were provided as part of the company’s response to clarification questions in TA881.[1] A plot showing the hazard functions for the models fitted to the TTD+PFS data is presented in CS Appendix J;[29] an updated plot was provided as part of the company’s clarification response.[35] The CS indicates that the expected shape of the hazard functions for OS and TTD was discussed with clinical experts; it is unclear from the CS whether the hazard plots were used to inform model selection for PFS.

## _4.2.4.2 Health-related quality of life_ 

## _Health state utility values_ 

Health state utility values were informed by EQ-5D-5L data collected in INVICTUS.[2] According to the CS,[3] EQ-5D-5L data were collected using an electronic PRO system at Cycle 1 on Day 1 and Day 15, on Day 1 of subsequent treatment cycles, and within 7 days after the last dose, at the end of treatment visit. EQ-5D-5L utility scores were calculated using the algorithm based on country-specific reference score sets reported by Van Hout _et al._[64] The EQ-5D-5L data were then mapped to the 3L version using the algorithm reported by Hernández Alava and Pudney.[71] Utility values for each model health state were based on the least squares mean (LSM) values from a mixed model for repeat measures (MMRM) analysis conducted by the company, which included treatment arm, treatment status, health state (PF/PD) and two-way and three-way interactions for these items as fixed effects. The CS states that the analysis used a _“compound symmetry within-subject correlation structure per treatment arm/treatment status/health state combination.”_ The company’s response to clarification question B14 states that treatment switching in the placebo treatment arm was formally incorporated in the MMRM model, but that dose escalation to ripretinib 150mg BID was not included.[35] The company’s clarification response also states that the chosen model was the only MMRM model considered; however, it was considered _“the most parsimonious MMRM model that would allow for full flexibility in health state utility estimations, whilst avoiding the potential risk of over fitting.”_ 

The CS[3] reports that the dataset used to inform health state utility values included “ _all EQ-5D measurements taken while patients were within each partition of the model.”_ The company’s clarification response (question B14)[35] presents the number of visits and patients by health status and treatment group which informed the MMRM analysis (see Table 30). Information regarding any exclusions of patients or time points, or imputation methods used to handle missing data are not mentioned in either the CS or the clarification response. As shown in the table, very few data points were available for patients with progressed disease who were not receiving ripretinib (N visits = 46; N patients = 43).
