## _Disutility values associated with adverse events_ 

The company’s model includes QALY losses associated with Grade ≥3 TEAEs occurring with an incidence of ≥5% in either treatment group during the double-blind phase of INVICTUS.[3] Disutility values for AEs were taken from external sources. The AE frequencies and disutility values applied in the model are shown in Table 32. The disutility for anaemia was based on a Short Form 6-Dimensions (SF-6D) value reported by reported by Harrow _et al._ ,[62] which, according to the CS,[3] was then re-scaled to the EQ-5D using a method previously described by Hoyle _et al._[73] Despite scrutinising each of these sources, the EAG was unable to determine how this re-scaling was done or how the resulting disutility value was estimated. The disutility value for abdominal pain was based on an EQ-5D VAS estimate for chest pain in people with lung cancer reported by Doyle _et al_ .[63] The CS states that the disutility for hypertension was also taken from Doyle _et al._ , although the EAG notes that this study does not report values for this type of AE; it appears that the company has assumed that the disutility for hypertension is equivalent to that for chest pain. Whilst this assumption has been applied in previous appraisals (e.g., NICE TA439[74] ), the justification for assuming hypertension and chest pain have equivalent HRQoL impacts is unclear. Overall disutilities attributable to AEs were estimated to be 0.019 for ripretinib, and 0.015 for BSC. Based on the description of the model in the CS, the company had intended to apply AE-related QALY losses in in the first model cycle based on an assumed duration of 28 days; however, the model is subject to an error whereby the QALY loss is applied in every model cycle (see Section 4.3.5, critical appraisal point 1).

## _4.2.4.3 Resource use and costs_ 

The model includes the following cost components: (i) drug acquisition costs associated with ripretinib and BSC (pain management medications); (ii) health state costs; (iii) pre-treatment costs; (iv) palliative treatment costs; (v) AE management costs and (vi) end-of-life care costs. ## _Drug acquisition costs (per cycle, ripretinib group only)_ 

The list price per pack of 90 x 50mg ripretinib tablets is £18,400.00 (30 days’ supply). The total acquisition costs for ripretinib are calculated in the model as a function of the list price of ripretinib, the probability of remaining on treatment in each cycle (based on the TTD function), the number of days per cycle, and a mean RDI of xxxxx from INVICTUS.[2] Wastage is calculated using an integer packbased approach which tracks whether a new pack of 90 ripretinib tablets is required in each 28-day model cycle (a new pack is not required every 10 model cycles). As ripretinib is an oral therapy, no administration costs are assumed. 

A Patient Access Scheme (PAS) has been agreed for ripretinib. This takes the form of a simple price discount of xxxxxx. The acquisition cost for ripretinib per 30-day pack including the PAS is estimated to be xxxxxxxxx.[3] 

## _BSC medications (per cycle, both treatment groups)_ 

BSC pain management costs were based on a survey of 15 physicians in England and Wales undertaken to inform TA488,[45] with additional information on dosing taken from TA730.[65] Drug costs were taken from the British National Formulary (BNF).[26] The most commonly prescribed dosage form of each product was determined using Prescription Cost Analysis data.[66] The CS[3] states that costing was based on the maintenance doses described in the SmPC for the most common indication of each product. Where a range of doses was available, the CS states that the lowest price for each medication was used; however, the EAG notes that this is not accurate as lower prices are available for several products in the Commercial Medicines Unit (CMU) electronic Market Information Tool (eMIT) (see Section 4.3.5). A breakdown of pain management drug costs applied in the model is shown in Table 34.

Pre-treatment costs are assumed to include CT scans, MRI scans, FBCs and LFTs. ## _4.2.5 Model evaluation methods_ 

The CS[3] presents ICERs for ripretinib versus BSC using both the deterministic and probabilistic versions of the model. The probabilistic ICER is based on 1,000 Monte Carlo samples. The results of the probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) are presented using a cost-effectiveness plane and costeffectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs). All model results presented in the CS include the PASdiscounted price for ripretinib and the list prices for other treatments. All ICERs presented in the CS include a decision modifier of 1.7 which is consistent with estimates obtained using the York QALY Shortfall Calculator.[76] 

The CS[3] presents the results of deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSAs) using a tornado plot and in tabular form. The CS also presents the results of 36 scenario analyses which explore the impact of: alternative discount rates; end-of-life care costs from Round _et al.;_[75] alternative parametric survival models for OS, PFS and TTD; alternative placebo group switching adjustment methods; alternative utility values; alternative methods for adjusting for the effect of IPDE on ripretinib OS and the inclusion of the costs of ripretinib 150mg BID dosing applied to 50% of the time spent  receiving post-progression ripretinib (based on an clinical input rather than the proportion observed in INVICTUS[2] ).

## **4.3 Critical appraisal of the company’s economic analysis** 

This section presents the EAG’s critical appraisal of the company’s original economic model, as described in the CS.[3] Section 4.3.1 summarises the EAG’s methods for the critical appraisal of the company’s model. Section 4.3.2 describes the EAG’s verification of the company’s model. Section 4.3.3 describes the correspondence between the CS, the model inputs and their original sources. Section 4.3.4 describes the extent to which the company’s economic analysis adheres to the NICE Reference Case.[77] Section 4.3.5 presents the main issues identified during the EAG’s critical appraisal of the company’s model. 

## _4.3.1 Critical appraisal methods_ 

The EAG adopted a number of approaches to explore, interrogate and critically appraise the company’s submitted economic analysis and the underlying model upon which this is based. These included: 

- Consideration of key items contained within published economic evaluation and health economic modelling checklists.[78, 79] 

- Scrutiny and discussion of the company’s model by the EAG. 

- Double-programming of the deterministic version of the company’s original model to fully assess the logic of the model structure, to draw out any unwritten assumptions and to identify any apparent errors in model implementation. 

- Examination of the correspondence between the description of the model reported in the CS[3] and the company’s executable model. 

- Where possible, checking parameter values used in the company’s model against their original data sources. 

- Replication of the base case results, PSA, DSAs and scenario analyses reported in the CS using the company’s executable model. 

- The use of expert clinical input to judge the credibility of the company’s economic analyses and the assumptions underpinning the model. 

## _4.3.2 Model verification by the EAG_ 

Table 42 presents a comparison of the results of the deterministic version of the company’s original model and the EAG’s double-programmed model. The results obtained from the EAG’s rebuilt model are similar to those generated using the company’s model. However, the EAG’s double-programming exercise led to the identification of several minor programming errors; these issues are discussed in detail in Section 4.3.5 (critical appraisal point 1).

## _4.3.3 Correspondence between the model, the CS and original sources of parameter values_ 

Where possible, the EAG checked the company’s model input values against their original sources, including the INVICTUS CSR.[2] The original version of the company’s model included some discrepancies – in particular, the version of the life tables used in the model reflected the UK population and were outdated, the unit costs obtained from NHS Cost Collection were based on an outdated version, and the drug prices did not consistently reflect the lowest prices from eMIT. Following the clarification round, the company submitted an updated economic model. The updated model is also subject to inconsistencies in that some of the drug costs do not correspond to the least expensive versions available, and the updated general population mortality risks are based on life tables for England and Wales rather than England only.[61] The EAG considers these to be minor discrepancies. The EAG notes that the NHS Cost collection online Power BI tool was unavailable for consultation after the clarification response was received, and therefore the EAG had to rely on screenshots provided by the company regarding the cost estimates that were updated at the clarification stage.[67]

## _4.3.5 Main issues identified from the EAG’s critical appraisal_ 

Box 1 summarises the main issues identified within the EAG’s critical appraisal of the company’s economic analyses. These issues are discussed in further detail in the subsequent sections. 

## **Box 1:  Main issues identified from the EAG’s critical appraisal** 

1. Model errors 

2. Concerns regarding the exclusion of a later data-cut of INVICTUS from the model 

3. Concerns regarding the company’s survival analysis 

4. Uncertainty around the commissioning of ripretinib 150mg BID dosing in the NHS 

5. Uncertainty around the effect on ripretinib 150mg BID dosing on OS 

6. Concerns relating to the modelled costs of drug wastage 

## **(1) Model errors** 

The EAG’s double-programming exercise identified a number of minor errors in the original version of the company’s executable model: 

- (a) The pain medication costs applied in the model do not reflect lowest drug prices listed in the current versions of the BNF or eMIT.[26, 80] 

- (b) The unit costs from the NHS Cost Collection[67] do not reflect the most up-to-date version. 

- (c) The model uses life tables for the UK rather than England.[61] The life table risks contained in the worksheet “Data Store” have not been linked to the life table risks applied as mortality constraints to the OS models. 

- (d) The general population mortality constraint applied to ripretinib OS is subject to a programming error which allows the modelled risk of death for people receiving ripretinib to drop below the general population mortality risk after 285 cycles. 

- (e) The CS[3] (Section 3.4.4) states that the model applies AE-related QALY loss once only in the first cycle. However, the executable model applies AE-related QALY losses in every model cycle. In addition, the formulae used to calculate per-cycle AE-related QALY losses include the incorrect use of brackets which means that the QALY loss is not scaled up to the model cohort size (1,000 patients); hence, changing the cohort size changes the ICER (which should not be the case). The AE-related QALY loss is also incorrectly applied to the half-cycle corrected trace, rather than the uncorrected model trace; this means that the total expected AErelated QALY loss is not applied to patients who progress or die in the first model cycle. 

- (f) The RDI estimates included in the model reflect the double-blind period of INVICTUS.[2] Given that the current model assumes that ripretinib treatment is permitted post-progression, the EAG believes that RDI estimates for the open-label period should be applied to post-progression ripretinib. 

119 



<!-- page 471 -->

- (g) The costs of pre-treatment are applied using the half-cycle corrected model trace, rather than the uncorrected trace. This means that patients who progress or die during the first model cycle do not incur these costs. 

- (h) The formulae which calculate the costs of palliative treatment use both the half-cycle corrected and the uncorrected trace. This introduces a minor inconsistency in the calculations. 

- (i) BSC costs are included in the ripretinib group in the PF and PD (off treatment) states but are excluded from PD (on treatment) state. The EAG believes that patients who continue to receive ripretinib following disease progression would also incur BSC costs. 

- (j) The model assumes that there are 52 weeks in a year; however, there are 52.18 weeks in a year. 

- (k) The approach used to sample health state utility values in the PSA ignores the logical ordering of the parameters (e.g., the sampled utility value for the PD state may be lower than the sampled utility value for the PF state in the same probabilistic model run). This issue could be resolved by sampling from difference distributions using the method described by Ren _et al._[81] 

During the clarification round, the EAG asked the company to confirm that these issues represent errors and to provide a corrected version of the model (see clarification response,[35] questions B19, B20, B22, B23, B24, B25, B26, B27, B28, B29 and B33). The company’s response acknowledges these issues. As part of its clarification response, the company submitted an updated model which addresses these errors. The EAG notes the following concerns regarding the updated model: 

- Issue (a). Some of the pain management drug costs still did not reflect the least expensive products. 

- Issue (b). The EAG was unable to check the NHS Cost Collection estimates because the Power BI tool was unavailable at the time of completion of the EAG report. 

- Issue (c). The updated model uses life tables for England and Wales rather than England only. 

- Issue (f). The RDI estimate from the open-label period of INVICTUS[2] does not appear to have been included in the updated model. 

- Issue (h). The palliative treatment costs in the revised model use the half-cycle corrected trace. However, this introduces a further minor error whereby the costs for patients who progress in the first cycle are omitted from the total costs. This issue is very minor. 

- Issue (j). The company’s clarification response states that this issue could not be addressed due to time constraints. 

The company’s revised model results are summarised separately in Section 5.1. 

120 



<!-- page 472 -->

## **(2) Concerns regarding the exclusion of a later data-cut of INVICTUS from the model** 

The data for TTD, PFS and OS used in the company’s model reflect the 15[th] January 2021 DCO of INVICTUS.[2] This is the same DCO used in the economic model used to inform TA881.[1] During the clarification round for the current appraisal, the EAG asked the company to clarify whether more recent data-cuts of INVICTUS are available, and if so, why these had not been used in the model (see clarification response,[35] question B1). The company’s response states that there is a later DCO from INVICTUS from May 2022, but these data have not been included in the model. This later DCO would have provided approximately 16 months of additional follow-up compared with the January 2021 DCO. The company’s clarification response includes additional clinical data from the May 2022 DCO on patient disposition, Kaplan-Meier plots for OS and an updated HR for OS (excluding adjustment for treatment switching onto ripretinib in the placebo group). 

The company’s clarification response[35] states that preparation and analysis for the CS for the current appraisal[3] began before the 2022 DCO analysis of INVICTUS became available. The clarification response also highlights that the HRs for OS for ripretinib versus placebo are similar between the January 2021 and May 2022 DCOs (0.41 versus xxxx, respectively). Despite this, the company states that it considers the May 2022 DCO to be less robust than the earlier January 2021 DCO, noting that the pre-specified end-of-study analysis included OS and safety, but not PFS or HRQoL; as such, incorporating the May 2022 data would result in different DCOs being applied between the clinical end points used in the model. The company’s response also argues that the 2022 DCO would increase the risk of bias and confounding in the OS data due to a greater reliance on data collection during the openlabel period of INVICTUS.[35] 

The EAG acknowledges that incorporating the later DCO into the economic model would require all of the company’s analyses of OS from INVICTUS[2] to be repeated, including the statistical adjustment of OS to account for treatment switching in the placebo group, the statistical adjustment of OS to account for IPDE to 150mg ripretinib BID dosing (applied in the company’s scenario analyses only) and updating the parametric survival models fitted to the adjusted OS data. However, the EAG believes that the company should have applied the latest DCO for OS, with appropriate statistical adjustments, as this would have provided additional information to inform long-term predictions of OS. Figure 32 presents overlaid Kaplan-Meier plots of ripretinib OS from the 2021 and 2022 DCOs; OS data for the placebo group are not presented here as they were not adjusted for treatment switching. 

The EAG considers that, despite the limitations of follow-up during the unblinded period, long-term follow-up data would provide valuable insights. In particular, such data could help clarify the trajectory of longer-term HRs and hazard shapes, both of which are important considerations for survival 

121 



<!-- page 473 -->

extrapolation. Specifically, an additional year of follow-up would better characterise the tail of the survival distribution which could help to inform parametric survival model selection. 

Intercurrent events such as IPDE in the experimental arm and treatment crossover in the control arm complicate interpretation of the ITT analysis. However, the company has attempted to address these issues using the two-stage adjustment method (Section 4.2.4), which the EAG deems reasonable. With longer follow-up, more patients are expected to progress, increasing the effective sample size for both IPDE and crossover adjustments. This would likely allow for more reliable estimates, provided potential biases are appropriately accounted for through the chosen covariates – which the EAG’s clinical advisors considered reasonable – and characterisation of longer-term treatment effects. In line with TSD 24,[47] which recommends presenting two-stage adjustment results both with and without re-censoring, longer-term data would be especially valuable to mitigate information loss in the re-censoring scenarios (i.e., EAG’s preferred scenarios for addressing treatment switching in the control arm and IPDE in the ripretinib arm). 

Although outcome measurement could be affected by the open-label nature of the follow-up data, the EAG notes that OS is a hard endpoint and therefore less susceptible to subjective influences. While the company stated concerns regarding the open-label nature of the data at the FAC stage of the appraisal, the EAG’s considers that the benefits of examining longer-term follow-up outweigh the risks. Excluding these data would constrain the understanding of longer-term survival outcomes and may increase decision uncertainty. Given the absence of alternative evidence on longer-term ripretinib use, the EAG considered that including the long-term data would have provided a more balanced basis for decisionmaking.

## **(3) Concerns regarding the company’s survival analysis** 

The EAG has several concerns regarding the parametric survival modelling presented in the CS.[3] These concerns are discussed below in terms of the general considerations around model fitting and selection set out in NICE DSU TSDs 14 and 21.[82, 83] 

122 



<!-- page 474 -->

**==> picture [343 x 261] intentionally omitted <==**

## _(a) Use of independent models fitted to data for each treatment group_ 

The company considered the potential for jointly fitted models for PFS and OS through consideration of log cumulative hazard plots, plots of Schoenfeld residuals and global Schoenfeld residuals tests. For PFS, the CS[3] states that the log-cumulative hazards were not strictly parallel, the Schoenfeld residuals plot suggests that the HR is likely to vary over time and the global Schoenfeld test suggested a _p_ -value which was less than 0.05. This indicates that the PH assumption may not hold. For OS, the CS states that the log-cumulative hazard plot and Schoenfeld residuals plot suggest that applying the PH assumption would be reasonable and the global Schoenfeld test suggests that the PH assumption cannot be ruled out ( _p_ >0.05). However, the company instead elected to fit separate parametric survival models to the OS data for each treatment group (including the statistical adjustment of the OS data to account for confounding due to switching in the placebo group). 

The EAG notes that the plots and tests undertaken by the company relate specifically to the assessment of PH models (the exponential, Weibull and Gompertz distributions). AFT models do not make the PH assumption; the appropriateness of using jointly fitted AFT models instead requires consideration of Q- Q plots, which have not been presented in the CS.[3] In general, the EAG prefers to avoid models which apply a constant HR or acceleration factor (AF), as this usually reflects an unnecessary and restrictive modelling assumption. As such, the EAG agrees with the company’s decision to fit independent models to the data for each treatment group. However, the EAG also notes that whilst a constant lifetime treatment effect parameter (e.g., an HR or AF) is not used in the economic model, it is important to consider what is implicitly being assumed about relative treatment effects for ripretinib versus BSC. Figure 33 shows that the independent log-logistic OS models implicitly suggest a time-varying HR for OS which favours ripretinib over BSC at all timepoints (i.e., the HR is consistently <1.0). In TA881,[1] one of the EAG’s clinical advisors commented that they would not expect a residual treatment effect on OS in patients after they have discontinued ripretinib. The company’s model predicts that virtually all patients will have discontinued ripretinib by 5 years; hence, the time-varying HR implied by the 

123 



<!-- page 475 -->

company’s OS model selection appears to reflect an optimistic scenario. However, the implied treatment effect is subject to uncertainty as the model predicts that almost all BSC-treated patients will have died within 2 years. 

**Figure 33: Time-varying HR for OS implied by independent log-logistic models used in the company’s base case analysis, generated by the EAG using the company’s corrected post-clarification version of the model***

## _(b) Range of models assessed_ 

The company fitted six standard parametric survival models to the available data on PFS and OS (see Figure 22, Figure 23, Figure 26 and Figure 27) and eight standard parametric survival models to the data on TTD+PFS (see Figure 19). Other more flexible survival distributions, e.g., RCS models, were not considered. The EAG notes that based on visual assessment alone, some of the fitted standard parametric survival models appear to provide a good fit to the PFS data in both groups. However, the overall visual fit of the models to the ripretinib OS data is poor, and the Kaplan-Meier functions suggest that there are potential turning points in the underlying hazard function which are not fully captured by the standard models. The use of more flexible parametric models may have been better able to reflect the observed ripretinib OS data. 

## _(c) Statistical and visual goodness-of-fit_ 

The EAG notes the following observations regarding the fitted parametric survival models: 

- _TTD+PFS (see Figure 19 and Table 26):_ The log-logistic model has the lowest AIC and BIC values. The company selected the exponential distribution for inclusion in the economic model. All of the models appear to slightly underestimate TTD in the first 12 months. The log-logistic 

124 



<!-- page 476 -->

and log-normal distributions have longer tails compared with the other models, indicating longer time on treatment. 

- _PFS (see Figure 22, Figure 23 and Table 27):_ The log-logistic model has the lowest combined AIC and BIC values across both treatment groups. The log-normal model provides similar combined AIC and BIC values, and the generalised gamma model provides a similar fit in terms of combined AIC, but not BIC. The company selected the log-normal distribution for inclusion in the economic model. All six fitted models appear to give similar projections for the BSC group, with virtually all patients having progressed or died within 12 months. With respect to the ripretinib group, the log-logistic and log-normal models have longer tails and provide more optimistic extrapolations compared with the other candidate models. These two models both appear to overestimate PFS compared with the observed data after around 1.5 years. 

- _OS (see Figure 26, Figure 27, and Table 28)._ The log-logistic model has the lowest combined AIC and BIC values. The log-normal model provides a similar fit in terms of combined AIC and BIC, whilst the exponential model has a similar combined BIC. The company selected the log-logistic distribution for inclusion in the economic model. Visually, all models provide broadly similar projections of OS for the BSC group, with very few patients surviving beyond 2 years. Within the ripretinib group, the models fall into two clusters, with the log-logistic, lognormal, Gompertz and generalised gamma models providing markedly more optimistic OS extrapolations than the Weibull and exponential models. All of the models for the ripretinib group appear to overestimate OS relative to the observed data after around one year. 

## _(d) Consideration of nature of hazards_ 

Modelled hazard plots for TTD are presented in CS Appendix J;[29] neither the CS[3] nor its appendices present empirical or modelled hazard plots for OS or PFS. However, plots of the unsmoothed and smoothed empirical hazards and the modelled hazards for PFS and OS were provided as part of the company’s response to clarification questions in TA881;[1] these plots have been reproduced in Figure 20, Figure 21, Figure 24 and Figure 25. These plots can be useful for assessing whether the hazard functions for the selected models are consistent with the underlying hazards in the observed data. With respect to these hazard plots, the EAG makes the following observations: 

- _TTD+PFS (see Figure 18):_ The smoothed empirical hazard for TTD+PFS increases until around 35 weeks (8 months) and then decreases beyond this time point. The company’s selected exponential TTD model assumes a constant hazard and is therefore inconsistent with the observed hazard. The generalised F, generalised gamma, log-normal and log-logistic distributions may better reflect the pattern in the observed hazard. 

- _PFS (see Figure 20 and Figure 21):_ The smoothed empirical hazard for PFS in both treatment groups appears to increase, decrease and then increase again. The log-normal distribution, which was selected for inclusion in the company’s base case analysis, assumes that the hazard 

125 



<!-- page 477 -->

increases and then decreases. The company’s clarification response in TA881[1] noted that only 8 patients in the placebo group remain at risk after 8 weeks; hence, the plot should be interpreted with caution. Notwithstanding this uncertainty, the modelled hazard for the log-normal distribution appears to be inconsistent with the empirical hazard for PFS in both groups. However, none of the fitted parametric survival models reflect this underlying pattern because, at most, these models can capture one turning point. It is possible that more flexible parametric models could have better reflected the empirical hazards. 

- _OS (see Figure 24 and Figure 25):_ The smoothed empirical hazard for OS in both treatment groups increases and then decreases. This is generally consistent with the underlying assumptions of the log-logistic model which was selected for inclusion in the company’s base case analysis. However, the EAG notes that the empirical hazard in both groups decreases more rapidly than the predicted hazards from the company’s log-logistic models. 

## _(e) Consideration of long-term clinical plausibility_ 

In TA881,[1] the ERG criticised the company’s model selection process because it appeared to have been based only on goodness of fit and did not explicitly include consideration of the clinical plausibility of the alternative survival distributions. The CS for the current appraisal[3] provides some, albeit limited, discussion regarding considerations of the clinical plausibility, stating that the log-logistic model for ripretinib provides a 10-year OS probability which is consistent with the upper end of the clinical experts’ estimates of OS at the company’s July 2024 advisory board meeting. The minutes of the 2022 and 2024 advisory board meetings held by the company[27, 40] include further details of the clinical experts’ views regarding potentially plausible models for OS. The OS models preferred by the company and the clinical experts who attended these meetings are summarised in Table 44, together with details of the final models selected for inclusion in the CS. As indicated in the table, the views regarding the most appropriate OS model varied between the company and the clinical experts across the meetings, with the log-normal, generalised gamma and exponential models each being preferred by the experts and/or the company. The company’s base case analysis for the current appraisal includes the log-logistic OS distribution which does not appear to have been preferred by the clinical experts at either the 2022 or 2024 advisory board meetings. Of particular note, the log-logistic OS model suggests that xxxx of patients receiving ripretinib will remain alive at 10 years. The minutes of the 2024 advisory board meeting[40] state that: xxx xxxxxxxx xxxxxxxxx xxx xxxx xxxx xxxxxxxx xxx xxxxxxxx xx xxx xxxx xxx xx xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx xx xxx xxxx xxxx xxx xxxx xxxx xxxxxxxxxx xxxxxxxx xxx xxxxxxx xxxxxxxxxx xxxx xx xxxxxxx xx xxx xxxx xx xxxxxxxxx xxxxxxx xxxxxxxxxx xxx xxxxxxxxxx xxxx 

xxxx xxxxxx xx xxxxx xxxxxxxxxxx The EAG notes that the costs of future effective subsequent-line treatments are not included in the company’s economic model and therefore the effects of such treatments on OS should not be considered a relevant factor in model selection. The company’s clarification response[35] (question B10) provides some further detail regarding the views of the clinical 

126 



<!-- page 478 -->

advisors at the 2024 advisory board meeting. Amongst the seven clinical advisors who attended the meeting, one advisor considered xx survival at 10-years to be plausible (as described above), one commented that xxx OS at 10 years was an overestimate and following the meeting, four clinical advisors provided estimates of 10-year OS for ripretinib of xxx xxxx xxx xxxx xxx, all of which are lower than the predicted OS from the log-logistic model selected by the company. Clinicians’ estimates of expected OS at 10 years were not reported in the minutes of the 2022 advisory board meeting. Based on the advisory board meeting minutes and the company’s clarification response, the company has selected a base case OS distribution which produces substantially more optimistic predictions of OS than the expected OS estimates suggested by most of the clinical experts who attended the 2024 advisory board meeting. 

Despite the consensus view from clinicians that the log-logistic model overestimates ripretinib OS, the company’s clarification response[35] states that _“Previous NICE TAs for advanced GIST indicate that clinicians repeatedly underestimate long term survival associated with TKI treatment.”_ In support of this argument, the company’s response highlights that observational studies of first-line imatinib have indicated a PFS probability of nearly 10% at 10 years[53, 84] and an observational study of second-line sunitinib has shown an OS probability of around 10% at 10 years,[85] despite lower expectations of longterm OS being provided by clinical experts during the NICE TAs of these treatments.[46, 86] One of the EAG’s clinical advisors commented that clinical expectations of OS during these earlier appraisals would not have accounted for the effects of other subsequent-line therapies which were not available at the time. The company’s clarification response also highlights that the ORR, median PFS and median OS for ripretinib in INVICTUS[2] are higher than estimates reported from pivotal trials of sunitinib and regorafenib, despite ripretinib being used in more heavily pre-treated patients who are more likely to harbour secondary drug-resistance mutations. The clarification response goes on to state that on the basis of the real-world estimates of OS for treatments used at earlier treatment lines, the greater benefit of ripretinib versus other TKIs, and uncertainty surrounding clinicians’ predicted OS, the company decided that a 10-year OS probability of xxxx was _“too low”_ and the estimate of xxxx based on the log-logistic model is plausible.

The EAG asked their clinical advisors for their views regarding the plausibility of the company’s model predictions of TTD, PFS and OS. Their views are summarised below. 

## _TTD_ 

- One of the EAG’s clinical advisors considered either the exponential or generalised gamma distributions to be potentially appropriate. The EAG was unable to obtain the view of the second clinical advisor regarding the TTD function. 

## _PFS_ 

- One of the EAG’s clinical advisors considered the company’s predictions of PFS based on the lognormal distributions (the yellow lines in Figure 22 and Figure 23) to be plausible for both treatment groups. The other clinical advisor preferred the generalised gamma model for ripretinib PFS and the Weibull model for BSC PFS. Both clinical advisors agreed that it was plausible that all patients receiving BSC would progress within one year and that a small proportion of patients receiving ripretinib could derive a long-term benefit in PFS. 

## _OS_ 

- Both of the EAG’s clinical advisors commented that they believed that continuing ripretinib beyond disease progression would lead to additional OS benefits. Both advisors also stated that they would expect ripretinib 150mg BID dosing to lead to some improvement in OS relative to 150mg QD dosing, although the magnitude of such benefit is unclear from the available INVICTUS data.[2] 

- The EAG’s first clinical advisor stated that in the 4L+ setting, it is likely that nearly all BSC-treated patients will have died within 1.5 years. They commented that for the BSC group, the log-normal and log-logistic distributions appear to be overly optimistic, whereas the Weibull and Gompertz distributions appear to be overly pessimistic. They considered the generalised gamma model to be the most plausible distribution. With respect to the ripretinib group, the clinical advisor considered that a predicted 10-year OS probability of xxxx was _“too optimistic”_ , even in the situation in which ripretinib is used post-progression. The clinical advisor instead considered the Weibull and exponential models to be more clinically plausible; these models suggest 10-year OS probabilities of xxxx and xxxx, respectively. 

- The EAG’s second clinical advisor considered that the Weibull and generalised gamma models provide the most plausible predictions of BSC OS, and the exponential and Weibull models provide the most plausible predictions of ripretinib OS, including the effects of post-progression treatment. 

- Overall, the EAG considers that the company’s selected log-logistic model generates predictions of  long-term OS for ripretinib which appear to be highly optimistic, as indicated by the EAG’s clinical advisors and the majority of clinical advisors who attended the company’s 2024 advisory board meeting.[40]

## _(f) Sensitivity analysis_ 

The CS[3] presents the results of a comprehensive range of scenario analyses which consider the use of all alternative parametric survival models for TTD, PFS and OS (see Table 41, Scenarios S4-S18). These analyses indicate that the ICER for ripretinib versus BSC is particularly sensitive to the selected model for OS. 

## _EAG’s conclusions regarding company’s survival modelling_ 

Overall, the EAG considers the company’s survival modelling to be limited, in particular due to: (i) the poor visual fit of the fitted models to the ripretinib OS data; (ii) the implicit assumption of a lifetime treatment effect on OS and (iii) the selection of the log-logistic model for the ripretinib group which produces predictions of OS which were considered to be implausibly optimistic by the EAG’s clinical advisors and which are higher that estimates of expected 10-year OS provided by most of the clinical experts consulted at the company’s 2024 advisory board meeting.

## **(4) Uncertainty around the commissioning of ripretinib 150mg BID dosing in the NHS** 

The company’s base case model uses the unadjusted OS data for the ripretinib arm of INVICTUS[2] and applies only the costs of ripretinib 150mg QD. Taken together, this assumes that the same OS outcomes observed in the ripretinib arm of INVICTUS (including the effects of post-progression 150mg BID dosing in some patients) can be achieved by using less of the drug (i.e., using QD dosing in all patients). The clinical advisors who attended the company’s 2024 advisory board meeting[40] agreed that dose escalation to ripretinib BID in the trial will have had a _“non-negligible effect”_ on OS. The EAG’s clinical advisors stated that they would expect BID dosing to improve OS, but they considered the magnitude of the benefit to be uncertain. The EAG’s clinical advisors also commented that they would dose-escalate to ripretinib 150mg BID for patients who are able to tolerate this higher dose if they were permitted to do so. Therefore, the EAG has concerns that the company’s base case model introduces an inconsistency between the health outcomes observed in the trial and the costs required to generate those health outcomes. Whilst the company’s base case analysis excludes any explicit consideration of the costs or effects of BID dosing, the CS[3] reports the results of six scenario analyses which attempt to adjust OS to account for the effects of BID dosing (see Table 41, Scenarios S30-35), as well as an additional scenario analysis in which the costs of BID dosing are included for 50% of patients’ postprogression ripretinib treatment time (see Table 41, Scenario S36). Most of the IPDE adjustment analyses presented in the CS have a relatively small impact on the ICER; however, the ICER for Scenario S36 is around £4,000 higher than the company’s base case estimate. As noted in Section 4.2.4, additional two-stage estimation analyses were conducted as part of the company’s response to clarification question B9;[35] however, ICERs were not provided in the company’s response document. 

During the clarification process, the EAG asked the company to calculate the proportion of postprogression ripretinib exposure time in INVICTUS[2] that patients spent receiving the BID dose and to explain why Scenario S36 (which includes the costs of BID dosing) was not applied in the company’s base case (see clarification response,[35] questions B16 and B12, respectively). The company’s response states that 60.1% of post-progression ripretinib exposure time was spent receiving BID dosing; this estimate is 10.1% higher than the proportion applied in Scenario S36. The company’s clarification response also states that the costs of BID dosing are not included in the base case model because: (i) the ripretinib 150mg BID dose reflects an off-licence use of the drug and that NICE can only issue guidance within the marketing authorisation for a given health technology, and (ii) the company is unclear how BID dosing would be commissioned in the NHS and whether off-licence use would be a barrier to the use of the higher dose. The company’s clarification response states that it has sought clarity from NHS England about whether BID dosing would be commissioned in the NHS but has not yet received a response. It also states that if BID dosing was commissioned by individual funding requests, _“its use in clinical practice is likely to be far lower than that captured in the model scenario”_ (50%). The company argues that there is too much uncertainty for Scenario S36 to be considered in the base case analysis. 

131 



<!-- page 483 -->

The EAG believes that this uncertainty can only be resolved by obtaining further input from NHS England regarding how ripretinib would be commissioned in the NHS. However, regardless of whether BID dosing would be routinely commissioned in practice, the EAG believes that the company’s base case model either underestimates the incremental costs or overestimates the incremental benefits of ripretinib: 

- (i) If BID dosing is not routinely commissioned by NHS England, the EAG’s preferred analysis would be to apply the OS data from the ripretinib arm of INVICTUS[2] including adjustment to account for BID dosing using the 2-stage method and to apply the costs of QD dosing to 100% of the total post-progression ripretinib treatment time. This approach would reflect the OS outcomes and costs associated with QD dosing only. 

- (ii) If BID dosing is routinely commissioned by NHS England, the EAG’s preferred analysis would be to apply the OS data from the ripretinib arm of INVICTUS[2] without adjustment for BID dosing and to include the costs of BID dosing for 60.1% of the total post-progression ripretinib treatment time. This approach would reflect the OS outcomes and costs associated with the combination of BID and QD dosing seen in the trial. 

The EAG’s exploratory analyses include scenarios which attempt to align health outcomes and costs in both of these commissioning situations (see Section 5.2, EAG’s preferred analysis “EA4” and sensitivity analysis “ASA1”). 

## **(5) Uncertainty around the effect on ripretinib 150mg BID dosing on OS** 

As detailed in Section 4.2.4, the company explored six scenario analyses across three methodological approaches to evaluate the impact of IPDE on OS: 

- Censored BID analyses (two scenarios: “open-label BID vs QD OS analysis [non-progressors + IPDE]” and “open-label BID vs QD OS analysis [non-progressors + QD]”) 

- Time-varying Cox models (two scenarios: treatment covariate only model; all covariates model) 

- Two-stage adjustments (two scenarios: simple model; complex model). 

Because the censored BID analyses selected patients based on post-randomisation characteristics, they are subject to selection bias and therefore cannot provide a causal estimate of the effect of IPDE on OS. It should also be noted that the “open-label BID vs QD OS analysis (non-progressors + IPDE)” analyses attempted to isolate the effect of BID dosing, rather than estimating OS had patients remained on QD dosing after progression (i.e., this is different from the other five IPDE scenario analyses). 

The scenario analyses using time-varying Cox models, including one with only IPDE as a covariate and a more complex model incorporating all covariates, also had methodological limitations. Specifically, simply including time-varying covariates in a Cox regression model does not adequately address time- 

132 



<!-- page 484 -->

varying confounding, as causal methods such as marginal structural models were not applied. As a result, the models yielded counterintuitive estimates suggesting that BID dosing was harmful, which contrasts with clinical expectations. 

The EAG considers the two-stage adjustment approach to be the most appropriate, in line with TSDs 16 and 24.[48, 70] Due to the small sample size, the company did not conduct IPCW adjusted analysis as an alternative approach, which the EAG considers to be reasonable. 

Although the two-stage adjustment reported in the CS[3] incorrectly implemented the time ratio in the economic model, the EAG considers the company’s corrected analysis provided in response to clarification question B9[35] to be appropriate. Nonetheless, considerable uncertainty remains and this is disccussed below. 

Six distributions were used to derive time ratios, each applied with and without re-censoring. Six parametric survival models for surival extraporation were then fitted to each counterfactual OS dataset, resulting in a total of 144 scenarios. In all scenarios, the time ratios exceeded 1.0, suggesting a beneficial effect of IPDE on OS. In the original CS,[3] the company selected one simple model (using the log-normal distribution) and one complex model (using the generalised gamma distribution) to derive time ratios. In the updated analysis provided as part of the company’s clarification response to question B9,[35] the company considered the simple model using the log-normal distribution with re-censoring as the preferred method for deriving counterfactual OS. However, no clear specification was provided regarding the preferred parametric model for the extrapolation of the adjusted survival data. Despite the updated ICERs not being presented in the company’s response, the updated executable model includes additional functionality which allowed the EAG to explore the ICERs associated with each of these scenarios. 

In contrast to the company’s preference, the EAG favours the complex model using the generalised gamma distribution to derive the time ratio, as it had the lowest AIC among all models assessed. Since these distributions were not used for survival extrapolation, statistical fit alone was sufficient for selection. However, this still led to 12 survival extrapolations to consider: counterfactual OS (using complex generalised gamma distribution) with and without re-censoring, with six potentially plausible parametric models fitted to the adjusted data. Among these 12 scenarios, the EAG prefers the loglogistic model with re-censoring for extrapolation (Figure 34 shows OS from six parametric models fitted to the counterfactual OS with re-censoring using the generalised gamma model). This model’s hazard function closely aligned with the smoothed empirical hazard (see Figure 35), and the extrapolation projected a 10-year survival that was similar to, but slightly lower than, the EAG’s preferred extrapolated unadjusted OS model (Figure 36) . 

133 



<!-- page 485 -->

The EAG notes the importance of presenting the results with and without re-censoring. While recensoring helps to reduce bias by breaking the dependency between treatment switching, censoring, and patient prognosis, thereby supporting the validity of estimated treatment effects, it comes at the cost of the loss of some longer-term data, and the extent of data loss increases with the magnitude of the estimated treatment effect (i.e., time ratios), introducing uncertainty into extrapolations. 

Therefore, in line with TSD 24,[70] the EAG prefers to present results both with and without re-censoring to support a balanced interpretation, as each approach may introduce bias in different directions and 

134 



<!-- page 486 -->

thus uncertainty remains. The EAG notes that the re-censoring scenario with the complex generalised gamma model for time ratio estimation and the log-logistic model for survival extrapolation generates a predicted probability of 10-year OS consistent with estimates provided by the EAG’s clinical advisors and most of the clinical advisors consulted by the company. The without re-censoring scenario generates a higher predicted probability of 10-year OS for all six parametric survival models compared to the equivalent models including re-censoring. Since the counterfactual OS curve based on the complex generalised gamma model may differ when re-censoring is excluded, the log-logistic model may no longer be the most clinically plausible option for survival extrapolation in that context. Model results for the complex generalised gamma model with and without re-censoring are included in the EAG’s additional sensitivity analyses (see Section 5.2.4). 

In summary, considerable uncertainty remains around the IPDE-adjusted OS scenarios. Additonally, the counterfactual OS estimates were based on point estimates of the time ratio. Although bootstrapping could offer a more comprehensive way to account for residual uncertainty, the EAG acknowledges that there are currently no readily available open-source tools to support such an implementation. 

## **(6) Concerns relating to the modelled costs of drug wastage** 

In TA881,[1] the company’s original model did not include any drug wastage; the ERG’s preferred model assumed that one-quarter of a pack of ripretinib would be wasted per patient initiating treatment. The Appraisal Committee concluded that it was appropriate to include drug wastage in the model, and that the ERG's estimate of 0.25 packs wasted per person was plausible. The company’s approach to modelling drug wastage for ripretinib in the current appraisal[3] is based on an integer pack-based approach. This approach tracks whether a new pack of 90 ripretinib tablets is required in each 28-day model cycle (including RDI adjustment), with a new pack being required in 9 of every 10 cycles. This pack-based approach leads to an estimate of 47% of a pack of ripretinib being wasted over a patient’s lifetime. This estimate is higher than the estimate previously accepted by the Appraisal Committee in TA881. The EAG is unsure why the company adopted the pack-based approach. Following the clarification round, the company amended its model to instead assume that 25% of a pack is wasted per patient initiating treatment with ripretinib (see clarification response,[35] question B25).

## **5.2 EAG exploratory analysis** 

## _5.2.1  EAG exploratory analysis - methods_ 

The EAG undertook exploratory analyses (EAs) using the updated version of the model which was provided as part of the company’s clarification response.[35] All analyses were undertaken by one modeller and checked by a second modeller. All analyses presented in this section reflect the PAS price of ripretinib. Results are presented with and without QALY weighting (decision modifier = 1.7). 

## _5.2.2  EAG’s preferred analysis_ 

The EAG’s preferred analysis is comprised of 3 sets of amendments to the company’s updated model. EA1 includes the correction of errors; EA2 and EA3 are conducted independently but include the error corrections from EA1. EA4 combines all of the EAG’s amendments together in a single analysis.

The following corrections were applied to the company’s updated model:

This analysis combines EAG analyses 1-3. The EAG’s preferred analysis was conducted using both the deterministic and probabilistic versions of the model. ## _5.2.3 EAG’s additional sensitivity analyses_ 

The EAG undertook the following additional sensitivity analyses using the deterministic version of the EAG’s preferred model (EA4a): 

- _ASA1a-f_ : These analyses apply alternative parametric survival models fitted to the BIDunadjusted OS data and include the costs of BID dosing for 60.1% of the post-progression treatment duration (this percentage is based on the experience of INVICTUS,[2] see clarification response,[35] question B16). These analyses are intended to reflect the situation whereby postprogression ripretinib 150mg BID dosing is permitted. 

139 



<!-- page 491 -->

- _ASA2a-f:_ These analyses apply alternative parametric survival models fitted to the BIDadjusted ripretinib OS data using the complex 2-stage method (generalised gamma) with recensoring and exclude the costs of BID dosing. These analyses are based on the same BID adjustment analysis as the EAG’s preferred model and explore the impact of selecting alternative parametric survival models fitted to the BID-adjusted OS data. 

- _ASA3a-f:_ These analyses apply alternative parametric survival models fitted to the BIDadjusted ripretinib OS data using the complex 2-stage method (generalised gamma) without recensoring and exclude the costs of BID dosing. These analyses are equivalent to ASA2 but remove the impact of re-censoring. 

- _ASA4a-f:_ These analyses were conducted to explore the impact of selecting alternative parametric survival models for TTD for ripretinib. 

- _ASA5a-f:_ These analyses were conducted to explore the impact of selecting alternative parametric survival models for PFS for both ripretinib and BSC. 

- _ASA6a-f:_ These analyses were conducted to explore the impact of alternative methods for adjusting BSC OS to account for treatment switching in the placebo group of INVICTUS.[2] 

- _ASA7:_ This analysis was conducted to explore the impact of applying an alternative health state utility value to the PD state based on the GRID study[88] (utility value PD off treatment for ripretinib and PD for BSC = 0.647 rather than 0.624). 

- _ASA8:_ These analyses explore the impact of all BID-adjustment models used to adjust OS and all parametric survival models fitted to the BID-adjusted OS data. Results for each analysis are presented graphically using separate plots which highlight the impact of including re-censoring. 

## _5.2.4  EAG exploratory analysis - results_ 

## 5.2.4.1  Results of the EAG’s preferred analysis 

The results of the EAG’s preferred analysis of ripretinib versus BSC are presented in Table 49. All ICERs including QALY weighting reflect a decision modifier of 1.7. Unless otherwise stated, all analyses are intended to reflect a situation whereby ripretinib is used at a dose of 150mg QD (i.e., where BID dosing is not used). Correcting the remaining errors in the company’s updated model leads to an estimated ICER for ripretinib versus BSC of £28,703 per QALY gained (EA1); this is slightly lower than the company’s base case ICER. The inclusion of the exponential model fitted to the BIDunadjusted ripretinib OS data and the generalised gamma model fitted to the switching-adjusted BSC OS data increases the ICER to £36,321 per QALY gained (EA2). The inclusion of the log-logistic model fitted to the BID-adjusted ripretinib OS data, whilst retaining the company’s preferred log-logistic model for BSC OS, leads to an ICER of £55,113 per QALY gained (EA3). The EAG’s preferred analysis (EA4b) which includes all of the EAG’s preferred assumptions (including BID-adjusted ripretinib OS) results in a probabilistic ICER of £55,470 per QALY gained. The ICER based on the deterministic version of the model is lower at £52,822 per QALY gained (EA4a).

## 5.2.4.2  Results of the EAG’s additional sensitivity analysis 

The results of ASA1-7 are shown in Table 50. The results indicate the following: 

- The selection of alternative parametric survival models fitted to the BID-unadjusted ripretinib OS data together with the inclusion of the costs of BID dosing for 60.1% of post-progression time leads to ICERs ranging from £31,457 to £43,807 per QALY gained (ASA1). These analyses reflect a situation whereby post-progression BID dosing is permitted. Whilst there is uncertainty around the effect of ripretinib 150mg BID dosing on long-term OS, it is noteworthy that all of these analyses result in ICERs which are lower than the EAG’s preferred (BIDadjusted) analysis. As expected, the ICER for ripretinib versus BSC is higher when either the exponential or Weibull models are selected as these distributions produce less favourable OS projections compared with the other survival models (see Figure 26). 

- The selection of alternative parametric survival models fitted to the BID-adjusted ripretinib OS data (with re-censoring) leads to ICERs ranging from £48,656 (log-normal) to £73,815 (Gompertz) per QALY gained (ASA2). The EAG’s preferred analysis applies the log-logistic model for ripretinib and is towards the lower end of this ICER range. 

141 



<!-- page 493 -->

- The selection of alternative parametric survival models fitted to the BID-adjusted ripretinib OS data (without re-censoring) leads to ICERs ranging from £21,813 to £45,589 per QALY gained (ASA3). These ICERs are markedly lower than the equivalent analyses in ASA2 which include re-censoring. 

- The selection of alternative parametric models for TTD leads to ICERs ranging from £52,469 (Weibull) to £61,355 (log-logistic) per QALY gained (ASA4). The EAG’s preferred analysis using the exponential model is towards the lower end of this range. 

- The model is not particularly sensitive to the selected parametric survival model for PFS, with all ICERs ranging from £52,473 (Weibull) to £55,031 (log-logistic) per QALY gained (ASA5). 

- The ICER is sensitive to the method used to adjust for treatment switching in the BSC group (ASA6). The ICER is substantially higher when the OS data are not adjusted (£154,896 per QALY gained). 

- The use of an alternative utility value for the PD (off treatment/BSC) state based on GRID has a minimal effect on the ICER (ASA7).

## **5.3 Decision modifiers** 

## _5.3.1 QALY weighting for severity_ 

Based on the characteristics of patients in INVICTUS (mean age = 60.1 years; 43.41% female) and the company’s mean estimate of the QALYs for the BSC comparator group (xxxx QALYs), the York Shortfall Calculator[76] suggests an absolute shortfall of xxxxx QALYs and a proportional shortfall of 

xxxxxx. This indicates that a decision modifier of 1.7 is appropriate. The EAG’s preferred analysis applies a generalised gamma distribution for OS in the BSC group resulting in less health gain in the comparator group (xxxx QALYs), thereby also indicating that a decision modifier of 1.7 is appropriate. 

## _5.3.2  Uncaptured benefits_ 

The CS[3] does not make a case that there are any relevant benefits of ripretinib which have not been captured in the ICER. 

146 



<!-- page 498 -->

## _5.3.4  Health inequalities_ 

The CS[3] states that there are no special considerations relating to health inequity or inequality. 

## **5.4 Confidential comparator and subsequent treatment prices** 

All analyses presented in this report include the proposed PAS for ripretinib. None of the other drugs included in the base case model are subject to comparator PAS discounts or confidential NHS prices. 

## **5.5 Discussion** 

The CS[3] includes an SLR of existing economic studies of treatments for GIST and details the methods and results of a _de novo_ model-based health economic analysis of ripretinib versus BSC in patients who have had at least three prior therapies for advanced or metastatic GIST, including imatinib. 

The company’s SLR identified one existing economic model of 4L+ ripretinib versus BSC (Liao _et al._[59] _)_ . This published economic analysis is limited due the absence of any statistical adjustment to account for confounding of the OS data caused by treatment switching in the placebo group of INVICTUS and because it excludes post-progression ripretinib costs from the intervention group of the model. 

The company’s economic model assesses the cost-effectiveness of ripretinib (plus BSC) versus BSC alone for the 4L+ treatment of patients with advanced GIST. The model uses a partitioned survival approach which includes four health states: (i) progression-free; (ii) progressed disease (on treatment); (iii) progressed disease (off treatment/BSC), and (iv) dead. The analysis adopts an NHS and PSS perspective, including QALYs accrued by GIST patients; caregiver effects are not included. Clinical outcomes for both treatment groups are based on parametric survival models fitted to data on PFS and OS from INVICTUS,[2] including the adjustment of OS in the BSC group to account for treatment switching using the two-stage estimation method (with re-censoring). Patients in the intervention group are assumed to receive treatment with ripretinib prior to and following disease progression. Whilst patients in INVICTUS were allowed to dose-escalate to ripretinib 150mg BID after progression, the company’s base case model does not include any statistical adjustment to account for the effect of BID dosing on OS, whilst the drug acquisition costs assume ripretinib 150mg QD dosing for all patients. Health state utility values are based on an MMRM fitted to EQ-5D-5L data (mapped to the 3L version) from INVICTUS; resource use and cost parameters were taken from a clinical expert survey used in TA488,[45] standard costing sources[26, 67] and other literature.[68] 

The probabilistic version of the company’s updated model suggests that the ICER for ripretinib versus BSC is expected to be £28,576 per QALY gained. The deterministic ICER is similar at £28,730 per QALY gained. 

147 



<!-- page 499 -->

The EAG critically appraised the company’s health economic analysis and double-programmed the deterministic version of the company’s model. The EAG notes the following key concerns regarding the company’s economic model: 

- The company’s model is informed by data from the January 2021 DCO of INVICTUS.[2] A later DCO of May 2022 is available for OS and safety data. However, this later data-cut has not been used in the company’s model. The EAG considers that the reliance on the 2021 DCO unnecessarily increases uncertainty around the modelled estimates of OS for ripretinib. 

- The company’s base case analysis uses the log-logistic distribution for ripretinib OS, based on the BID-unadjusted OS data. This model suggests a predicted probability of OS at 10 years of xxxx. The clinical experts who attended the company’s 2024 advisory board meeting stated that a predicted probability of OS at 10 years for ripretinib of xxx was an overestimate and that xxxx was more realistic. One clinician considered that an estimate of xx was plausible because treatments are improving and new options are being developed; however, the EAG notes that this expert’s estimate does not reflect expected OS if ripretinib was included in the current treatment pathway for GIST.[40] The EAG’s clinical advisors preferred the selection of the exponential and Weibull models fitted to the BID-unadjusted ripretinib OS data. These models are less optimistic than the company’s selected log-logistic distribution as they suggest predicted probabilities of OS at 10 years of approximately xx. 

- Clinical experts consulted by the company and the EAG have indicated that ripretinib 150mg BID dosing is expected to lead to improved OS compared with 150mg QD dosing. However, BID dosing represents an off-label use of ripretinib. The EAG’s clinical advisors stated that they would want to use BID dosing where clinically appropriate if the commissioning route for ripretinib allowed this. There remains uncertainty around whether NHS England will commission BID dosing. The company’s base case analysis uses the BID-unadjusted OS data from INVICTUS[2] (which includes the effects of BID dosing in some patients) and includes the costs of ripretinib 150mg QD dosing only. Taken together, the company’s model assumes that the outcomes observed in INVICTUS (including the effects of post-progression ripretinib 150mg BID dosing in some patients) can be achieved by using the 150mg QD dose in all patients. The EAG believes that these assumptions result in an inconsistency between the outcomes observed in the trial and the resources required to generate those outcomes. As part of its clarification response,[35] the company conducted additional analyses to adjust the OS data to account for BID dosing using the two-stage estimation method and refitted survival models to the BID-adjusted ripretinib OS data. These analyses form part of the EAG’s preferred analyses, based on the assumption that only QD dosing would be commissioned. The EAG’s sensitivity analyses include the use of parametric survival models fitted to the BID-unadjusted OS data and the inclusion of the costs of BID dosing in 60.1% of the post-progression ripretinib 

148 



<!-- page 500 -->

treatment time, based on INVICTUS. The latter analyses may be more relevant for decisionmaking if BID dosing is commissioned. 

The EAG undertook exploratory analyses using the company’s updated model to address the issues described above. The EAG’s preferred model includes: (i) the correction of errors; (ii) the selection of an alternative model for OS in the BSC group (OS data adjusted for switching using the simple twostage estimation method [log-normal] with re-censoring; generalised gamma model fitted to the switching-adjusted data) and (iii) the selection of an alternative model for OS in the ripretinib group (OS data adjusted for ripretinib 150mg BID dosing using the complex two-stage estimation method [generalised gamma] with re-censoring; log-logistic model fitted to the BID-adjusted data). The probabilistic version of the EAG’s preferred model suggests that the ICER for ripretinib versus BSC is expected to be £55,470 per QALY gained. The deterministic version of the model suggests an ICER of £52,822 per QALY gained. These estimates are substantially higher than the company’s base case ICER. 

The EAG’s preferred analyses assume that BID dosing would not be commissioned in the NHS. However, this assumption may not be appropriate. The EAG’s additional sensitivity analyses indicate that fitting survival models to the BID-unadjusted OS data for ripretinib and including the costs of BID dosing for 60.1% of the ripretinib post-progression treatment time leads to lower ICERs which range from £31,457 to £43,807 per QALY gained. These analyses may be more relevant for decision-making if BID dosing is permitted. The EAG’s other sensitivity analyses indicate that the ICER is sensitive to the choice of parametric survival model for OS, whether the adjustment model for OS to account for the effects of BID dosing includes re-censoring, whether the BSC OS data are adjusted for treatment switching, and the choice of parametric survival model selected for TTD.

## **External Assessment Group addendum – comments on the company’s updated base case analysis** 

**Produced by** Sheffield Centre for Health and Related Research (SCHARR), The University of Sheffield **Authors** Paul Tappenden, Professor of Health Economic Modelling, SCHARR, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK Jen-Yu Amy Chang, Research Fellow, SCHARR, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK Aline Navega Biz, Research Fellow, SCHARR, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK **Correspondence Author** Paul Tappenden, Professor of Health Economic Modelling, SCHARR, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK **Date completed** 25[th] September 2025 

1 



<!-- page 508 -->

## **1. Introduction** 

In September 2025, the company submitted an addendum which contains the results of its updated base case analysis[1] together with an updated version of the executable model. The company’s updated base case analysis is based on the deterministic version of EAG’s preferred model (see EAG report,[2] Table 49, Scenario EA4a), but features two differences: 

- (1) The EAG’s preferred analysis (EA4) applied a two-stage adjustment to account for intra-patient dose escalation (IPDE) in the ripretinib arm of the INVICTUS trial[3] using a complex generalised gamma model _with re-censoring_ and the _log-logistic_ model for extrapolation. In contrast, the company has retained the two-stage adjustment using the complex generalised gamma model but has selected the _without re-censoring_ scenario and adopted the _log-normal_ model for extrapolation of the adjusted data. 

- (2) The company has increased the Patient Access Scheme (PAS) discount for ripretinib from xxx to xxx. 

The company’s addendum document is limited to a table which contains the results of model analyses. It does not contain any explanatory text regarding why the company prefers to exclude re-censoring from the ripretinib IPDE adjustment model or why the parametric survival model used for extrapolation of the adjusted data has been changed. The EAG also notes that the version of the model submitted by the company does not include the correction of errors implemented by the EAG (see EAG report,[2] Section 5.2.2, EA1). 

## **2. EAG comments on the company’s updated analysis** 

As discussed in the EAG report,[2] re-censoring is applied to guard against informative censoring in the counterfactual dataset, although this comes at the cost of losing longer-term survival information which is needed for extrapolation.[4] Decision Support Unit (DSU) Technical Support Document (TSD) 24 recommends presenting results with and without re-censoring for two-stage adjustment analyses.[5] As such, the EAG acknowledges that it is appropriate to present the two-stage-IPDE-adjusted results for ripretinib without re-censoring. However, the EAG believes that the scenario including re-censoring should be preferred for the reasons described below. 

Firstly, the company’s updated base case model (including two-stage adjustment with the complex generalised gamma without re-censoring; log-normal extrapolation) results in a 10-year probability of overall survival (OS) for ripretinib-treated patients of xxxxx (see Figure 1); this is more optimistic than the consensus estimate of xxxx provided by clinical experts at the company’s 2024 advisory board meeting.[6] The EAG’s preferred analysis (including two-stage adjustment with the complex generalised gamma with re-censoring; log-logistic extrapolation) results in a predicted 10-year OS probability of xxxxx which is similar to, albeit slightly lower than, the consensus estimate obtained from the clinicians 

2 



<!-- page 509 -->

consulted by the company. The EAG also notes that based on the unadjusted ripretinib OS data, the EAG’s clinical advisors’ preferred OS models for extrapolation (Weibull and exponential) suggested 10-year OS probabilities of xxxx and xxxx, respectively. 

Secondly, the EAG notes that the smoothed empirical hazard of the counterfactual Kaplan-Meier function for OS in the without re-censoring scenario (see Figure 2, provided as part of the company’s clarification response[7] ) suggests an initial increase up to around 40 weeks, followed by another rise at approximately 93 weeks. The late upward turning point may be an artefact of data sparsity at later follow-up time points, right-censoring, and/or bandwidth choice for smoothing, and is not necessarily a true rise in risk. Nonetheless, a true late hazard increase may be clinically possible (e.g., due to treatment effect waning). Without more mature OS data, the EAG cannot conclude either way. More mature follow-up would provide greater confidence in the extrapolation. The EAG also notes that none of the survival extrapolation models that capture the initial hazard increase (the log-logistic, log-normal, and the generalised gamma distributions) provide a satisfactory fit to the without re-censoring two-stage adjusted data (i.e., the timing of the first peak of hazard increase). Among the standard extrapolation models assessed in this scenario, the log-logistic model appears to be provide a better fit than the lognormal model, as its hazard peak aligns more closely with the empirical hazard (Figure 2), and survival is closer to the counterfactual Kaplan-Meier curve for the majority of the follow-up period (Figure 3), though overall fit remains sub-optimal. The predicted 10-year OS under the log-logistic model in the without re-censoring scenario (xxxxx) still exceeds the aforementioned expert consensus estimate (xxxx). As previously shown in Figure 34 and Figure 35 of the EAG report,[2] the with re-censoring scenario—using the complex generalised gamma model for IPDE adjustment and the log-logistic model for extrapolation—generates a predicted probability of 10-year OS of xxxxx, which was consistent with estimates provided by the EAG’s clinical advisors and most of the clinical advisors consulted by the company. 

The EAG considers that the point estimate of the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) may fall between £44,964 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained (the EAG’s preferred scenario: twostage adjustment of the IPDE using a complex generalised gamma model with re-censoring and loglogistic extrapolation) and £29,717 per QALY gained (the equivalent scenario but excluding recensoring). However, the EAG regards its preferred model specification as being the most appropriate, given the sub-optimal fit of the extrapolation models in the without re-censoring scenario and the more optimistic 10-year OS predictions compared with clinical expert opinion obtained by the company and the EAG.

## **3. Updated model results** 

The results of the company’s updated base case analysis and the EAG’s exploratory analysis, including the EAG’s preferred analysis (EA4a), are shown in Table 1. All of these analyses include a decision modifier of 1.7. The deterministic version of the company’s updated base case model suggests that the ICER for ripretinib versus best supportive care (BSC) is £29,350 per QALY gained. This is markedly lower that the EAG’s preferred ICER of £44,964 per QALY gained. The probabilistic versions of the company’s updated base case model and the EAG’s preferred model result in higher ICERs of £30,232 and £47,162 per QALY gained, respectively (see Table 2). 

The EAG also conducted an additional analysis, starting from the company’s updated base case scenario, whereby the parametric survival model used for extrapolation of the adjusted ripretinib OS data was changed to the log-logistic distribution. This had only a minor impact on the ICER (company’s base case ICER = £29,350; log-logistic model ICER = £29,717 per QALY gained). 

The company’s addendum also includes the results of several other scenario analyses. However, these are based on the EAG’s preferred analysis (EA4a) including the updated ripretinib PAS rather than the company’s updated base case analysis. For completeness, these scenarios have been reproduced in Table 3.

14

are appropriately accounted for through the chosen covariates – which the EAG’s clinical advisors considered reasonable – and characterisation of longer-term treatment effects. In line with TSD24 guidance,47 which recommends presenting two-stage adjustment results both with and without re-censoring, longer-term data would be especially valuable to mitigate information loss in the re-censoring scenarios (i.e., EAG’s preferred scenarios for addressing treatment switching in the control arm and IPDE in the ripretinib arm). Although outcome measurement could be affected by the open-label nature of the follow-up data, the EAG notes that OS is a hard endpoint and therefore less susceptible to subjective influences. 

15 



<!-- page 532 -->

While the company has stated concerns regarding the open-label nature of the data at the fact check stage of the appraisal, the EAG’s considers that the benefits of examining longer-term follow-up outweigh the risks. Excluding these data would constrain the understanding of longerterm survival outcomes and may increase decision uncertainty. Given the absence of alternative evidence on longer-term ripretinib use, the EAG considered that including the long-term data provides a more balanced basis for decision-making.”
